docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
coola is a lightweight Python library to compare, hash and summarize complex and nested data structures. It provides simple, extensible functions that work on objects containing PyTorch tensors, NumPy arrays, pandas/polars DataFrames, and other scientific computing objects:

  • Compare: objects_are_equal, objects_are_allclose, assert_objects_equal and compare check equality (exact or with a tolerance) and tell where two objects differ.
  • Hash: hash_object computes a deterministic hash of a nested object.
  • Summarize: summarize creates a short, readable description of a large structure for logs.

Quick Links:

  • User Guide
  • Installation
  • Features
  • Contributing

docs.title: Why coola?
docs.text:
Python's native equality operator (==) doesn't work well with complex nested structures containing tensors, arrays, or DataFrames. You'll often encounter errors or unexpected behavior. coola solves this with intuitive comparison functions:

Check exact equality:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> import torch
>>> from coola.equality import objects_are_equal
>>> data1 = {"torch": torch.ones(2, 3), "numpy": np.zeros((2, 3))}
>>> data2 = {"torch": torch.ones(2, 3), "numpy": np.zeros((2, 3))}
>>> objects_are_equal(data1, data2)
True

Compare with numerical tolerance:

>>> from coola.equality import objects_are_allclose
>>> data1 = {"value": 1.0}
>>> data2 = {"value": 1.0 + 1e-9}
>>> objects_are_allclose(data1, data2)
True

Assert equality in your tests, with the path of the difference:

>>> from coola.equality import assert_objects_equal
>>> actual = {"users": [{"id": 1, "score": 95}, {"id": 2, "score": 87}]}
>>> expected = {"users": [{"id": 1, "score": 95}, {"id": 2, "score": 88}]}
>>> assert_objects_equal(actual, expected)
Traceback (most recent call last):
    ...
AssertionError: objects are not equal at actual['users'][1]['score']
numbers are different:
  actual   : 87
  expected : 88

assert_objects_allclose does the same with a tolerance.

Get the difference as data:

>>> from coola.equality import compare
>>> result = compare(actual, expected)
>>> result.equal
False
>>> result.path
('users', 1, 'score')
>>> print(result.reason)
numbers are different:
  actual   : 87
  expected : 88

Hash and summarize:

>>> from coola.hashing import hash_object
>>> from coola.summary import summarize
>>> len(hash_object(actual))
64
>>> print(summarize(actual, max_depth=2))
<class 'dict'> (length=1)
  (users): <class 'list'> (length=2)
      (0): {'id': 1, 'score': 95}
      (1): {'id': 2, 'score': 87}

compare(actual, expected) explains the first difference (its path and its reason), and assert_objects_equal(actual, expected) raises an AssertionError with the same message.

See the user guide for detailed examples.

docs.title: Features
docs.text: coola provides a comprehensive set of utilities for working with complex data structures:

docs.title: 🔍 Equality Comparison
docs.text:
Compare complex nested objects with support for multiple data types:

  • Exact equality: objects_are_equal() for strict comparison
  • Approximate equality: objects_are_allclose() for numerical tolerance
  • Assertions for tests: assert_objects_equal() and assert_objects_allclose() raise an AssertionError with the path of the difference
  • Structured results: compare() returns a ComparisonResult with the path and the reason
  • Extensible: Add custom equality testers for your own types

Learn more →

Supported types: JAX • NumPy • pandas • polars • PyArrow • PyTorch • xarray • Python built-ins (dict, list, tuple, set, etc.)

Learn more about supported types →

docs.title: 📊 Data Summarization
docs.text:
Generate human-readable summaries of nested data structures for debugging and logging:

  • Configurable depth control
  • Type-specific formatting
  • Truncation for large collections

Learn more →

docs.title: 🔄 Data Conversion
docs.text:
Transform data between different nested structures:

  • Convert between list-of-dicts and dict-of-lists formats
  • Useful for working with tabular data and different data representations

Learn more →

docs.title: 🗂️ Mapping Utilities
docs.text:
Work with nested dictionaries efficiently:

  • Flatten nested dictionaries into flat key-value pairs
  • Extract specific values from complex nested structures
  • Filter dictionary keys based on patterns or criteria, rename keys and merge mappings

Learn more →

docs.title: 🔁 Iteration
docs.text:
Traverse nested data structures systematically:

  • Depth-first search (DFS) traversal for nested containers
  • Breadth-first search (BFS) traversal for level-by-level processing
  • Filter and extract specific types from heterogeneous collections

Learn more →

docs.title: 📈 Reduction
docs.text:
Compute statistics on sequences with flexible backends:

  • Calculate min, max, mean, median, quantile, std on numeric sequences
  • Support for multiple backends: native Python, NumPy, PyTorch
  • Consistent API regardless of backend choice

Learn more →

docs.title: #️⃣ Hashing
docs.text:
Compute stable hashes of nested objects:

  • Hash dicts, lists, sets, dataclasses, pydantic models, arrays and data frames
  • Independent of the insertion order of mappings and sets
  • Extensible with custom hashers

Learn more →

docs.title: 🆔 Identifiers
docs.text:
Generate unique identifiers: ULID, UUID (v5, v7), Snowflake, ObjectId, and checksummed and content-based identifiers.

Learn more →

docs.title: 💾 Data Loading and Saving
docs.text:
Load and save JSON, pickle, text and PyTorch files with atomic writes, an overwrite policy and optional durability (fsync).

Learn more →

docs.title: 🎲 Random Number Generators
docs.text:
Seed, save and restore the random number generators of random, NumPy and PyTorch in one call.

Learn more →

docs.title: 🔧 Recursive Transformation and Validation
docs.text:
• Apply a function to every leaf of a nested structure
  • Validate arguments with clear error messages

Learn more about transformation → · Learn more about validation →

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text:
Contributions are welcome! We appreciate bug fixes, feature additions, documentation improvements, and more. Please check the contributing guidelines for details on:

  • Setting up the development environment
  • Code style and testing requirements
  • Submitting pull requests

Whether you're fixing a bug or proposing a new feature, please open an issue first to discuss your changes.

docs.title: API Stability
docs.text: Important: As coola is under active development, its API is not yet stable and may change between releases. We recommend pinning a specific version in your project’s dependencies to ensure consistent behavior.

docs.title: Get Started
docs.text: We highly recommend installing coola in a virtual environment to avoid dependency conflicts.

docs.title: Using uv (recommended)
docs.text:
uv is a fast Python package installer and resolver:

uv pip install coola

Install with several optional dependencies:

uv pip install coola[all,jax,numpy,packaging,pandas,polars,pyarrow,pydantic,torch,xarray,testing,colorlog,rich]  # "all" installs everything

Install with specific optional dependencies:

uv pip install coola[numpy,torch]  # with NumPy and PyTorch

docs.title: First steps
docs.text:
After the installation, compare, hash and summarize a nested object:

>>> from coola.equality import assert_objects_equal, compare, objects_are_equal
>>> from coola.hashing import hash_object
>>> from coola.summary import summarize
>>> actual = {"scores": [95, 87]}
>>> expected = {"scores": [95, 88]}
>>> objects_are_equal(actual, expected)
False
>>> compare(actual, expected).path
('scores', 1)
>>> assert_objects_equal(actual, expected)  # in a test: the AssertionError shows the path
Traceback (most recent call last):
    ...
AssertionError: objects are not equal at actual['scores'][1]
numbers are different:
  actual   : 87
  expected : 88
>>> len(hash_object(actual))
64
>>> print(summarize(actual))
<class 'dict'> (length=1)
  (scores): [95, 87]

docs.title: Using pip
docs.text:
Alternatively, you can use pip:

pip install coola

Install with several optional dependencies:

pip install coola[all,jax,numpy,packaging,pandas,polars,pyarrow,pydantic,torch,xarray,testing,colorlog,rich]  # "all" installs everything

Install with specific optional dependencies:

pip install coola[numpy,torch]  # with NumPy and PyTorch

docs.title: Installing from source
docs.text:
To install coola from source, you can follow the steps below.

First, clone the git repository:

git clone git@github.com:durandtibo/coola.git
cd coola

Note: coola requires Python 3.11 or higher.

It is recommended to create a virtual environment (this step is optional). To create a virtual environment, you can use the following command:

make setup-venv

This command automatically creates a virtual environment using uv. When the virtual environment is created, you can activate it with the following command:

source .venv/bin/activate

Then, you should install the required packages to use coola with the following command:

inv env.install --groups dev,docs

This command will install all the required packages. You can also use this command to update the required packages. This command will check if there is a more recent package available and will install it. Finally, you can test the installation with the following command:

inv test.unit --cov

docs.title: How to Add Support for a New Library
docs.text:
This page is the checklist to add support for a new optional library (a "backend", such as NumPy, PyTorch or pandas) to coola. A backend is supported by several packages, each with its own registry, and it is easy to add the equality support and forget the others.

To teach coola about one of your own classes, without changing coola, see How to Add Support for a New Type instead.

In this page, <pkg> is the name of the library, e.g. pandas.

docs.title: 1. Declare the optional dependency
docs.text:
1. Add the extra to [project.optional-dependencies] of pyproject.toml, e.g. <pkg> = ["<pkg>>=1.0"]. The all extra, the CI jobs that test each dependency with its supported versions, and dev/config/package_versions.json (updated by a bot) follow from it.
  2. Create src/coola/utils/imports/<pkg>.py, copied from pandas.py. It defines check_<pkg>, is_<pkg>_available, <pkg>_available and raise_<pkg>_missing_error. Decorate is_<pkg>_available with availability_cache (not with functools.cache), so that clear_availability_caches knows about it. Export the four names in src/coola/utils/imports/__init__.py.
  3. Create src/coola/utils/fallback/<pkg>.py, copied from pandas.py: a fake module with fake classes that raise MissingPackageError, used when the library is not installed. It must have every attribute of the library that is used in an annotation or a class X(Base[pkg.Type]) statement, because these are evaluated when the module is imported.
  4. Add the marks for the tests to src/coola/testing/fixtures.py, and the two names to __all__:
<pkg>_available, <pkg>_not_available = requires(is_<pkg>_available(), "<pkg>")

docs.title: 2. Equality
docs.text:
1. Create src/coola/equality/tester/<pkg>.py. For a library of tables (data frames, series, columnar arrays), write an adapter (follow pandas.py, polars.py or pyarrow.py): a class with a kind_name (the plural word used in the reasons), a same_structure(other, ctx) method and a columns() method that yields Columns, and a function that builds it from an object. A column is numeric or duration (compared by the numeric kernel, with the tolerance and equal_nan; the null values are given as a mask) or exact (compared by the equals of the library). Register TableEqualityTester(adapter) for the types of the library.
  2. For an array library, write a tester that derives from BaseEqualityTester (follow numpy.py): it checks the data type and the shape, then compares the values with the shared kernel, and returns a verdict (ctx.fail(reason, *path) returns False) or the child pairs. For an optional library, __init__ calls check_<pkg>(). Export the tester in equality/tester/__init__.py as a lazy name.
  3. Register the tester: add a get_default_testers function to equality/tester/<pkg>.py that returns the {type: tester} mapping of the library (and returns {} if is_<pkg>_available() is False), and add the library to _LAZY_TESTERS in equality/tester/interface.py.
  4. Document the behavior of the library in the table "Behavior by type".

docs.title: 3. The other packages
docs.text:
Decide for each package whether the library needs an entry, and write the decision down in the pull request.

Package What to do Default coola.summary Add a BaseMetadataSummarizer in summary/<pkg>.py that describes the metadata (shape, dtype, columns) in _describe, export it as a lazy name, and register it with a get_default_summarizers function and the _LAZY_SUMMARIZERS table of summary/interface.py. Without it, the summary is the str of the object, which can be very long. coola.hashing Nothing by default: there is no canonical byte form for arrays and data frames. Document how to register a hasher with register_hashers. The type is not hashable. coola.recursive Nothing: the objects of the library are leaves, passed to the function. Leaf. coola.iterator Nothing: the objects are leaves, and are not expanded. Leaf. coola.random If the library has a global random number generator, add a BaseRandomManager in random/<pkg>.py, and register it in random/interface.py (the manager is imported with import_object, because the RNG of the library must be seeded even if the library is imported later). Not managed. coola.reducer If the library can compute statistics, subclass BaseReducer in reducer/<pkg>.py (the six computations, _sort, optionally _prepare). Its results must agree with NativeReducer (see tests/unit/reducer/test_consistency.py). Not supported.

docs.title: Lazy imports
docs.text:
Importing coola must not import the optional libraries, because it can take seconds (for example torch). The modules that need a library import it at the top, as usual, with the fallback module when it is not installed. What is lazy is who imports these modules:

  • Package exports. The __init__.py of a package lists the names that are defined in a module of an optional library in a _LAZY_EXPORTS table, and defines __getattr__ and __dir__ with lazy_exports. The names stay in __all__, and from coola.equality.tester import TorchTensorEqualityTester works as before, but the module is imported when the name is used. Import the names for the type checkers in the if TYPE_CHECKING: block.
  • Registries. The default registries do not import the modules of the optional libraries. registry.register_lazy(packages, "package.module:get_default_...") registers a group of entries that is built the first time the registry looks for a type whose class (or one of its base classes) comes from one of the packages, or needs the whole registry (len, iteration, items). An object cannot have a type of a library that was not imported, so a library is only imported by the registry if the program already imported it. The entries that are already registered are not replaced.
  • Code that handles the objects of a library only if they exist. Use sys.modules.get("numpy") instead of importing the library (see coola.utils.conversion).

docs.title: 4. Tests and documentation
docs.text:
1. Write the unit tests next to the existing ones, with the mark of step 1 (@<pkg>_available), and an import guard for the library as in the other test files. Test with and without the library: the CI runs the tests with the required dependencies only.
  2. Every new public class and function must be in the __all__ of its module and of its package: tests/unit/test_public_api.py checks it.
  3. Check that importing coola and its subpackages does not import the library: add the library to OPTIONAL_LIBRARIES of tests/integration/test_lazy_imports.py.
  4. Update the user guide pages of the packages you touched, and the "Supported Types" list of docs/docs/uguide/equality.md.

docs.title: Summary of the files
docs.text: Step Files Dependency pyproject.toml, utils/imports/<pkg>.py, utils/imports/__init__.py, utils/fallback/<pkg>.py, testing/fixtures.py Equality equality/_helpers/<pkg>.py (the kernel, if the library has arrays), equality/tester/<pkg>.py, equality/tester/__init__.py, equality/tester/interface.py Summary summary/<pkg>.py, summary/__init__.py, summary/interface.py Others (optional) random/<pkg>.py, random/interface.py, reducer/<pkg>.py Tests and docs tests/unit/..., docs/docs/uguide/*.md

docs.title: Architecture and Design
docs.text: This document describes the internal architecture and design principles of coola.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
coola is designed around a flexible, extensible comparison framework that can handle various data types through a plugin-like architecture. The core design follows these principles:

  1. Separation of concerns: Comparison logic is separated from data type handling
  2. Extensibility: New data types can be added without modifying core code
  3. Type safety: Strong type checking to prevent subtle bugs
  4. Composability: Complex comparisons are built from simpler ones

docs.title: 1. Comparison Functions
docs.text:
The main entry points for users:

  • objects_are_equal: Checks exact equality
  • objects_are_allclose: Checks equality within tolerance

These functions provide a simple interface while delegating to the internal comparison system.

docs.title: 2. Testers
docs.text: A tester implements the comparison logic for one type (or family of types). Testers live in coola.equality.tester.

docs.title: BaseEqualityTester
docs.text:
Abstract base class defining the tester interface:

class BaseEqualityTester(ABC, Generic[T]):
    @abstractmethod
    def objects_are_equal(self, actual: T, expected: T, ctx: Engine) -> bool | Iterator[tuple]:
        """A verdict, or the child pairs (actual, expected, path part) that must all be equal."""

docs.title: BaseEqualityTester and the engine
docs.text:
The Python testers use the engine (coola.equality.engine.Engine). The engine owns the invariants of a comparison: identity, strict type, depth, cycles and the location of the first difference. A tester that derives from BaseEqualityTester never recurses: its objects_are_equal(actual, expected, ctx) receives two objects of the same type and the engine, and returns a verdict (True, or ctx.fail(reason, *path), which returns False) or the child pairs (actual, expected, path part) that must all be equal, produced lazily. The engine keeps the child iterators on an explicit stack, so there is no RecursionError whatever the nesting, and a comparison stops at the first difference.

class PointTester(BaseEqualityTester[Point]):
    def objects_are_equal(self, actual, expected, ctx):
        return ((actual.coords, expected.coords, AttributeName("coords")),)

The testers of NumPy, PyTorch, JAX and xarray use the engine too: an array tester checks the data type and the shape (and the device for a tensor), then compares the elements with the shared kernel; the location of a difference is the index of the first element that differs, looked up only when the difference is explained. #### Built-in Testers

  • DefaultEqualityTester: Fallback for any type (== on two objects of the same type)
  • MappingEqualityTester, OrderedMappingEqualityTester (also checks the key order, used for OrderedDict), SequenceEqualityTester and SetEqualityTester: Return the children of mappings, sequences and sets
  • DataclassEqualityTester, ObjectAttributesEqualityTester and PydanticModelEqualityTester: Return the fields or the attributes as children
  • ScalarEqualityTester, DifferenceCloseEqualityTester, EqualEqualityTester, EqualNanEqualityTester, TolerantEqualEqualityTester: Numbers and objects with an equal method
  • Array testers for NumPy, PyTorch, xarray and JAX (for example NumpyArrayEqualityTester, TorchTensorEqualityTester)
  • TableEqualityTester: pandas, polars and PyArrow tables, with one adapter per library

docs.title: EqualityTesterRegistry
docs.text:
The registry maps types to testers. It is a TypeRegistry (coola.registry):

  • find_equality_tester(data_type) returns the tester for the most specific registered type, walking the Method Resolution Order (MRO); object is registered with DefaultEqualityTester, so a tester is always found
  • objects_are_equal(actual, expected, config) finds the tester for type(actual) and delegates (a tester that uses the engine runs a nested Engine) to it
  • Lookup results are cached per type, and the cache is cleared whenever the registry changes

get_default_registry() returns the global registry. Testers for optional libraries are only registered when the library is installed. register_equality_testers(mapping, *, exist_ok=False) adds testers to it. A test that registers a tester should not leak it: use coola.utils.singleton.temporary_default_registries() (see the testing guide), or work on get_default_registry().copy().

docs.title: EqualityConfig
docs.text:
A frozen dataclass that carries the comparison settings. It can be shared between comparisons and threads; the state of one comparison (the cache of testers, the first failure) lives in the Engine:

@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class EqualityConfig:
    registry: EqualityTesterRegistry  # defaults to the default registry
    tolerance: Tolerance = Tolerance()  # rtol, atol
    equal_nan: bool = False
    max_depth: int = 100

The tester reads the settings from the engine (ctx.atol, ctx.rtol, ctx.equal_nan).

docs.title: 5. Comparison Results
docs.text: compare returns a ComparisonResult, and assert_objects_equal / assert_objects_allclose raise an AssertionError with a description of the difference.

docs.title: Data Flow
docs.text:
Here's how a comparison flows through the system:

User calls objects_are_equal(obj1, obj2)
    ↓
Creates EqualityConfig with settings (and the registry)
    ↓
Runs Engine(config).run(obj1, obj2)
    ↓
For each pair: identity, strict type, tester lookup (cached per call, MRO lookup)
    ↓
Calls tester.objects_are_equal(obj1, obj2, engine): a verdict, or the child pairs
(pushed on the explicit stack, depth first)
    ↓
Returns boolean result

docs.title: 1. Strategy Pattern
docs.text: Testers implement different comparison strategies for different types, allowing the algorithm to vary independently from the clients that use it.

docs.title: 2. Template Method
docs.text:
Many testers follow a template:

  1. Check types match
  2. Check metadata (shape, dtype, etc.)
  3. Check values
  4. Optionally show differences

docs.title: 3. Registry Pattern
docs.text: The tester registry allows runtime type-to-tester mapping, enabling extensibility.

docs.title: 4. Visitor Pattern
docs.text: The recursive nature of comparison through nested structures follows a visitor-like pattern.

docs.title: Adding Support for New Types
docs.text:
To add support for a custom type:

  1. Implement a Tester:
from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
from coola.equality.tester import BaseEqualityTester


class MyTypeEqualityTester(BaseEqualityTester[MyType]):
    def equal(self, other: object) -> bool:
        return type(other) is type(self)

    def objects_are_equal(self, actual: MyType, expected: object, config: EqualityConfig) -> bool:
        # Type check
        if type(actual) is not type(expected):
            return False

        # Custom comparison logic
        return actual.compare_to(expected)
  1. Register the Tester:
from coola.equality.tester import register_equality_testers

register_equality_testers({MyType: MyTypeEqualityTester()})

To avoid modifying the global registry, create a EqualityTesterRegistry, register the tester on it and pass it with registry=.

  1. Use it:
from coola.equality import objects_are_equal

objects_are_equal(obj1, obj2)

See the extending guide for more details.

docs.title: Checklist: writing a tester
docs.text:
• Return a verdict (ctx.fail(reason) for a difference) or the child pairs (actual, expected, path part); never recurse: the engine checks the identity, the type, the depth and the cycles
  • Use AttributeName for an attribute and ctx.fail(reason, *path) for the location inside a leaf (the index in an array)
  • Build the reason lazily (a callable), so objects_are_equal formats nothing
  • Honour ctx.equal_nan and the tolerance (ctx.rtol, ctx.atol: |a - e| <= atol + rtol * max(|a|, |e|)), or document that your tester ignores them

docs.title: Strict Type Checking
docs.text:
coola enforces strict type checking:

  • 1 (int) ≠ 1.0 (float) ≠ True (bool)
  • list ≠ tuple
  • dict ≠ OrderedDict
  • two OrderedDicts with the same items in a different order are different (the order of the keys of a dict is ignored)

This prevents subtle bugs from type coercion.

docs.title: Type Hierarchy Support
docs.text:
Through MRO-based lookup, coola supports inheritance:

  • A tester for Sequence applies to list, tuple, etc.
  • More specific testers override general ones
  • Custom subclasses inherit parent testers

docs.title: Early Exit
docs.text:
Testers check fast properties first:

  1. Type check (very fast)
  2. Metadata checks (fast: shape, dtype, device)
  3. Value comparison (potentially slow)

docs.title: Lazy Evaluation
docs.text: Comparisons short-circuit on first difference when possible.

docs.title: Caching
docs.text: The registry caches tester lookups by type for performance.

docs.title: Recursive Transformation
docs.text: recursive_apply uses one engine (coola.recursive.engine) and one extension point. A transformer only describes the shape of a type: expand(data) returns None for a leaf, or the children and the function that rebuilds the container from the transformed children. The engine owns the invariants: the transformer lookup (by MRO, cached for the call), the call of func on the leaves, the cycle check and the depth (an explicit stack, so there is no RecursionError). This is the same split as the equality engine, where a tester returns the child pairs.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: summarize uses one engine (coola.summary.engine), one extension point and one option object (SummaryConfig). A summarizer only describes one type: summarize(data, config, *, compact) returns a str for a leaf, or a Node (a header, the lazy (label, child) pairs and their number) for a container. The engine owns the invariants: the summarizer lookup (by MRO), the display depth, max_items and max_characters, the cycle check, the layout, and the errors (a summarizer that raises is replaced by a placeholder). It walks the nodes with an explicit stack, so there is no RecursionError. A container at the display depth is shown on one line by CompactRepr, whose work is bounded by max_items, so the cost depends on the size of the summary and not on the size of the data. This is the same split as the equality and the recursive engines.

docs.title: Depth
docs.text: The engine does not recurse (see Design of coola.equality), so a deep structure cannot overflow the interpreter stack. EqualityConfig.max_depth (default 100) bounds the work on a pathological structure and raises MaxDepthExceededError, a plain Exception.

docs.title: Graceful Degradation
docs.text:
When a specific tester is not available, coola falls back to:

  1. More general tester (via MRO)
  2. DefaultEqualityTester (registered for object), which uses ==

docs.title: Informative Messages
docs.text:
When the comparison explains the difference (compare, assert_*), testers report:

  • What objects differ
  • Where in the structure the difference is
  • The actual values that differ

docs.title: Testing Strategy
docs.text:
The coola codebase uses:

  1. Unit tests: Test individual testers in isolation
  2. Integration tests: Test complete comparison workflows
  3. Property-based tests: Test invariants (reflexivity, symmetry of the exact comparison, and monotonicity of *_allclose: a larger atol or rtol never turns a True into False). The unit tests also walk the default registry: every tester of a built-in type must be reflexive on a sample of its type (NATIVE_SAMPLES in tests/unit/equality/tester/test_interface.py)
  4. Cross-library tests: Test integration with PyTorch, NumPy, etc.

docs.title: Core Dependencies
docs.text: • Python 3.11+: Core language features

docs.title: Optional Dependencies
docs.text:
• torch: PyTorch tensor support
  • numpy: NumPy array support
  • pandas: DataFrame support
  • polars: Polars DataFrame support
  • xarray: xarray support
  • jax: JAX array support
  • pyarrow: PyArrow table support

Each optional dependency is only imported when used (lazy loading): import coola and the import of its subpackages do not import any of them. The __init__.py files expose the names that need a library with lazy_exports, and the default registries load the entries of a library the first time they look for one of its types (register_lazy). See Lazy imports.

docs.title: Module Organization
docs.text:
coola/
├── equality/             # Equality and tolerance comparison
│   ├── interface.py      # objects_are_equal, objects_are_allclose
│   ├── result.py         # compare, assert_objects_equal, ...
│   ├── config.py         # EqualityConfig
│   ├── tester/           # Type-specific testers and the registry
│   └── handler/          # Helpers: numeric kernels, formatting, path parts
├── registry/             # Generic registries and type dispatch
├── summary/, hashing/, recursive/, iterator/, nested/, random/, reducer/
├── io/, factory/, identifier/, display/, validation/, testing/
└── utils/                # Utility functions

docs.title: Design of coola.equality
docs.text: The package is small on purpose: one engine, one extension point, one numeric rule and one table algorithm.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
1. Performance is a requirement. Both the passing and the failing path are measured by the benchmarks; a simpler design that is slower is rejected.
  2. Early exit. Two objects are different as soon as one difference is found: nothing after it is visited, converted or formatted.
  3. First difference only, on demand. objects_are_equal and objects_are_allclose build no message and no path; only compare and assert_* explain, and only the first difference.
  4. Equality drives hashing, not the reverse. hash_object is aligned with equality, never the other way round.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
objects_are_equal / objects_are_allclose / compare / assert_objects_equal / assert_objects_allclose
        |   one EqualityConfig (frozen) and one Engine per call
        v
Engine.run(actual, expected)    explicit stack of child iterators; one loop
        |   identity -> type -> tester lookup (cached per call) -> verdict or children
        v
Tester.objects_are_equal(actual, expected, ctx) -> bool | Iterator[(actual, expected, path part)]
        |   leaves: numbers, arrays, scalars       containers: sequence, mapping, set, object, table
        v
numeric kernel (NumPy, torch, JAX)      adapters: pandas, polars, pyarrow -> table

Four rules follow from it:

  1. One extension point: the tester. A tester is a class with one method.
  2. The engine owns the invariants: identity, strict type, depth, cycles, path and first failure. A tester cannot forget them because it never recurses.
  3. A container decomposes, it does not recurse: it returns the child pairs that must all be equal, lazily and in the order the first difference is wanted.
  4. coola owns the semantics, the libraries own the structure: every number goes through the kernel; a library says whether two frames have the same columns, never whether 1 is close to 2.

docs.title: The engine
docs.text:
The engine is one loop over a stack of child iterators (depth first, so the first difference in iteration order is the one reported). For each pair:

  1. actual is expected: equal.
  2. type(actual) is not type(expected): different.
  3. The tester is looked up in a per-call dict[type, tester] filled from the registry the first time a type is met, so the registry lookup is paid once per type. A registration made during a comparison is seen by the next call.
  4. The tester is called. A bool is the verdict. An iterator is a container: if its pair is already on the stack the pair is equal (cycle); if the stack is max_depth deep, MaxDepthExceededError is raised; otherwise it is pushed and the loop continues with its first child.
  5. On False, the path is built once from the path parts of the stack, the part of the failing pair and the parts given to ctx.fail.

Consequences: the stack use is constant, RecursionError cannot happen, and explaining costs nothing in the loop. ctx.fail(reason, *path) returns False; reason can be a callable that is called only when the difference is explained.

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text: There is one record, the first failure (path, reason): no list of reports and no message per parent level. Values in a reason go through one bounded formatter, so a failure in a million-element array formats a few values, not the array. A path part is a key or a position (['a'], [3]), AttributeName("x") (.x) or Element(2) ({2}). An array reports its index. A table is a leaf and names only the first differing column; the user finds the row with the library (for example DataFrame.compare).

docs.title: The numeric kernel
docs.text:
NumPy, torch and JAX share one formula:

close = (a == b) | (finite & (|a - b| <= atol + rtol * max(|a|, |b|))) | (isnan(a) & isnan(b) if equal_nan)
Dtype Preparation Rule bool none exact signed and unsigned integers exact difference in integers kernel, tolerance in float64 float16, bfloat16, float32 cast to float64 kernel float64, complex128 none (complex64 is cast up) kernel timedelta64 integer nanoseconds; NaT mask apart kernel; NaT by equal_nan datetime64, str, bytes, void none exact; NaT by equal_nan object none cells are children of the engine

Python scalars use the same formula; Decimal, Fraction and timedelta keep a difference-based rule.

docs.title: Tables
docs.text:
pandas, polars and PyArrow share one algorithm in TableEqualityTester, which takes an adapter per library: check the structure (shape, names, dtypes, index), then compare the columns lazily, one by one, each by its kind, and stop at the first column that differs. A Series or an Array is a one-column table.

Kind Dtypes Comparison numeric integers, floats, nullable and Arrow numerics null masks equal, then the kernel duration timedelta64, polars Duration, Arrow duration kernel on integer nanoseconds exact booleans, strings, categories, instants, nested and object the library's equals; never sees the tolerance or equal_nan

Nested and object columns are the one place where the library decides. attrs, flags and Arrow schema metadata are ignored. Adding a library means writing one adapter of about 40 lines.

docs.title: Module layout
docs.text:
coola/equality/
  interface.py   the five functions
  config.py      Tolerance, EqualityConfig
  engine.py      Engine, Element
  result.py      ComparisonResult
  tester/        base, registry, one module per family (default, scalar, collection, difference,
                 dataclass, object, equal, tolerant), per library (numpy, torch, jax, xarray,
                 pydantic), and table.py with the adapters pandas.py, polars.py, pyarrow.py
  _helpers/      private helpers (formatting, numeric kernel, comparison keys)

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text: Decision Reason Iterative engine, not recursion constant stack, one place for depth, cycles and path One tester method returns a verdict or an iterator one extension point No show_difference and no logger; compare and assert_* explain no cost on the fast path, thread safe bool and every Enum are exact they are labels, not quantities Masked arrays compare the data under the mask, the mask and fill value no hidden difference Small floats are cast to float64 no overflow of the tolerance at the edge of the range Integer difference is exact no rounding of large integers Tables are one leaf, reported by column simple and fast; the library finds the row Time resolution is part of the dtype as in NumPy Library testers are public users can compose, subclass or register them max_depth=100 and MaxDepthExceededError are kept bound the work on pathological structures

docs.title: Design of coola.factory
docs.text: The package builds an object from a fully qualified name. It is small on purpose and has no state: it keeps no registry, cache or singleton, and it imports the standard library and coola.utils.imports only. A configuration names the code to run, so every change is judged first by what the data can make the process do. The three entry points (factory, resolve_object and is_object_config) are compositions of functions that each own one invariant: import_object is the only place that imports a target (allow-list checked before the import, one ImportError for a missing target), and instantiate_object is the only place that calls one (abstract classes refused, the _init_ rule, the target's keywords never shadowed by a parameter of the API). The allow-list is a filter on a path and always comes from the caller's code, never from the data. See the user guide for the properties of the package.

docs.title: Design of coola.io
docs.text: The package reads and writes one value to one file, and a write either happens completely or leaves the target as it was. The base classes own the invariants and a format only describes how to turn a value into a file and back. BaseLoader.load is a template method: it converts the path (str, file:// URI or os.PathLike) and calls the _load(Path) of the format, so a format cannot forget the conversion. BaseFileSaver.save writes to a hidden temporary file next to the target and commits it with one atomic operation (os.link for exist_ok=False, os.replace for exist_ok=True), then removes the temporary file, so a reader sees the old file or the new one and two concurrent saves never mix. There is no lock, no lock file and no thread: the commit already decides every race, and a caller that needs mutual exclusion around a read-modify-write uses its own lock. equal(), repr and str are written once in the base classes from _display_fields(); a format that has no configuration defines nothing. TextSaver accepts a str only. Optional libraries (torch) are imported lazily. See the user guide for the properties of the package.

docs.title: Design of coola.hashing
docs.text:
The package has one engine, one extension point and one encoding rule. A hasher only describes the content of a type: encode(data) returns the bytes of a leaf (tagged(tag, payload)) or a Node(tag, children, ordered, group). The engine (coola.hashing.engine) owns everything else: the dispatch by type (once per type and per call), the digests, the order rule, the cycles, the shared containers, the depth and the placeholder of ignore_unhashable. This is the same split as equality (the engine owns identity, type, depth and cycles; a tester returns the child pairs) and recursive (a transformer returns the children).

hash_object(data, *, registry=None, length=64, ignore_unhashable=False)
        |   validates length; one registry; one call = one engine run
        v
digest_of(data, registry, ...)       explicit stack of frames; per-call type -> hasher cache and memo
        |-- hasher   = registry.find_hasher(type(data))     MRO, fallbacks, Enum rule
        |-- encoding = hasher.encode(data)                  pure: no registry, no recursion
        |        bytes -> leaf:  digest = BLAKE2b(0x00 + encoding)
        |        Node  -> push the children; when done:
        |                 digest = BLAKE2b(0x01 + tag + 0x00 + entries of the children)
        |                 (an entry is 0xFF + digest, or size + leaf for a leaf of at most 64 bytes)
        v
the 64-byte digest of the root  ->  hex()[:length]
Decision Why encode returns a description, the engine hashes cycles, depth, sharing, length and the placeholder cannot be forgotten A leaf of at most 64 bytes is inlined in the preimage of its parent a flat container makes one BLAKE2b call instead of one per item One 64-byte digest, cut at the end by length a hasher never sees length; a short hash is the start of a longer one The format version is the BLAKE2b person parameter two formats can never be confused; a change is one constant A shared container is hashed once per call (a memo by id) a hash is pure, so the memo is invisible; a DAG is linear A cycle raises ValueError the digest of a container in a cycle would depend on where it is reached Secrets are types with a hasher (SecretHasher) the policy is the one of the registry, wherever the secret is __coola_hash__ returns the content of a custom object, not a hash the object cannot bypass the engine and does not forward any option Only the compare=True fields of a dataclass equal dataclasses have the same hash

See the user guide for the properties of the package.

docs.title: Why Strict Type Checking?
docs.text:
Rationale: Prevents subtle bugs from implicit type coercion. In scientific computing, knowing that 1 (int) and 1.0 (float) are treated differently can catch numerical issues.

Trade-off: Less convenient for some use cases, but more explicit and safe.

docs.title: Why Registry-Based Dispatch?
docs.text:
Rationale: Allows extensibility without modifying core code. Users can add support for their own types.

Trade-off: Slightly more complex than if/else chains, but much more maintainable.

The registries are TypeRegistry objects (coola.registry). A lookup follows the Method Resolution Order of the type, then the fallback predicates (for the types that cannot be a key, such as every dataclass), then object. The handlers of the optional libraries are registered lazily (register_lazy), so importing coola imports none of these libraries. The state of a registry is a dictionary that is replaced on every write, so a lookup takes no lock; the registries survive os.fork and pickle. See the registry guide.

docs.title: Future Directions
docs.text:
Potential areas for enhancement:

  1. Parallel comparison: For large independent comparisons
  2. Streaming comparison: For very large objects that don't fit in memory
  3. Approximate structural matching: For comparing objects with similar but not identical structure
  4. Diff generation: Not just boolean result, but detailed diff
  5. Performance optimizations: Cython/Numba for hot paths

docs.title: Package Layering
docs.text:
Packages fall into two groups:

  • Core: registry (type-based dispatch), utils (generic helpers), display and validation. These must not import from any feature package.
  • Features: equality, hashing, summary, recursive, iterator, random, nested, reducer, io, factory, identifier and testing. Only equality, hashing, summary, recursive and iterator are built on registry; reducer and random are standalone helpers. identifier depends on hashing (the stable identifiers are built on hash_object), and hashing must not import identifier.

There is no exception: coola.registry imports no feature package. display and utils currently import each other, so they are kept in the same group.

The contract is enforced with import-linter (configured in pyproject.toml). Run it with:

lint-imports

docs.text:
To contribute to coola's architecture:

  1. Understand the existing patterns
  2. Follow the established conventions

  4. Write tests for new components

See the contributing guide for more details.

docs.title: Development Guide
docs.text: This guide covers setting up your development environment and common development tasks.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Python 3.11 or higher
  • uv for dependency management
  • Git for version control
  • Basic knowledge of Python and testing

docs.title: 1. Fork and Clone
docs.text:
# Fork the repository on GitHub, then clone your fork
git clone https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/coola.git
cd coola

docs.title: 2. Set Up Virtual Environment
docs.text:
The project uses uv for dependency management. First, install uv if you don't have it:

curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

Create and set up the virtual environment:

make setup-venv

This will create a virtual environment and install all dependencies, including development tools.

Activate the virtual environment:

source .venv/bin/activate

docs.title: 3. Install Dependencies
docs.text:
If you already have a virtual environment and just want to install dependencies:

# Install core dependencies
inv env.install --no-optional-deps

# Install with documentation dependencies
inv env.install --groups dev,docs

docs.title: 4. Set Up Pre-commit Hooks
docs.text:
pre-commit install

This will automatically run code quality checks before each commit.

docs.title: Running Tests
docs.text:
Run all unit tests:

inv test.unit

Run tests with coverage:

inv test.unit --cov

Run specific test file:

pytest tests/unit/equality/test_interface.py

Run specific test:

pytest tests/unit/equality/test_interface.py::test_objects_are_equal_false_different_type

docs.title: Code Quality
docs.text:
Check code formatting (Ruff):

inv format.check-python

Fix code formatting:

inv format.fix-python

Run linter (Ruff):

inv lint.check-python

Check the package layering and import cycles:

lint-imports
inv imports.check-cycles

Format docstrings:

inv format.fix-docstrings

Run all pre-commit checks:

pre-commit run --all-files

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
Build documentation locally:

mkdocs serve -f docs/mkdocs.yml

Then open http://127.0.0.1:8000 in your browser.

Build documentation without serving:

mkdocs build -f docs/mkdocs.yml

Run doctests:

inv test.doctest

docs.title: Type Checking
docs.text:
coola uses ty for type checking (see the ci-type-checking workflow). You can run type checking locally:

ty check

docs.title: Writing Good Tests
docs.text:
1. Use descriptive names:
def test_objects_are_equal_with_identical_dicts_returns_true(): ...


def test_objects_are_equal_with_different_types_returns_false(): ...
  1. Test edge cases:
  2. Empty collections
  3. None values
  4. Large data

  5. Deeply nested structures

import pytest
import torch
from coola.equality import objects_are_equal


@pytest.fixture
def sample_tensor():
    return torch.randn(10, 10)


def test_tensor_comparison(sample_tensor):
    result = objects_are_equal(sample_tensor, sample_tensor)
    assert result is True

def test_failure_case():

docs.title: Migration Guide: v0.11 to v1.0
docs.text: This guide explains how to migrate your code from coola version 0.11.x to version 1.0.x. Version 1.0 includes significant API reorganization to improve maintainability and extensibility.

docs.title: Overview of Changes
docs.text:
The main changes in version 1.0 are:

  1. Module reorganization: Better structured package hierarchy
  2. Import path changes: Top-level imports moved to subpackages
  3. Naming changes: More consistent naming conventions (e.g., comparators → tester)
  4. Removed features: Some modules were removed or merged (e.g., formatters)
  5. New equality engine: One extension point (the tester), one iterative engine, no handler chain
  6. Explanations on demand: show_difference is replaced by compare and assert_objects_equal

docs.title: Quick Migration Checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Update imports for equality functions (coola → coola.equality)
  • [ ] Update imports for summarization (coola.summarizers → coola.summary)
  • [ ] Replace uses of formatters with summary functions
  • [ ] Rewrite custom comparators, testers and handlers as testers that return a verdict or child pairs (section 3)
  • [ ] Replace show_difference=True by compare(...) or assert_objects_equal(...) (section 4)
  • [ ] Update module names (reduction → reducer)

docs.title: 1. Top-Level Imports Removed
docs.text:
The main equality functions are no longer available at the top level.

Before (v0.11):

from coola import objects_are_equal, objects_are_allclose

After (v1.0):

from coola.equality import objects_are_equal, objects_are_allclose

Migration: Add .equality to your import statements.

docs.title: 2. Module Reorganization
docs.text:
Several modules have been renamed or reorganized:

Feature v0.11 v1.0 Status Equality functions module coola.comparison (internal) coola.equality Renamed Comparators coola.equality.comparators coola.equality.tester Renamed Formatters coola.formatters N/A Removed* Summarizers coola.summarizers coola.summary Renamed Reduction coola.reduction coola.reducer Renamed

*Use coola.summary instead of the removed formatters module.

Note: In v0.11, equality functions were available both at the top level (from coola import) and in coola.comparison module. In v1.0, they are only in coola.equality.

docs.title: 3. Equality Comparison System
docs.text: The equality comparison system has been redesigned with a cleaner architecture.

docs.title: Basic Usage (No Breaking Changes)
docs.text:
If you only use the basic equality functions, the migration is simple:

Before (v0.11):

from coola import objects_are_equal, objects_are_allclose

objects_are_equal(actual, expected)
objects_are_allclose(actual, expected, rtol=1e-5, atol=1e-8)

After (v1.0):

from coola.equality import objects_are_equal, objects_are_allclose

objects_are_equal(actual, expected)
objects_are_allclose(actual, expected, rtol=1e-5, atol=1e-8)

The function signatures and behavior remain the same.

docs.title: Custom Equality Testers
docs.text:
The comparator system has been replaced by testers that use an engine. A tester never recurses and never checks the identity, the type, the depth or the cycles: the engine does. The tester receives two objects of the same type and the engine (ctx), and returns either a verdict or the child pairs (actual, expected, path part) that must all be equal.

Before (v0.11):

from coola.equality.comparators import BaseEqualityComparator


class PointComparator(BaseEqualityComparator):
    def clone(self):
        return PointComparator()

    def equal(self, other):
        return isinstance(other, PointComparator)

    def object_equal(self, tester, object1, object2, show_difference=False):
        if not isinstance(object2, Point):
            return False
        return tester.object_equal((object1.x, object1.y), (object2.x, object2.y))

After (v1.0):

>>> from coola.equality import AttributeName, BaseEqualityTester, compare, objects_are_equal
>>> class Point:
...     def __init__(self, x, y):
...         self.x = x
...         self.y = y
>>> class PointEqualityTester(BaseEqualityTester[Point]):
...     def objects_are_equal(self, actual, expected, ctx):
...         return (
...             (actual.x, expected.x, AttributeName("x")),
...             (actual.y, expected.y, AttributeName("y")),
...         )
>>> from coola.equality import get_default_registry
>>> registry = get_default_registry().copy()
>>> registry.register(Point, PointEqualityTester())  # or register_equality_testers({...})
>>> objects_are_equal(Point(1, 2.0), Point(1, 2.0), registry=registry)
True
>>> result = compare(Point(1, 2.0), Point(1, 3.0), registry=registry)
>>> result.path
('y',)

A leaf tester returns a verdict and gives the reason with ctx.fail, which returns False. The reason can be a function: it is called only when the difference is explained.

class VersionEqualityTester(BaseEqualityTester[Version]):
    def objects_are_equal(self, actual, expected, ctx):
        return actual.number == expected.number or ctx.fail(
            lambda: f"versions differ: {actual.number} vs {expected.number}"
        )

Migration of the v1.0 pre-release API (handlers and chain testers):

Before After BaseChainEqualityTester, HandlerEqualityTester, create_chain A BaseEqualityTester with one method objects_are_equal(a, e, ctx) BaseEqualityHandler, SameObjectHandler, SameTypeHandler, ... Removed: the engine checks the identity and the type config.registry.objects_are_equal(a, b, config) (recursion) Return the child pair (a, b, path part) report_difference(config, message, path=...) return ctx.fail(reason, *path) check_recursion_depth, track_comparison, HandlerCycleError Removed: the engine owns the depth and the cycles tester.equal(other) tester == other (same type and same attributes) EqualityConfig(atol=..., rtol=...), config.reports EqualityConfig(tolerance=Tolerance(...)); the config is frozen Engine(registry, config) Engine(config, explaining=False) PandasDataFrameEqualityTester, PolarsSeriesEqualityTester, ... TableEqualityTester(adapter), registered by the default registry from coola.equality.handler import ... Private (coola.equality._helpers); use coola.equality MaxDepthExceededError is a RecursionError A plain Exception; there is no RecursionError from the engine

docs.title: Type-Specific Classes
docs.text:
Before (v0.11):

from coola.equality.comparators import (
    TorchTensorComparator,
    NumpyArrayComparator,
    MappingEqualityComparator,
    SequenceEqualityComparator,
)

After (v1.0):

from coola.equality import (
    TorchTensorEqualityTester,
    NumpyArrayEqualityTester,
    MappingEqualityTester,
    SequenceEqualityTester,
)

Migration: Replace Comparator with EqualityTester in class names. The pandas, polars and PyArrow testers are one TableEqualityTester with an adapter per library.

docs.title: Changes of the results
docs.text:
The rules are the same for every container and every library. A comparison can change in these cases:

  • bool and the members of an enum.Enum are labels: the tolerance never applies to them (also IntEnum, numpy.bool_ and pandas booleans).
  • An integer difference is computed in integers: 2**62 and 2**62 + 1 are different with atol=0.5 in an array, as they are in a list.
  • float16, bfloat16 and float32 are compared in double precision (no wrong True at the edge of the range).
  • MappingProxyType and array.array are compared like a mapping and a sequence.
  • pandas, polars and PyArrow numbers follow the tolerance; the nested and object cells are compared by the library (equals), without tolerance. The tolerance does not apply to an index.
  • A table (data frame, series, index, Arrow table) is one leaf of the explanation: the path stops at the table and the reason names the first column that differs.
  • OrderedDict keeps its order, a dict does not. A cycle is equal. A nesting deeper than max_depth raises MaxDepthExceededError.

docs.title: 4. Explaining a Difference: show_difference Removed
docs.text:
show_difference=True (a log message) is replaced by two functions that explain the first difference only, on demand: compare returns a ComparisonResult and assert_objects_equal / assert_objects_allclose raise an AssertionError. objects_are_equal and objects_are_allclose format nothing.

Before:

import logging

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)
objects_are_equal(actual, expected, show_difference=True)

After:

>>> from coola.equality import compare, assert_objects_equal
>>> result = compare({"a": [1, 2, 3]}, {"a": [1, 2, 4]})
>>> result.equal
False
>>> result.path
('a', 2)
>>> print(result.format_message())
objects are not equal at actual['a'][2]
numbers are different:
  actual   : 3
  expected : 4
>>> assert_objects_equal({"a": 1}, {"a": 2})
Traceback (most recent call last):
    ...
AssertionError: objects are not equal at actual['a']
numbers are different:
  actual   : 1
  expected : 2

compare(actual, expected, rtol=0.0, atol=0.0, ...) takes the same keywords as objects_are_allclose (exact by default). ComparisonResult has equal, path (keys, positions, AttributeName, Element) and reason, and no actual / expected fields.

docs.title: 5. Formatters Removed
docs.text:
The coola.formatters module has been removed. Use coola.summary for text representation instead.

Before (v0.11):

from coola.formatters import Formatter, DefaultFormatter

formatter = DefaultFormatter()
formatted_output = formatter.format(obj)

After (v1.0):

from coola.summary import summarize

summary_output = summarize(obj)

Migration:

  • Replace formatter calls with summarize() function
  • The summarize() function provides similar text representation functionality
  • If you need custom formatting logic, implement a custom BaseSummarizer

docs.title: 6. Summarization
docs.text:
The summarization module has been renamed from summarizers to summary.

Before (v0.11):

from coola import summary

summary_text = summary(value, max_depth=2)

After (v1.0):

from coola.summary import summarize

summary_text = summarize(value, max_depth=2)

Changes:

  • Module renamed: coola.summarizers → coola.summary
  • Function renamed: summary() → summarize()
  • Top-level import removed: use from coola.summary import summarize

docs.title: 7. Reduction
docs.text:
The reduction module has been renamed from reduction to reducer.

Before (v0.11):

from coola.reduction import Reduction

# Use the global reducer
Reduction.reducer  # Access current reducer

After (v1.0):

from coola.reducer import auto_reducer, NativeReducer, NumpyReducer

# Create reducer instances directly
reducer = auto_reducer()  # Automatically selects best available backend
# Or use specific reducers:
# reducer = NativeReducer()    # Pure Python
# reducer = NumpyReducer()     # NumPy backend
# reducer = TorchReducer()     # PyTorch backend

Migration:

  • Update module name: coola.reduction → coola.reducer
  • The Reduction class pattern has been replaced with direct reducer instances
  • Use auto_reducer() for automatic backend selection

Changes of the reducers:

  • auto_reducer() returns NumpyReducer if NumPy is installed, else NativeReducer. It no longer returns TorchReducer when PyTorch is installed (it is slower on a list and slow to import): create TorchReducer() explicitly for tensors that live on a device.
  • BaseBasicReducer is removed. Subclass BaseReducer, which now owns the checks (empty input, iterator, options, shape) and calls the private computations _max, _mean, _median, _min, _quantile, _std and _sort. _is_empty and _check_values are removed; implement _prepare to convert or validate the input if needed.
  • sort(values, *, descending=False): descending is keyword-only.
  • EmptySequenceError is a ValueError.
  • The input is a sequence of real numbers (list, tuple, range) or a one-dimensional array / tensor for the backend. An iterator, a set, a str, an n-d or 0-d array, a complex number, an integer beyond 64 bits (NumPy and PyTorch) or a Decimal raise TypeError or ValueError with the same text in every backend (they used to return a value or raise AttributeError, RuntimeError, ...). NativeReducer rejects arrays and tensors: use NumpyReducer or TorchReducer.
  • quantile raises ValueError for a quantile outside [0, 1] (or NaN) in the three backends, before the values are read.
  • NativeReducer.mean uses statistics.fmean: it is much faster and the last bit of a float mean can differ.

docs.title: 8. New Features in v1.0
docs.text:
Several new modules have been added in v1.0:

  • coola.iterator: DFS/BFS traversal of nested structures
  • coola.recursive: Recursive processing utilities
  • coola.registry: Generic registry implementations

These are new additions and don't require migration from v0.11.

docs.title: Pattern 1: Simple Equality Checks
docs.text:
Before:

from coola import objects_are_equal
import torch

result = objects_are_equal({"a": torch.tensor([1, 2, 3])}, {"a": torch.tensor([1, 2, 3])})

After:

from coola.equality import objects_are_equal
import torch

result = objects_are_equal({"a": torch.tensor([1, 2, 3])}, {"a": torch.tensor([1, 2, 3])})

docs.title: Pattern 2: Tolerance-Based Comparison
docs.text:
Before:

from coola import objects_are_allclose
import numpy as np

result = objects_are_allclose(np.array([1.0, 2.0]), np.array([1.0001, 2.0001]), atol=1e-3)

After:

from coola.equality import objects_are_allclose
import numpy as np

result = objects_are_allclose(np.array([1.0, 2.0]), np.array([1.0001, 2.0001]), atol=1e-3)

docs.title: Pattern 3: Summarization
docs.text:
Before:

from coola import summary

text = summary([1, 2, 3, {"key": "value"}], max_depth=2)
print(text)

After:

from coola.summary import summarize

text = summarize([1, 2, 3, {"key": "value"}], max_depth=2)
print(text)

docs.title: Pattern 4: Custom Comparators/Testers
docs.text: See Custom Equality Testers above: a tester has one method objects_are_equal(actual, expected, ctx) that returns a verdict or the child pairs.

docs.title: Testing Your Migration
docs.text:
After migrating your code, ensure everything works correctly:

  1. Update imports: Run your code to check for import errors
  2. Run tests: Ensure all existing tests pass
  3. Check functionality: Verify equality checks produce the same results
  4. Review custom code: If you have custom comparators/testers, review and test thoroughly

docs.title: Getting Help
docs.text:
If you encounter issues during migration:

  • Check the documentation for detailed API reference
  • Review the examples for common usage patterns
  • Open an issue on GitHub if you need help

docs.title: API Stability Note
docs.text:
⚠️ Important: This migration guide is for the 1.0 release series. The current version is an alpha/pre-release.

  • The API structure described in this guide reflects the 1.0 design
  • The changes from v0.11 documented here are stable and will remain in the 1.0 series
  • Minor refinements may occur before the final 1.0.0 stable release
  • For production use, monitor the releases page and consider pinning to a specific version

docs.title: Migration Guide: v1.1 to v2.0
docs.text: This guide explains how to migrate your code from coola version 1.1.x to version 2.0.x.

docs.title: Overview of Changes
docs.text: The main changes in version 2.0 are the expand protocol of coola.recursive (the engine now recurses, and a transformer only describes the children of one object) and the single child finder of coola.iterator (one registry and one find_children for dfs_iterate and bfs_iterate). coola.factory has one way to import a target, one way to call it and one way to ask what it builds. coola.random has one seed domain, a strict set_rng_state and one registry type that subclasses coola.registry.Registry. coola.summary has one engine, one extension point (a summarizer returns a string or a Node) and one option object (SummaryConfig): the options are the keyword arguments of summarize. coola.registry has one storage class (Registry) and one dispatch class (TypeRegistry): the registries of the packages are TypeRegistry subclasses, a type that cannot be a key (every dataclass) is registered as a fallback predicate, and the registries can be pickled.

docs.title: Migration Checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Port the custom coola.recursive transformers to expand (section 1)
  • [ ] Port the custom coola.iterator iterators and child finders to find_children (section 2)
  • [ ] Replace _init_: __new__ and the _init_ names that start with _ by a public class method, and resolve the nested configurations before passing them under an allow-list (section 3)
  • [ ] Replace the removed names of coola.random, and give set_rng_state a state with the registered keys (section 4)
  • [ ] Port the custom coola.summary summarizers to summarize(data, config, *, compact), move the options of the summarizers to the arguments of summarize, and read the new layout (section 5)

  • [ ] Replace DataclassMarker, find, resolve_or, BaseTypeDispatchRegistry, the equal_nan argument of equal and the positional exist_ok (section 6)

  • [ ] Port the custom coola.hashing hashers to encode, replace SupportsHash.hash by __coola_hash__, move the secret policy to the registry, and replace the removed names (section 7). Every hash and every stable identifier changes.

  • [ ] Rename load to _load in the custom coola.io loaders, drop their equal, remove lock=, import add_uuid_suffix from coola.utils.path, and call str() before save_text (section 8)
  • [ ] Replace generate_uuid4, generate_nano_id, generate_prefixed_id and generate_obfuscated_id (section 9)

docs.title: 1. Recursive Transformers: the expand Protocol
2. Iterators: One Child Finder for Both Orders
3. Factory: Strict Contracts
docs.text:
Before After A target cannot receive an argument named obj or cls It receives every key that is not reserved, whatever its name _init_="__new__" or a name that starts with _ TypeError: use a public class method or static method _allowed_prefixes_ in the configuration of resolve_object (used when the caller has none) Ignored: the allow-list always comes from the caller factory(..., _allowed_prefixes_=[...]) with an argument that is {"_target_": ...} ValueError: resolve the nested configuration first resolve_object with a nested configuration and allowed_prefixes ValueError (same reason) A dict with _target_ and a dict subclass cls Built (the key _target_ is reserved) A dict without _target_ Returned if it is an instance of cls, else TypeError Counter({"_target_": 2}) passed to resolve_object Resolved as a configuration Missing module or attribute of a target ImportError: The target object does not exist: ... everywhere A target that returns A \| B with no subclass of cls Refused before the call is_object_config({"_target_": 5}, int) False (was TypeError) Explicit _init_="__init__" with resolve_object The target is checked, like the default

Before:

resolve_object({"_target_": "mypkg.Model", "_init_": "__new__"})

After:

resolve_object({"_target_": "mypkg.Model", "_init_": "from_config", "config": {...}})

An allow-list is a filter on a path, not a sandbox: never allow a prefix that contains a function that resolves its arguments ("coola", "coola.factory", pickle, eval, ...).

docs.title: 4. Random: One Seed Domain, One Registry
docs.text:
Before After RandomRandomManager (coola.random.random) PythonRandomManager (coola.random.python) numpy_seed(seed) and torch_seed(seed) NumpyRandomManager().seed(seed) and TorchRandomManager().seed(seed) random_seed(seed, manager) random_seed(seed, *, registry=None) register_managers(mapping, True) register_managers(mapping, exist_ok=True) manager.manual_seed(-1), 1.5, True, 2**63 accepted or folded TypeError / ValueError: every entry validates the seed NumPy: manual_seed(2**32 + 1) gives the numbers of manual_seed(1) A seed >= 2**32 is split in two 32-bit words: its numbers change registry.has_manager(key) and registry.find_manager(key) key in registry (or registry.has(key)) and registry[key] set_rng_state with different keys logs a warning and restores a part of the state ValueError, nothing restored; all the managers are restored before an error is raised get_random_seed(seed) in [-2**63, 2**63 - 1) In [0, 2**63 - 1), valid for manual_seed: the value for a given seed changes get_torch_generator(random_seed=1, device) (not exported) get_torch_generator(seed, *, device="cpu") from coola.random; seed is required repr(RandomManagerRegistry) has a (state): Registry(...) line The managers are listed directly

A state saved with torch and restored on a machine without torch now raises a ValueError. Restore it into a registry with the same keys.

docs.title: 5. Summary: One Engine, One Option Object
6. Registry: Two Classes, Fallbacks, Pickling
docs.text:
Before After registry.register(DataclassMarker, handler) registry.register_fallback(dataclasses.is_dataclass, handler) from coola.registry import DataclassMarker Removed; the dataclass handler is in registry.fallbacks(), not in items() / len() BaseTypeDispatchRegistry, registry.find(t), registry.resolve_or(t) Removed; the registries of the packages are TypeRegistry subclasses: use registry.resolve(t) registry.register(key, value, True), register_many(mapping, True) exist_ok is keyword-only: register(key, value, exist_ok=True) registry.equal(other, equal_nan=True) registry.equal(other): the entries are compared with ==, and a registry equals its copy except RuntimeError around AlreadyRegisteredError AlreadyRegisteredError is a ValueError only A hasher for object makes the hashing fallbacks unreachable object is the last resort everywhere: type > fallback > object HasherRegistry.register_fallback(predicate, hasher) accepts a duplicate predicate A duplicate predicate raises AlreadyRegisteredError (exist_ok=True replaces it, keeping its place) HasherRegistry.unregister_fallback(predicate) returns None It returns the hasher and raises KeyNotRegisteredError for an unknown predicate repr(registry) printed (state): TypeRegistry(...); a hashing fallbacks list One display: one (key): value line per entry, then (fallback) lines and the pending lazy groups register_lazy(["builtins", "decimal"], f) then register_lazy("builtins", g) failed Both groups stay and load; register_lazy is a method of TypeRegistry only pickle.dumps(registry) and copy.deepcopy(registry) raised TypeError They work; a spawn worker can receive a registry

Before:

from coola.registry import DataclassMarker

registry.register(DataclassMarker, MyDataclassHandler())

After:

from dataclasses import is_dataclass

registry.register_fallback(is_dataclass, MyDataclassHandler())

A handler registered for the type of a dataclass still has priority over the fallback. A fallback also supports the virtual subclasses of an abstract base class (the MRO lookup does not call issubclass): registry.register_fallback(lambda t: issubclass(t, Sequence), handler).

docs.title: 7. Hashing: One Engine, encode, a New Format
docs.text:
Every hash value changes (new encoding, format version coola-hash-2, short leaves inlined in the preimage of their parent), so every stable identifier changes too: generate_stable_content_id and generate_stable_uuid5 return other values. Regenerate any stored hash or identifier.

Before After Hasher.hash(data, registry, *, length, ignore_unhashable) Hasher.encode(data): returns tagged(tag, payload) (a leaf) or Node(tag, children) A hasher calls registry.hash(child, length=..., ignore_unhashable=...) The children are in the Node; the engine hashes them hash_string, hash_bytes, hash_tagged, hash_enum, hash_path Removed: use hash_object; tagged and digest are the building blocks of a hasher SupportsHash.hash(registry, length, ignore_unhashable), HashableHasher __coola_hash__(self) -> object (the content, not a hash), SupportsCoolaHash, ContentHasher PydanticModelHasher(on_secret=...), hash_pydantic_model, unwrap_secrets SecretHasher(on_secret) and get_secret_hashers(on_secret), registered in a registry "exclude" removed the key or the item of a secret "exclude" hashes a constant: the position of a secret is kept A secret in a dict or a dataclass raised, or was TypeNotRegisteredError The policy of the registry applies wherever the secret is hash_object(data, registry, 32), register_hashers(mapping, True) Keyword-only: hash_object(data, registry=registry, length=32), register_hashers(mapping, exist_ok=True) HasherRegistry.hash(data, 16) HasherRegistry.hash(data, length=16) ValueError("... nested too deeply") at about 500 levels No limit: the traversal uses an explicit stack A DAG costs one visit per path A shared container is hashed once length applied to every node: hash(x, length=16) was not a prefix of length=128 One digest cut at the end: a hash is the start of the longer ones A dataclass field with compare=False was hashed Only the compare=True fields are hashed memoryview hashed like bytes; UserString and MappingProxyType failed Own tag (memoryview), UserString and MappingProxyType are hashed A pandas object named NaN and one named None had different hashes Same hash

Before:

class PointHasher(BaseHasher[Point]):
    def hash(self, data, registry, *, length=64, ignore_unhashable=False):
        return registry.hash((data.x, data.y), length=length, ignore_unhashable=ignore_unhashable)

After:

class PointHasher(BaseHasher[Point]):
    def encode(self, data):
        return Node("Point", [data.x, data.y])

To reveal or exclude secrets, build a registry:

registry = get_default_registry().copy()
registry.register_many(get_secret_hashers("reveal"), exist_ok=True)
hash_object(model, registry=registry)

docs.title: 8. I/O: Template Methods, No Lock
9. Identifier: Four Generators Removed
docs.text:
generate_uuid4, generate_nano_id, generate_prefixed_id, generate_obfuscated_id and decode_obfuscated_id are removed: each is a line of the standard library or, for the obfuscated identifiers, an affine map that two known pairs break. The stable identifiers keep their values.

Before After generate_uuid4() str(uuid.uuid4()) generate_nano_id(n, a) secrets.token_urlsafe(16), or "".join(secrets.choice(a) for _ in range(n)) generate_prefixed_id f"cus_{generate_ulid()}" generate_obfuscated_id a library made for it (sqids), or a keyed permutation; never an affine map

docs.title: coola.display
docs.text: Contain display shared helpers.

docs.title: coola.display.BaseDisplayMixin
docs.text:
Bases: ABC

Abstract base for display mixins.

__repr__ and __str__ are defined here: they get the fields from _display_fields and delegate the layout to _render_fields. Subclasses must implement _render_fields to choose the layout. Classes that use a layout mixin override _display_fields to return the values to show; by default no field is shown.

docs.title: coola.display.InlineDisplayMixin
docs.text:
Bases: BaseDisplayMixin

Mixin that renders __repr__ and __str__ on a single line.

All fields are displayed inline. Best suited for simple objects with few, short fields where a compact single-line format aids readability. Override _display_fields to choose the fields to show; by default none is shown, which suits stateless classes.

Example 
>>> from coola.display import InlineDisplayMixin
>>> from typing import Any
>>> class MyClass(InlineDisplayMixin):
...     def __init__(self, key1: str, key2: str) -> None:
...         self.key1 = key1
...         self.key2 = key2
...     def _display_fields(self) -> dict[str, Any]:
...         return {"key1": self.key1, "key2": self.key2}
...
>>> obj = MyClass(key1="value1", key2="value2")
>>> print(repr(obj))
MyClass(key1='value1', key2='value2')
>>> print(str(obj))
MyClass(key1=value1, key2=value2)
>>> class NoFields(InlineDisplayMixin):
...     pass
...
>>> print(repr(NoFields()))
NoFields()

docs.title: coola.display.MultilineDisplayMixin
docs.text:
Bases: BaseDisplayMixin

Mixin that renders __repr__ and __str__ in multiline dict format.

Each field is displayed on its own indented line. Best suited for objects with several fields or deeply nested values where a single-line format would be hard to read. Override _display_fields to choose the fields to show; by default none is shown.

Example 
>>> from coola.display import MultilineDisplayMixin
>>> from typing import Any
>>> class MyClass(MultilineDisplayMixin):
...     def __init__(self, key1: str, key2: str) -> None:
...         self.key1 = key1
...         self.key2 = key2
...     def _display_fields(self) -> dict[str, Any]:
...         return {"key1": self.key1, "key2": self.key2}
...
>>> obj = MyClass(key1="value1", key2="value2")
>>> print(repr(obj))
MyClass(
  (key1): value1
  (key2): value2
)
>>> print(str(obj))
MyClass(
  (key1): value1
  (key2): value2
)

docs.title: coola.display.repr_pydantic_model
docs.text:
repr_pydantic_model(
    model: BaseModel,
    *,
    sort: bool = True,
    exclude_none: bool = False,
    exclude_secret: bool = True,
    exclude_fields: list[str] | None = None,

Return a formatted, single-line repr-style representation of a pydantic model.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default model BaseModel

The pydantic model to format.

required sort bool

If True, sort fields by name.

True exclude_none bool

If True, omit fields whose value is None.

False exclude_secret bool

If True, omit fields typed as a secret type (SecretStr, SecretBytes, Secret) entirely, rather than showing the masked value.

True exclude_fields list[str] | None

Optional list of field names to omit. A RuntimeWarning is emitted for names that are not fields of the model; a field already omitted by exclude_none or exclude_secret is not reported.

None
