docs.title: coola.display.colorlog
docs.text: Provide utilities for configuring Python's logging output.

docs.title: coola.display.colorlog.configure_colorlog_logging
docs.text:
configure_colorlog_logging(
    level: int = INFO, force: bool = False, **kwargs: Any
) -> None

Configure the root logger, using a coloured formatter when available.

If the colorlog package is installed and sys.stderr is attached to a terminal, attaches a colorlog.StreamHandler with per-level colours for both the log metadata (level, logger name, line number) and the message itself. If colorlog is not installed, or output is not a terminal (e.g. redirected to a file or running in CI), falls back to plain logging.basicConfig with no formatting, to avoid emitting raw ANSI escape codes into non-interactive output.

The coloured handler writes to stream if given, and to sys.stderr otherwise; the terminal check applies to this stream. If handlers, filename, filemode, format or style is given, the caller controls the output and the call is forwarded to logging.basicConfig without a coloured handler. datefmt is used by the coloured formatter.

Note

logging.basicConfig is a no-op if the root logger already has handlers configured. Pass force=True to remove existing handlers and reconfigure unconditionally.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default level int

Minimum log level for the root logger. Accepts any constant from logging (e.g. logging.DEBUG, logging.WARNING). Defaults to logging.INFO.

INFO force bool

When True, removes any existing handlers before applying the new configuration, ensuring this call always takes effect. Defaults to False.

False **kwargs Any

Additional keyword arguments passed to logging.basicConfig (e.g. stream, filename, datefmt).

{} Example 
>>> import logging
>>> from coola.display.colorlog import configure_colorlog_logging
>>> configure_colorlog_logging(level=logging.DEBUG)

docs.title: coola.equality
docs.text:
Utilities to compare nested objects for exact or tolerant equality.

The package exports the comparison functions, the result, the configuration, the engine, the testers and the registry. The testers of the optional libraries (NumPy, PyTorch, JAX, xarray, pydantic) are imported the first time they are used.

docs.title: coola.equality.AttributeName
docs.text:
Bases: str

Name of an attribute in the location of a difference.

It is a str that marks a path component as an attribute (a dataclass field, for example) rather than a key or an index, so a path is formatted as ['a'][2].x and not as ['a'][2]['x'].

Example 
>>> from coola.equality._helpers.utils import AttributeName
>>> AttributeName("x") == "x"
True

docs.title: coola.equality.BaseEqualityTester
docs.text:
Bases: InlineDisplayMixin, ABC, Generic[T]

Define the base class to implement an equality operator.

The engine owns the invariants of a comparison (identity, strict type, depth, cycles, location of the first difference). A tester never recurses: objects_are_equal receives the two objects, which have the same type, and the engine, and returns

  • a verdict: True, or ctx.fail(reason, *path) (which returns False) for a leaf;
  • or the child pairs (actual, expected, path part) that must all be equal, produced lazily and in the order the first difference is wanted, for a container.

Two testers are equal if they have the same type and the same attributes. A child class with parameters must override _display_fields.

Example 
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.engine import Engine
>>> from coola.equality.tester import BaseEqualityTester, get_default_registry
>>> class PointTester(BaseEqualityTester[tuple]):
...     def objects_are_equal(self, actual, expected, ctx):
...         return ((actual[0], expected[0], 0), (actual[1], expected[1], 1))
...
>>> registry = get_default_registry().copy()
>>> registry.register(tuple, PointTester(), exist_ok=True)
>>> Engine(EqualityConfig(registry=registry)).run((1, 2), (1, 2))
True
>>> Engine(EqualityConfig(registry=registry)).run((1, 2), (1, 3))
False
>>> PointTester() == PointTester()
True

docs.title: coola.equality.BaseEqualityTester.objects_are_equal abstractmethod
docs.text:
objects_are_equal(
    actual: T, expected: T, ctx: Engine
) -> bool | Iterator[tuple[object, object, object]]

Test two objects that have the same type.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default actual T

The actual object.

required expected T

The expected object, with the same type.

required ctx Engine

The Engine of the comparison.

required

Returns:

Type Description bool | Iterator[tuple[object, object, object]]

A verdict, or the child pairs that must all be equal.

Example 
>>> import numpy as np
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.engine import Engine

>>> engine = Engine(EqualityConfig())
>>> tester = NumpyArrayEqualityTester()
>>> tester.objects_are_equal(np.ones(2), np.ones(2), engine)
True
>>> tester.objects_are_equal(np.ones(2), np.zeros(2), engine)
False

docs.text:
Describe the outcome of comparing two objects.

bool(result) is True if the objects are equal, so the result can be used as a drop-in replacement for the bool returned by objects_are_equal.

Attributes:

Name Type Description equal bool

True if the objects are equal.

path tuple[object, ...]

The location of the first difference, e.g. ("a", 2) for actual["a"][2]. The attributes (the fields of a dataclass) are AttributeName instances and are formatted as .name, and the elements of a set are Element instances formatted as {value}. Empty if equal, or if the difference is at the root.

A description of the first difference found, or None if the objects are equal.

>>> from coola.equality import compare
>>> result = compare({"a": [1, 2, 3]}, {"a": [1, 2, 4]})
>>> bool(result)
False
>>> result.path
('a', 2)
>>> result.format_path()

docs.title: coola.equality.DataclassEqualityTester
docs.text:
Bases: BaseEqualityTester[Any]

Implement an equality tester for dataclass instances.

The two instances have the same type, and the tester compares their fields, in the order of declaration. The fields with compare=False are ignored. The fields are compared with the engine, so they support the tolerance and equal_nan, and the location of a difference is the name of the field.

Example 
>>> from dataclasses import dataclass
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.engine import Engine
>>> from coola.equality.tester import get_default_registry
>>> @dataclass
... class Point:
...     x: float
...
>>> engine = Engine(EqualityConfig())
>>> engine.run(Point(1.0), Point(1.0))
True
>>> engine.run(Point(1.0), Point(2.0))
False

docs.title: coola.equality.DefaultEqualityTester
docs.text:
Bases: BaseEqualityTester[object]

Implement a default equality tester.

This tester serves as the fallback for types without specialized equality testers. It uses Python's built-in == operator to test equality between two objects of the same type. The engine checks the identity and the type before the tester is called.

This tester is registered for the object type in the default registry, making it the catch-all for unregistered types via Python's MRO.

Raises:

Type Description TypeError

if == raises a TypeError or a ValueError, or returns a value that cannot be converted to a bool (for example an array). False would claim that the objects are different when they were not compared at all.

Example 
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.engine import Engine
>>> from coola.equality.tester import DefaultEqualityTester, get_default_registry
>>> engine = Engine(EqualityConfig())
>>> tester = DefaultEqualityTester()
>>> tester.objects_are_equal("meow", "meow", engine)
True
>>> tester.objects_are_equal("meow", "meov", engine)
False

docs.title: coola.equality.DifferenceCloseEqualityTester
docs.text:
Bases: BaseEqualityTester[Any]

Implement an equality tester for decimal.Decimal, fractions.Fraction and datetime.timedelta.

These types have no allclose, so the tester compares their difference with the tolerance (see difference_close). A Decimal NaN is equal to a NaN only if equal_nan is True, and atol of a timedelta is a number of seconds.

This tester is registered for Decimal, Fraction and timedelta in the default registry.

Example 
>>> from coola.equality import Tolerance
>>> from decimal import Decimal
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.engine import Engine
>>> from coola.equality.tester import DifferenceCloseEqualityTester, get_default_registry
>>> registry = get_default_registry()
>>> tester = DifferenceCloseEqualityTester()
>>> tester.objects_are_equal(
...     Decimal("1.0"), Decimal("1.00001"), Engine(EqualityConfig())
... )
False
>>> tester.objects_are_equal(
...     Decimal("1.0"), Decimal("1.00001"), Engine(EqualityConfig(tolerance=Tolerance(atol=1e-3)))
... )
True

docs.title: coola.equality.Engine
docs.text:
Run the comparison of two objects.

One engine runs one comparison. For each pair of objects, the engine checks the identity, the strict type, finds the tester (the lookup is cached for the call) and calls it. A tester that uses the engine returns either a bool (the verdict) or an iterator of (actual, expected, path part) child pairs that must all be equal. The iterators are kept on an explicit stack, depth first, so the first difference in iteration order is the one found and nothing after it is visited. The stack use is constant: there is no RecursionError whatever the nesting.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default config EqualityConfig

The settings of the comparison (the registry that finds the tester of a type, the tolerance, equal_nan and max_depth). A config is immutable and can be shared.

required explaining bool

If True, the reasons are built and the first difference is recorded in failure.

False

Attributes:

Name Type Description atol

The absolute tolerance.

rtol

The relative tolerance.

equal_nan

If True, two NaNs are equal.

explaining

If True, the reasons are built.

failure tuple[tuple[object, ...], str | None] | None

None or, after a difference was found, the pair (path, reason) of the first difference.

Example 
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.engine import Engine
>>> Engine(EqualityConfig()).run([1, {"a": 2}], [1, {"a": 2}])
True
>>> Engine(EqualityConfig()).run([1, {"a": 2}], [1, {"a": 3}])
False

docs.title: coola.equality.EqualEqualityTester
docs.text:
Bases: BaseEqualityTester[object]

Implement an equality tester for objects with equal method.

This tester is designed for objects that implement an equal(other) method for equality comparison. The two objects have the same type (the engine checks it) and the tester calls the equal method of the first one. An object without a callable equal is different.

Example 
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.engine import Engine
>>> from coola.equality.tester import EqualEqualityTester, get_default_registry
>>> class MyFloat:
...     def __init__(self, value: float) -> None:
...         self._value = float(value)
...     def equal(self, other: object) -> bool:
...         if type(other) is not type(self):
...             return False
...         return self._value == other._value
...
>>> engine = Engine(EqualityConfig())
>>> tester = EqualEqualityTester()
>>> tester.objects_are_equal(MyFloat(42), MyFloat(42), engine)
True
>>> tester.objects_are_equal(MyFloat(42), MyFloat(1), engine)
False

docs.title: coola.equality.EqualNanEqualityTester
docs.text:
Bases: BaseEqualityTester[object]

Implement an equality tester for objects with equal method that supports NaN equality.

This tester is designed for objects that implement an equal(other, equal_nan) method. The tester calls the equal method of the first object with equal_nan of the comparison. An object without a callable equal is different.

Example 
>>> import math
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.engine import Engine
>>> from coola.equality.tester import EqualNanEqualityTester, get_default_registry
>>> class MyFloat:
...     def __init__(self, value: float) -> None:
...         self._value = float(value)
...     def equal(self, other: object, equal_nan: bool = False) -> bool:
...         if type(other) is not type(self):
...             return False
...         if equal_nan and math.isnan(self._value) and math.isnan(other._value):
...             return True
...         return self._value == other._value
...
>>> registry = get_default_registry()
>>> tester = EqualNanEqualityTester()
>>> nan1, nan2 = MyFloat(float("nan")), MyFloat(float("nan"))
>>> tester.objects_are_equal(nan1, nan2, Engine(EqualityConfig()))
False
>>> tester.objects_are_equal(nan1, nan2, Engine(EqualityConfig(equal_nan=True)))
True

Define the config to control the comparison rules.

The config is immutable: it can be shared between comparisons and threads. The state of one comparison lives in the Engine.

create_default_registry() tolerance Tolerance

Tolerance() equal_nan bool

False max_depth int

docs.title: coola.equality.EqualityTesterRegistry
docs.text:
Bases: TypeRegistry[BaseEqualityTester[Any]]

Registry that manages and dispatches equality testers based on data type.

This registry maintains a mapping from Python types to equality tester instances and uses the Method Resolution Order (MRO) for type lookup. When checking equality, it automatically selects the most specific registered equality tester for the data's type, falling back to parent types or a default tester if needed.

The registry includes an internal cache for type lookups to optimize performance in applications that repeatedly check equality of similar data structures.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default initial_state dict[type, T] | None

Optional initial mapping of types to equality testers. If provided, the state is copied to prevent external mutations.

None

Attributes:

Name Type Description _state dict[K, V]

Internal mapping of registered types to equality testers

Example

Basic usage:

>>> from coola.equality.tester import (
...     EqualityTesterRegistry,
...     SequenceEqualityTester,
...     DefaultEqualityTester,
... )
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> registry = EqualityTesterRegistry(
...     {object: DefaultEqualityTester(), list: SequenceEqualityTester()}
... )
>>> registry
EqualityTesterRegistry(
  (<class 'object'>): DefaultEqualityTester()
  (<class 'list'>): SequenceEqualityTester()
)
>>> config = EqualityConfig()
>>> registry.objects_are_equal([1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 3], config=config)
True

docs.text:
find_equality_tester(
    data_type: type,
) -> BaseEqualityTester[Any]

Type-specific alias for find: find the appropriate equality tester for a given type.

See TypeRegistry.resolve for the full behavior description (MRO resolution, caching, and the KeyError on no match).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default data_type type

The Python type to find an equality tester for

required

Returns:

Type Description BaseEqualityTester[Any]

The most specific registered equality tester for this type, a parent

BaseEqualityTester[Any]

type's tester via MRO, or the default tester

Example 
>>> from collections.abc import Sequence
>>> from coola.equality.tester import (
...     EqualityTesterRegistry,
...     SequenceEqualityTester,
...     DefaultEqualityTester,
... )
>>> registry = EqualityTesterRegistry({object: DefaultEqualityTester()})
>>> registry.register(Sequence, SequenceEqualityTester())
>>> # Sequence is not in list's MRO, so the registry falls back to DefaultEqualityTester
>>> tester = registry.find_equality_tester(list)
>>> tester
DefaultEqualityTester()

docs.title: coola.equality.EqualityTesterRegistry.objects_are_equal
docs.text:
objects_are_equal(
    actual: object, expected: object, config: EqualityConfig
) -> bool

Check if two objects are equal by recursively comparing their structure.

This is the main entry point for equality checking. It automatically: 1. Determines the actual object's type 2. Finds the appropriate equality tester 3. Delegates to that tester's objects_are_equal method 4. The tester recursively processes nested structures

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default actual object

The actual object.

required expected object

The expected object.

required config EqualityConfig

The equality configuration.

required

Returns:

Type Description bool

True if the objects are equal according to the registered testers,

bool

False otherwise

Example

Checking if two lists of integers are equal:

>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.tester import get_default_registry
>>> registry = get_default_registry()
>>> config = EqualityConfig()
>>> registry.objects_are_equal([1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 3], config=config)
True

Checking if two lists of tensors are equal:

>>> import torch
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.tester import get_default_registry
>>> registry = get_default_registry()
>>> config = EqualityConfig()
>>> registry.objects_are_equal(
...     [torch.ones(2, 3), torch.zeros(2)],
...     [torch.ones(2, 3), torch.zeros(2)],
...     config=config,
... )
True

docs.title: coola.equality.JaxArrayEqualityTester
docs.text:
Bases: BaseEqualityTester[ndarray]

Implement an equality tester for jax.numpy.ndarray.

Two arrays are equal if they have the same data type, the same shape and equal elements. The numbers are compared with the tolerance and equal_nan of the comparison, and a boolean array is exact. The location of a difference is the index of the first element that differs. Without 64-bit mode, JAX has no float64: the tolerance is computed in the widest dtype JAX has.

Example 
>>> import jax.numpy as jnp
>>> from coola.equality import compare
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.engine import Engine
>>> from coola.equality.tester import JaxArrayEqualityTester, get_default_registry
>>> engine = Engine(EqualityConfig())
>>> tester = JaxArrayEqualityTester()
>>> tester.objects_are_equal(jnp.ones((2, 3)), jnp.ones((2, 3)), engine)
True
>>> tester.objects_are_equal(jnp.ones((2, 3)), jnp.zeros((2, 3)), engine)
False
>>> compare(jnp.ones((2, 3)), jnp.zeros((2, 3))).path
(0, 0)

docs.title: coola.equality.MappingEqualityTester
docs.text:
Bases: BaseEqualityTester['Mapping[Any, Any]']

Implement a mapping equality tester.

This tester handles dictionary-like objects (dict, Mapping ABC). The two mappings must have the same keys, and the values of the same key are compared in the order of actual. The keys are compared with their type, like the elements of sets: {1: "a"} and {True: "a"} are not the same mapping. With equal_nan=True, two NaN keys are the same key.

Example 
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.engine import Engine
>>> from coola.equality.tester import get_default_registry
>>> registry = get_default_registry()
>>> engine = Engine(EqualityConfig())
>>> engine.run({"a": 1, "b": 2}, {"a": 1, "b": 2})
True
>>> engine.run({"a": 1, "b": 2}, {"a": 1, "b": 4})
False

docs.title: coola.equality.NumpyArrayEqualityTester
docs.text:
Bases: BaseEqualityTester[ndarray]

Implement an equality tester for numpy.ndarray.

Two arrays are equal if they have the same data type, the same shape and equal elements. The numbers are compared with the tolerance and equal_nan of the comparison (a boolean, a string and an instant are exact; atol of a duration is a number of seconds). The elements of an object array are compared by the engine, one by one. The location of a difference is the index of the first element that differs (the position in the flattened array for an object array).

Example 
>>> import numpy as np
>>> from coola.equality import compare
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.engine import Engine
>>> from coola.equality.tester import NumpyArrayEqualityTester, get_default_registry
>>> engine = Engine(EqualityConfig())
>>> tester = NumpyArrayEqualityTester()
>>> tester.objects_are_equal(np.ones((2, 3)), np.ones((2, 3)), engine)
True
>>> tester.objects_are_equal(np.ones((2, 3)), np.zeros((2, 3)), engine)
False
>>> compare(np.ones((2, 3)), np.zeros((2, 3))).path
(0, 0)

docs.title: coola.equality.NumpyMaskedArrayEqualityTester
docs.text:
Bases: BaseEqualityTester[MaskedArray]

Implement an equality tester for numpy.ma.MaskedArray.

Two masked arrays are equal if they have the same data type, the same shape, the same data (the masked values are compared too), the same mask and the same fill_value. The location of a difference is .data, .mask or .fill_value, and then the index in the array.

Example 
>>> import numpy as np
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.engine import Engine
>>> from coola.equality.tester import get_default_registry
>>> engine = Engine(EqualityConfig())
>>> engine.run(
...     np.ma.array([1, 2, 3], mask=[0, 0, 1]), np.ma.array([1, 2, 3], mask=[0, 0, 1])
... )
True
>>> engine.run(
...     np.ma.array([1, 2, 3], mask=[0, 0, 1]), np.ma.array([1, 2, 3], mask=[0, 1, 1])
... )
False

docs.text:
Bases: BaseEqualityTester[object]

Implement an equality tester for numpy.timedelta64 and numpy.datetime64 scalars.

NaT is equal to NaT only if equal_nan is True. A numpy.timedelta64 is a duration: the tolerances apply (atol is a number of seconds). A numpy.datetime64 is an instant and is compared exactly.

Example 
>>> from coola.equality import Tolerance
>>> import numpy as np
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.engine import Engine
>>> from coola.equality.tester import NumpyTimeScalarEqualityTester, get_default_registry
>>> tester = NumpyTimeScalarEqualityTester()
>>> engine = Engine(EqualityConfig(tolerance=Tolerance(atol=1.0)))
>>> tester.objects_are_equal(np.timedelta64(1, "s"), np.timedelta64(2000, "ms"), engine)
True
>>> tester.objects_are_equal(
...     np.datetime64("2020-01-01"), np.datetime64("2020-01-02"), engine
... )
False

docs.title: coola.equality.ObjectAttributesEqualityTester
docs.text:
Bases: BaseEqualityTester[Any]

Implement an equality tester for objects without value semantics.

A plain class, an exception or a functools.partial is equal to another object only if it is the same object, unless the class defines __eq__. This tester compares the attributes instead: the entries of vars, the slots, the args of an exception and the content of a functools.partial (see get_object_attributes). The attributes are compared through the registry, so the tolerance and equal_nan apply to them.

It is not registered by default, because it changes the result for the classes that rely on the identity: register it for the classes that must be compared by their attributes. The two objects have the same type, the same attribute names and equal values. The location of a difference is the name of the attribute.

Example 
>>> from coola.equality import objects_are_equal
>>> from coola.equality.tester import (
...     DefaultEqualityTester,
...     EqualityTesterRegistry,
...     ObjectAttributesEqualityTester,
... )
>>> class Point:
...     def __init__(self, x):
...         self.x = x
...
>>> registry = EqualityTesterRegistry({object: DefaultEqualityTester()})
>>> objects_are_equal(Point(1), Point(1), registry=registry)
False
>>> registry.register(Point, ObjectAttributesEqualityTester())
>>> objects_are_equal(Point(1), Point(1), registry=registry)
True
>>> objects_are_equal(Point(1), Point(2), registry=registry)
False

docs.title: coola.equality.OrderedMappingEqualityTester
docs.text:
Bases: MappingEqualityTester

Implement an ordered mapping equality tester.

This tester behaves like MappingEqualityTester, and additionally requires the keys to be in the same order. It is registered for collections.OrderedDict, for which Python's == is also order-sensitive.

Example 
>>> from collections import OrderedDict
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.engine import Engine
>>> from coola.equality.tester import get_default_registry
>>> engine = Engine(EqualityConfig())
>>> engine.run(OrderedDict(a=1, b=2), OrderedDict(a=1, b=2))
True
>>> engine.run(OrderedDict(a=1, b=2), OrderedDict(b=2, a=1))
False

docs.title: coola.equality.PydanticModelEqualityTester
docs.text:
Bases: BaseEqualityTester[BaseModel]

Implement an equality tester for pydantic.BaseModel.

The two models must have the same type, the same field values and the same extra values. The values are compared with the registry, so they support the tolerance and equal_nan. The private attributes are not compared, as the fields are what the model validates and serializes. The other entries of the instance __dict__ (for example the value of a functools.cached_property that was read on one model only) are ignored too. The location of a difference is the name of the field, or model_extra.

Example 
>>> from pydantic import BaseModel
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.engine import Engine
>>> from coola.equality.tester import PydanticModelEqualityTester, get_default_registry
>>> class Point(BaseModel):
...     x: float
...     y: float
...
>>> engine = Engine(EqualityConfig())
>>> engine.run(Point(x=1.0, y=2.0), Point(x=1.0, y=2.0))
True
>>> engine.run(Point(x=1.0, y=2.0), Point(x=1.0, y=3.0))
False

docs.title: coola.equality.ScalarEqualityTester
docs.text:
Bases: BaseEqualityTester[float]

Implement a scalar equality tester.

This tester handles numeric scalar types (int, float, complex) with support for NaN equality and tolerance-based comparisons. Two NaNs are equal only if equal_nan is True, a bool and an enum member are labels and are compared exactly, and the other numbers are close if |a - b| <= atol + rtol * max(|a|, |b|).

This tester is registered for int, float and complex in the default registry.

Example 
>>> from coola.equality import Tolerance
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.engine import Engine
>>> from coola.equality.tester import ScalarEqualityTester, get_default_registry
>>> registry = get_default_registry()
>>> tester = ScalarEqualityTester()
>>> tester.objects_are_equal(42.0, 42.0, Engine(EqualityConfig()))
True
>>> tester.objects_are_equal(42.0, 1.0, Engine(EqualityConfig()))
False
>>> tester.objects_are_equal(42.0, 42.0001, Engine(EqualityConfig(tolerance=Tolerance(atol=1e-3))))
True

docs.title: coola.equality.SequenceEqualityTester
docs.text:
Bases: BaseEqualityTester['Sequence[Any]']

Implement a sequence equality tester.

This tester handles sequence types (list, tuple, deque, Sequence ABC). The two sequences must have the same length, and the items are compared in order. A sequence of exact scalars (int, str, bytes, bool and None) is compared at once.

Example 
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.engine import Engine
>>> from coola.equality.tester import get_default_registry
>>> engine = Engine(EqualityConfig())
>>> engine.run([1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 3])
True
>>> engine.run([1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 4])
False
>>> engine.run([1, 2, 3], [1, 2])
False

docs.title: coola.equality.SetEqualityTester
docs.text:
Bases: BaseEqualityTester['AbstractSet[Any]']

Implement a set equality tester.

This tester handles set and frozenset. Unlike ==, the elements are matched by hash and type, so equal_nan applies to them (the tolerance does not). The location of a difference is the element of actual that has no match in expected.

Example 
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.engine import Engine
>>> from coola.equality.tester import get_default_registry
>>> engine = Engine(EqualityConfig())
>>> engine.run({1, 2, 3}, {1, 2, 3})
True
>>> engine.run({1, 2, 3}, {1, 2, 4})
False

docs.title: coola.equality.TableEqualityTester
docs.text:
Bases: BaseEqualityTester[Any]

Implement an equality tester for the tables of pandas, polars and pyarrow.

The structure is compared first, then the columns one by one, each by its kind (see Column). The comparison stops at the first column that differs. A table is a leaf for the engine: the difference is reported as a whole, with the name of the first column that differs, and no row. The user finds the row with the tools of the library (DataFrame.compare, polars.testing, Table.equals).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default adapter Callable[[Any], Table]

The function that converts an object to a Table.

required Example 
>>> import pandas as pd
>>> from coola.equality import compare
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.engine import Engine
>>> from coola.equality.tester import TableEqualityTester, get_default_registry
>>> from coola.equality.tester.pandas import pandas_frame
>>> engine = Engine(EqualityConfig())
>>> tester = TableEqualityTester(pandas_frame)
>>> tester.objects_are_equal(
...     pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2]}), pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2]}), engine
... )
True
>>> tester.objects_are_equal(
...     pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2]}), pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 3]}), engine
... )
False
>>> print(compare(pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2]}), pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 3]})).reason)
tables have different values: column 'a' differs

docs.text:
Define the tolerance of a comparison.

Two numbers actual and expected are close if |actual - expected| <= atol + rtol * max(|actual|, |expected|) (the numpy.isclose rule made symmetric). The default is no tolerance (exact comparison).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default rtol float

The relative tolerance parameter. Must be non-negative and finite. Defaults to 0.0.

0.0 atol float

The absolute tolerance parameter. Must be non-negative and finite. Defaults to 0.0.

0.0

Raises:

Type Description TypeError

If rtol or atol is not a real number (a bool is rejected).

ValueError

If rtol or atol is negative or not finite.

Example

>>> Tolerance()
Tolerance(rtol=0.0, atol=0.0)
>>> Tolerance.numpy_default()

docs.title: coola.equality.TolerantEqualEqualityTester
docs.text:
Bases: BaseEqualityTester[object]

Implement an equality tester for objects that support both allclose and equal methods.

This tester is designed for objects that implement both an allclose(other, rtol, atol, equal_nan) method for tolerance-based comparison and an equal(other, equal_nan) method for exact comparison. The tester calls allclose when a tolerance is not zero, otherwise equal. An object that does not have both methods is different.

Example 
>>> from coola.equality import Tolerance
>>> import math
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.engine import Engine
>>> from coola.equality.tester import TolerantEqualEqualityTester, get_default_registry
>>> class MyFloat:
...     def __init__(self, value: float) -> None:
...         self._value = float(value)
...     def allclose(
...         self,
...         other: object,
...         rtol: float = 1e-5,
...         atol: float = 1e-8,
...         equal_nan: bool = False,
...     ) -> bool:
...         if type(other) is not type(self):
...             return False
...         if equal_nan and math.isnan(self._value) and math.isnan(other._value):
...             return True
...         return math.isclose(self._value, other._value, rel_tol=rtol, abs_tol=atol)
...     def equal(self, other: object, equal_nan: bool = False) -> bool:
...         if type(other) is not type(self):
...             return False
...         if equal_nan and math.isnan(self._value) and math.isnan(other._value):
...             return True
...         return self._value == other._value
...
>>> registry = get_default_registry()
>>> tester = TolerantEqualEqualityTester()
>>> tester.objects_are_equal(MyFloat(42), MyFloat(42), Engine(EqualityConfig()))
True
>>> tester.objects_are_equal(MyFloat(1.0), MyFloat(1.4), Engine(EqualityConfig()))
False
>>> tester.objects_are_equal(
...     MyFloat(1.0), MyFloat(1.4), Engine(EqualityConfig(tolerance=Tolerance(atol=0.5)))
... )
True

docs.title: coola.equality.TorchPackedSequenceEqualityTester
docs.text:
Bases: BaseEqualityTester[PackedSequence]

Implement an equality tester for torch.nn.utils.rnn.PackedSequence.

This tester compares the data tensor and the metadata of two packed sequences: batch_sizes, sorted_indices and unsorted_indices. The location of a difference is the name of the attribute.

Example 
>>> import torch
>>> from torch.nn.utils.rnn import pack_padded_sequence
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.engine import Engine
>>> from coola.equality.tester import get_default_registry
>>> engine = Engine(EqualityConfig())
>>> def make(value):
...     return pack_padded_sequence(
...         torch.tensor([[1.0, value], [3.0, 4.0]]),
...         lengths=torch.tensor([2, 1]),
...         batch_first=True,
...         enforce_sorted=False,
...     )
...
>>> engine.run(make(2.0), make(2.0))
True
>>> engine.run(make(2.0), make(5.0))
False

docs.title: coola.equality.TorchTensorEqualityTester
docs.text:
Bases: BaseEqualityTester[Tensor]

Implement an equality tester for torch.Tensor.

Two tensors are equal if they have the same data type, shape, device, layout and equal elements. The numbers are compared with the tolerance and equal_nan of the comparison, and a boolean tensor is exact. The tensors on the meta device have no data: only the metadata is compared. The location of a difference is the index of the first element that differs.

Example 
>>> import torch
>>> from coola.equality import compare
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.engine import Engine
>>> from coola.equality.tester import TorchTensorEqualityTester, get_default_registry
>>> engine = Engine(EqualityConfig())
>>> tester = TorchTensorEqualityTester()
>>> tester.objects_are_equal(torch.ones(2, 3), torch.ones(2, 3), engine)
True
>>> tester.objects_are_equal(torch.ones(2, 3), torch.zeros(2, 3), engine)
False
>>> compare(torch.ones(2, 3), torch.zeros(2, 3)).path
(0, 0)

docs.title: coola.equality.compare
docs.text:
compare(
    actual: object,
    expected: object,
    *,
    rtol: float = 0.0,
    atol: float = 0.0,
    equal_nan: bool = False,
    max_depth: int = 100,
    registry: EqualityTesterRegistry | None = None,
) -> ComparisonResult

Compare two objects and explain the first difference.

Exact equality is used by default. Set rtol or atol to compare within a tolerance: rtol=1e-5 and atol=1e-8 are the defaults of objects_are_allclose. Comparison stops at the first difference, and only this difference is explained.

Note

The difference is the first failure recorded by the engine (ctx.fail of a tester). Nothing is logged, and no global state is modified, so this function can be called concurrently from several threads.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default actual object

The actual object.

required expected object

The expected object.

required rtol float

The relative tolerance parameter. Must be non-negative.

0.0 atol float

The absolute tolerance parameter. Must be non-negative.

0.0 equal_nan bool

If True, treat two NaN values as equal.

False max_depth int

The nesting limit: the maximum nesting level of the compared objects. A deeper structure raises MaxDepthExceededError (it is not a display depth like the max_depth of summarize). Must be positive. See the "Common options" section of the equality user guide. Defaults to 100.

100 registry EqualityTesterRegistry | None

Registry used to resolve type-specific equality testers. If None, the default registry is used.

None

Returns:

Type Description ComparisonResult

The comparison result.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If rtol or atol is negative, or if max_depth is not positive.

MaxDepthExceededError

If the nesting of the objects exceeds max_depth.

Example 
>>> from coola.equality import compare
>>> compare([1, 2], [1, 2]).equal
True
>>> result = compare({"a": 1}, {"a": 2})
>>> result.path
('a',)
>>> result.equal
False
>>> compare(1.0, 1.0 + 1e-9).equal
False
>>> compare(1.0, 1.0 + 1e-9, rtol=1e-5, atol=1e-8).equal
True

docs.title: coola.equality.get_default_registry
docs.text:
get_default_registry() -> EqualityTesterRegistry

Get or create the default global registry with common Python types.

Returns a singleton registry instance that is pre-configured with equality testers for Python's built-in types including sequences (list, tuple), mappings (dict), and scalar types (int, float).

This function uses a singleton pattern to ensure the same registry instance is returned on subsequent calls, which is efficient and maintains consistency across an application.

Returns:

Type Description EqualityTesterRegistry

A EqualityTesterRegistry instance with equality testers registered for: - Scalar types (int, float) - Sequences (list, tuple, deque, array.array, Sequence ABC) - Mappings (dict, OrderedDict, MappingProxyType, Mapping ABC) - Third-party library types (numpy, torch, pandas, polars, jax, xarray, pyarrow)

Notes

The singleton pattern means modifications to the returned registry affect all future calls to this function. If you need an isolated registry, create a new EqualityTesterRegistry instance directly.

Example 
>>> from coola.equality.tester import get_default_registry
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> registry = get_default_registry()
>>> # Registry is ready to use with common Python types
>>> config = EqualityConfig()
>>> registry.objects_are_equal([1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 3], config)
True
>>> registry.objects_are_equal([1, 2, 3], [1, 1], config)
False

docs.title: coola.equality.objects_are_allclose
docs.text:
objects_are_allclose(
    actual: object,
    expected: object,
    *,
    rtol: float = 1e-05,
    atol: float = 1e-08,
    equal_nan: bool = False,
    max_depth: int = 100,
    registry: EqualityTesterRegistry | None = None,
) -> bool

Indicate if two objects are equal within a tolerance.

Note

The types are compared first, so 1 and 1.0 are different (as are [1] and [1.0]), even with a tolerance. A boolean is a label, not a quantity: True and False are never close, even with atol=1 (also for numpy.bool_ and for boolean arrays).

An object is always equal to itself, even if it contains NaN and equal_nan=False: [n] equals [n] for n = float("nan"), but not [float("nan")]. Two distinct objects that contain NaN are equal only with equal_nan=True.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default actual object

The actual object.

required expected object

The expected object.

required rtol float

The relative tolerance parameter. Must be non-negative.

1e-05 atol float

The absolute tolerance parameter. Must be non-negative.

1e-08 equal_nan bool

If True, treat two NaN values as equal.

False max_depth int

The nesting limit: the maximum nesting level of the compared objects. A deeper structure raises MaxDepthExceededError (it is not a display depth like the max_depth of summarize). Must be positive. See the "Common options" section of the equality user guide. Defaults to 100.

100 registry EqualityTesterRegistry | None

Registry used to resolve type-specific equality testers. If None, the default registry is used.

None

Returns:

Type Description bool

True if the two objects are equal within tolerances, otherwise

bool

False.

Raises:

Type Description TypeError

If rtol or atol is not a real number, or if max_depth is not an int (a bool is rejected).

ValueError

If rtol or atol is negative, or if max_depth is not positive.

MaxDepthExceededError

If the nesting of the objects exceeds max_depth.

Example 
>>> from coola.equality import objects_are_allclose
>>> objects_are_allclose([1.0, 2.0], [1.0 + 1e-8, 2.0])
True
>>> objects_are_allclose([1.0, 2.0], [1.0, 2.1], atol=1e-3, rtol=0.0)
False
>>> objects_are_allclose([float("nan")], [float("nan")], equal_nan=False)
False
>>> objects_are_allclose([float("nan")], [float("nan")], equal_nan=True)
True

docs.title: coola.equality.engine
docs.text:
Implement the engine that runs a comparison with an explicit stack.

The engine owns the invariants of a comparison: identity, strict type, depth, cycles and the location of the first difference. A tester that uses the engine never recurses: it returns a verdict, or the child pairs that must all be equal.

docs.title: coola.equality.engine.Element dataclass
docs.text:
Location of an element of a set in the path of a difference.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default value object

The element.

required Example 
>>> from coola.equality import Element
>>> Element(2)
Element(value=2)

docs.title: coola.equality.engine.Engine
docs.text:
Run the comparison of two objects.

One engine runs one comparison. For each pair of objects, the engine checks the identity, the strict type, finds the tester (the lookup is cached for the call) and calls it. A tester that uses the engine returns either a bool (the verdict) or an iterator of (actual, expected, path part) child pairs that must all be equal. The iterators are kept on an explicit stack, depth first, so the first difference in iteration order is the one found and nothing after it is visited. The stack use is constant: there is no RecursionError whatever the nesting.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default config EqualityConfig

The settings of the comparison (the registry that finds the tester of a type, the tolerance, equal_nan and max_depth). A config is immutable and can be shared.

required explaining bool

If True, the reasons are built and the first difference is recorded in failure.

False

Attributes:

Name Type Description atol

The absolute tolerance.

rtol

The relative tolerance.

equal_nan

If True, two NaNs are equal.

explaining

If True, the reasons are built.

failure tuple[tuple[object, ...], str | None] | None

None or, after a difference was found, the pair (path, reason) of the first difference.

Example 
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.engine import Engine
>>> Engine(EqualityConfig()).run([1, {"a": 2}], [1, {"a": 2}])
True
>>> Engine(EqualityConfig()).run([1, {"a": 2}], [1, {"a": 3}])
False

docs.title: coola.equality.tester
docs.text:
Type-aware equality testers used by coola.equality.

This package exposes a registry-based dispatch system with built-in testers for common Python containers and optional scientific types. Extend the default behavior by registering custom testers in the default registry.

Example 
>>> from coola.equality.tester import get_default_registry
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> registry = get_default_registry()
>>> config = EqualityConfig()
>>> # Compare lists with nested structures
>>> registry.objects_are_equal([1, {"a": 2}], [1, {"a": 2}], config)
True

docs.title: coola.equality.tester.BaseEqualityTester
docs.text:
Bases: InlineDisplayMixin, ABC, Generic[T]

Define the base class to implement an equality operator.

The engine owns the invariants of a comparison (identity, strict type, depth, cycles, location of the first difference). A tester never recurses: objects_are_equal receives the two objects, which have the same type, and the engine, and returns

  • a verdict: True, or ctx.fail(reason, *path) (which returns False) for a leaf;
  • or the child pairs (actual, expected, path part) that must all be equal, produced lazily and in the order the first difference is wanted, for a container.

Two testers are equal if they have the same type and the same attributes. A child class with parameters must override _display_fields.

Example 
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.engine import Engine
>>> from coola.equality.tester import BaseEqualityTester, get_default_registry
>>> class PointTester(BaseEqualityTester[tuple]):
...     def objects_are_equal(self, actual, expected, ctx):
...         return ((actual[0], expected[0], 0), (actual[1], expected[1], 1))
...
>>> registry = get_default_registry().copy()
>>> registry.register(tuple, PointTester(), exist_ok=True)
>>> Engine(EqualityConfig(registry=registry)).run((1, 2), (1, 2))
True
>>> Engine(EqualityConfig(registry=registry)).run((1, 2), (1, 3))
False
>>> PointTester() == PointTester()
True

>>> import numpy as np

docs.title: coola.equality.tester.DataclassEqualityTester
docs.text:
Bases: BaseEqualityTester[Any]

Implement an equality tester for dataclass instances.

The two instances have the same type, and the tester compares their fields, in the order of declaration. The fields with compare=False are ignored. The fields are compared with the engine, so they support the tolerance and equal_nan, and the location of a difference is the name of the field.

Example 
>>> from dataclasses import dataclass
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.engine import Engine
>>> from coola.equality.tester import get_default_registry
>>> @dataclass
... class Point:
...     x: float
...
>>> engine = Engine(EqualityConfig())
>>> engine.run(Point(1.0), Point(1.0))
True
>>> engine.run(Point(1.0), Point(2.0))
False

docs.title: coola.equality.tester.DefaultEqualityTester
docs.text:
Bases: BaseEqualityTester[object]

Implement a default equality tester.

This tester serves as the fallback for types without specialized equality testers. It uses Python's built-in == operator to test equality between two objects of the same type. The engine checks the identity and the type before the tester is called.

This tester is registered for the object type in the default registry, making it the catch-all for unregistered types via Python's MRO.

Raises:

Type Description TypeError

if == raises a TypeError or a ValueError, or returns a value that cannot be converted to a bool (for example an array). False would claim that the objects are different when they were not compared at all.

Example 
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.engine import Engine
>>> from coola.equality.tester import DefaultEqualityTester, get_default_registry
>>> engine = Engine(EqualityConfig())
>>> tester = DefaultEqualityTester()
>>> tester.objects_are_equal("meow", "meow", engine)
True
>>> tester.objects_are_equal("meow", "meov", engine)
False

docs.title: coola.equality.tester.DifferenceCloseEqualityTester
docs.text:
Bases: BaseEqualityTester[Any]

Implement an equality tester for decimal.Decimal, fractions.Fraction and datetime.timedelta.

These types have no allclose, so the tester compares their difference with the tolerance (see difference_close). A Decimal NaN is equal to a NaN only if equal_nan is True, and atol of a timedelta is a number of seconds.

This tester is registered for Decimal, Fraction and timedelta in the default registry.

Example 
>>> from coola.equality import Tolerance
>>> from decimal import Decimal
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.engine import Engine
>>> from coola.equality.tester import DifferenceCloseEqualityTester, get_default_registry
>>> registry = get_default_registry()
>>> tester = DifferenceCloseEqualityTester()
>>> tester.objects_are_equal(
...     Decimal("1.0"), Decimal("1.00001"), Engine(EqualityConfig())
... )
False
>>> tester.objects_are_equal(
...     Decimal("1.0"), Decimal("1.00001"), Engine(EqualityConfig(tolerance=Tolerance(atol=1e-3)))
... )
True

docs.title: coola.equality.tester.EqualEqualityTester
docs.text:
Bases: BaseEqualityTester[object]

Implement an equality tester for objects with equal method.

This tester is designed for objects that implement an equal(other) method for equality comparison. The two objects have the same type (the engine checks it) and the tester calls the equal method of the first one. An object without a callable equal is different.

Example 
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.engine import Engine
>>> from coola.equality.tester import EqualEqualityTester, get_default_registry
>>> class MyFloat:
...     def __init__(self, value: float) -> None:
...         self._value = float(value)
...     def equal(self, other: object) -> bool:
...         if type(other) is not type(self):
...             return False
...         return self._value == other._value
...
>>> engine = Engine(EqualityConfig())
>>> tester = EqualEqualityTester()
>>> tester.objects_are_equal(MyFloat(42), MyFloat(42), engine)
True
>>> tester.objects_are_equal(MyFloat(42), MyFloat(1), engine)
False

docs.title: coola.equality.tester.EqualNanEqualityTester
docs.text:
Bases: BaseEqualityTester[object]

Implement an equality tester for objects with equal method that supports NaN equality.

This tester is designed for objects that implement an equal(other, equal_nan) method. The tester calls the equal method of the first object with equal_nan of the comparison. An object without a callable equal is different.

Example 
>>> import math
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.engine import Engine
>>> from coola.equality.tester import EqualNanEqualityTester, get_default_registry
>>> class MyFloat:
...     def __init__(self, value: float) -> None:
...         self._value = float(value)
...     def equal(self, other: object, equal_nan: bool = False) -> bool:
...         if type(other) is not type(self):
...             return False
...         if equal_nan and math.isnan(self._value) and math.isnan(other._value):
...             return True
...         return self._value == other._value
...
>>> registry = get_default_registry()
>>> tester = EqualNanEqualityTester()
>>> nan1, nan2 = MyFloat(float("nan")), MyFloat(float("nan"))
>>> tester.objects_are_equal(nan1, nan2, Engine(EqualityConfig()))
False
>>> tester.objects_are_equal(nan1, nan2, Engine(EqualityConfig(equal_nan=True)))
True

docs.title: coola.equality.tester.EqualityTesterRegistry
docs.text:
Bases: TypeRegistry[BaseEqualityTester[Any]]

Registry that manages and dispatches equality testers based on data type.

This registry maintains a mapping from Python types to equality tester instances and uses the Method Resolution Order (MRO) for type lookup. When checking equality, it automatically selects the most specific registered equality tester for the data's type, falling back to parent types or a default tester if needed.

The registry includes an internal cache for type lookups to optimize performance in applications that repeatedly check equality of similar data structures.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default initial_state dict[type, T] | None

Optional initial mapping of types to equality testers. If provided, the state is copied to prevent external mutations.

None

Attributes:

Name Type Description _state dict[K, V]

Internal mapping of registered types to equality testers

Example

Basic usage:

>>> from coola.equality.tester import (
...     EqualityTesterRegistry,
...     SequenceEqualityTester,
...     DefaultEqualityTester,
... )
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> registry = EqualityTesterRegistry(
...     {object: DefaultEqualityTester(), list: SequenceEqualityTester()}
... )
>>> registry
EqualityTesterRegistry(
  (<class 'object'>): DefaultEqualityTester()
  (<class 'list'>): SequenceEqualityTester()
)
>>> config = EqualityConfig()
>>> registry.objects_are_equal([1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 3], config=config)
True

docs.title: coola.equality.tester.EqualityTesterRegistry.find_equality_tester
docs.text:
find_equality_tester(
    data_type: type,
) -> BaseEqualityTester[Any]

Type-specific alias for find: find the appropriate equality tester for a given type.

See TypeRegistry.resolve for the full behavior description (MRO resolution, caching, and the KeyError on no match).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default data_type type

The Python type to find an equality tester for

required

Returns:

Type Description BaseEqualityTester[Any]

The most specific registered equality tester for this type, a parent

BaseEqualityTester[Any]

type's tester via MRO, or the default tester

Example 
>>> from collections.abc import Sequence
>>> from coola.equality.tester import (
...     EqualityTesterRegistry,
...     SequenceEqualityTester,
...     DefaultEqualityTester,
... )
>>> registry = EqualityTesterRegistry({object: DefaultEqualityTester()})
>>> registry.register(Sequence, SequenceEqualityTester())
>>> # Sequence is not in list's MRO, so the registry falls back to DefaultEqualityTester
>>> tester = registry.find_equality_tester(list)
>>> tester
DefaultEqualityTester()

docs.title: coola.equality.tester.EqualityTesterRegistry.objects_are_equal
docs.text:
objects_are_equal(
    actual: object, expected: object, config: EqualityConfig
) -> bool

Check if two objects are equal by recursively comparing their structure.

This is the main entry point for equality checking. It automatically: 1. Determines the actual object's type 2. Finds the appropriate equality tester 3. Delegates to that tester's objects_are_equal method 4. The tester recursively processes nested structures

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default actual object

The actual object.

required expected object

The expected object.

required config EqualityConfig

The equality configuration.

required

Returns:

Type Description bool

True if the objects are equal according to the registered testers,

bool

False otherwise

Example

Checking if two lists of integers are equal:

>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.tester import get_default_registry
>>> registry = get_default_registry()
>>> config = EqualityConfig()
>>> registry.objects_are_equal([1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 3], config=config)
True

Checking if two lists of tensors are equal:

>>> import torch
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.tester import get_default_registry
>>> registry = get_default_registry()
>>> config = EqualityConfig()
>>> registry.objects_are_equal(
...     [torch.ones(2, 3), torch.zeros(2)],
...     [torch.ones(2, 3), torch.zeros(2)],
...     config=config,
... )
True

docs.title: coola.equality.tester.JaxArrayEqualityTester
docs.text:
Bases: BaseEqualityTester[ndarray]

Implement an equality tester for jax.numpy.ndarray.

Two arrays are equal if they have the same data type, the same shape and equal elements. The numbers are compared with the tolerance and equal_nan of the comparison, and a boolean array is exact. The location of a difference is the index of the first element that differs. Without 64-bit mode, JAX has no float64: the tolerance is computed in the widest dtype JAX has.

Example 
>>> import jax.numpy as jnp
>>> from coola.equality import compare
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.engine import Engine
>>> from coola.equality.tester import JaxArrayEqualityTester, get_default_registry
>>> engine = Engine(EqualityConfig())
>>> tester = JaxArrayEqualityTester()
>>> tester.objects_are_equal(jnp.ones((2, 3)), jnp.ones((2, 3)), engine)
True
>>> tester.objects_are_equal(jnp.ones((2, 3)), jnp.zeros((2, 3)), engine)
False
>>> compare(jnp.ones((2, 3)), jnp.zeros((2, 3))).path
(0, 0)

docs.title: coola.equality.tester.MappingEqualityTester
docs.text:
Bases: BaseEqualityTester['Mapping[Any, Any]']

Implement a mapping equality tester.

This tester handles dictionary-like objects (dict, Mapping ABC). The two mappings must have the same keys, and the values of the same key are compared in the order of actual. The keys are compared with their type, like the elements of sets: {1: "a"} and {True: "a"} are not the same mapping. With equal_nan=True, two NaN keys are the same key.

Example 
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.engine import Engine
>>> from coola.equality.tester import get_default_registry
>>> registry = get_default_registry()
>>> engine = Engine(EqualityConfig())
>>> engine.run({"a": 1, "b": 2}, {"a": 1, "b": 2})
True
>>> engine.run({"a": 1, "b": 2}, {"a": 1, "b": 4})
False

docs.title: coola.equality.tester.NumpyArrayEqualityTester
docs.text:
Bases: BaseEqualityTester[ndarray]

Implement an equality tester for numpy.ndarray.

Two arrays are equal if they have the same data type, the same shape and equal elements. The numbers are compared with the tolerance and equal_nan of the comparison (a boolean, a string and an instant are exact; atol of a duration is a number of seconds). The elements of an object array are compared by the engine, one by one. The location of a difference is the index of the first element that differs (the position in the flattened array for an object array).

Example 
>>> import numpy as np
>>> from coola.equality import compare
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.engine import Engine
>>> from coola.equality.tester import NumpyArrayEqualityTester, get_default_registry
>>> engine = Engine(EqualityConfig())
>>> tester = NumpyArrayEqualityTester()
>>> tester.objects_are_equal(np.ones((2, 3)), np.ones((2, 3)), engine)
True
>>> tester.objects_are_equal(np.ones((2, 3)), np.zeros((2, 3)), engine)
False
>>> compare(np.ones((2, 3)), np.zeros((2, 3))).path
(0, 0)

docs.title: coola.equality.tester.NumpyMaskedArrayEqualityTester
docs.text:
Bases: BaseEqualityTester[MaskedArray]

Implement an equality tester for numpy.ma.MaskedArray.

Two masked arrays are equal if they have the same data type, the same shape, the same data (the masked values are compared too), the same mask and the same fill_value. The location of a difference is .data, .mask or .fill_value, and then the index in the array.

Example 
>>> import numpy as np
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.engine import Engine
>>> from coola.equality.tester import get_default_registry
>>> engine = Engine(EqualityConfig())
>>> engine.run(
...     np.ma.array([1, 2, 3], mask=[0, 0, 1]), np.ma.array([1, 2, 3], mask=[0, 0, 1])
... )
True
>>> engine.run(
...     np.ma.array([1, 2, 3], mask=[0, 0, 1]), np.ma.array([1, 2, 3], mask=[0, 1, 1])
... )
False

docs.title: coola.equality.tester.NumpyTimeScalarEqualityTester
docs.text:
Bases: BaseEqualityTester[object]

Implement an equality tester for numpy.timedelta64 and numpy.datetime64 scalars.

NaT is equal to NaT only if equal_nan is True. A numpy.timedelta64 is a duration: the tolerances apply (atol is a number of seconds). A numpy.datetime64 is an instant and is compared exactly.

Example 
>>> from coola.equality import Tolerance
>>> import numpy as np
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.engine import Engine
>>> from coola.equality.tester import NumpyTimeScalarEqualityTester, get_default_registry
>>> tester = NumpyTimeScalarEqualityTester()
>>> engine = Engine(EqualityConfig(tolerance=Tolerance(atol=1.0)))
>>> tester.objects_are_equal(np.timedelta64(1, "s"), np.timedelta64(2000, "ms"), engine)
True
>>> tester.objects_are_equal(
...     np.datetime64("2020-01-01"), np.datetime64("2020-01-02"), engine
... )
False

docs.title: coola.equality.tester.ObjectAttributesEqualityTester
docs.text:
Bases: BaseEqualityTester[Any]

Implement an equality tester for objects without value semantics.

A plain class, an exception or a functools.partial is equal to another object only if it is the same object, unless the class defines __eq__. This tester compares the attributes instead: the entries of vars, the slots, the args of an exception and the content of a functools.partial (see get_object_attributes). The attributes are compared through the registry, so the tolerance and equal_nan apply to them.

It is not registered by default, because it changes the result for the classes that rely on the identity: register it for the classes that must be compared by their attributes. The two objects have the same type, the same attribute names and equal values. The location of a difference is the name of the attribute.

Example 
>>> from coola.equality import objects_are_equal
>>> from coola.equality.tester import (
...     DefaultEqualityTester,
...     EqualityTesterRegistry,
...     ObjectAttributesEqualityTester,
... )
>>> class Point:
...     def __init__(self, x):
...         self.x = x
...
>>> registry = EqualityTesterRegistry({object: DefaultEqualityTester()})
>>> objects_are_equal(Point(1), Point(1), registry=registry)
False
>>> registry.register(Point, ObjectAttributesEqualityTester())
>>> objects_are_equal(Point(1), Point(1), registry=registry)
True
>>> objects_are_equal(Point(1), Point(2), registry=registry)
False

docs.title: coola.equality.tester.OrderedMappingEqualityTester
docs.text:
Bases: MappingEqualityTester

Implement an ordered mapping equality tester.

This tester behaves like MappingEqualityTester, and additionally requires the keys to be in the same order. It is registered for collections.OrderedDict, for which Python's == is also order-sensitive.

Example 
>>> from collections import OrderedDict
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.engine import Engine
>>> from coola.equality.tester import get_default_registry
>>> engine = Engine(EqualityConfig())
>>> engine.run(OrderedDict(a=1, b=2), OrderedDict(a=1, b=2))
True
>>> engine.run(OrderedDict(a=1, b=2), OrderedDict(b=2, a=1))
False

docs.title: coola.equality.tester.PydanticModelEqualityTester
docs.text:
Bases: BaseEqualityTester[BaseModel]

Implement an equality tester for pydantic.BaseModel.

The two models must have the same type, the same field values and the same extra values. The values are compared with the registry, so they support the tolerance and equal_nan. The private attributes are not compared, as the fields are what the model validates and serializes. The other entries of the instance __dict__ (for example the value of a functools.cached_property that was read on one model only) are ignored too. The location of a difference is the name of the field, or model_extra.

Example 
>>> from pydantic import BaseModel
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.engine import Engine
>>> from coola.equality.tester import PydanticModelEqualityTester, get_default_registry
>>> class Point(BaseModel):
...     x: float
...     y: float
...
>>> engine = Engine(EqualityConfig())
>>> engine.run(Point(x=1.0, y=2.0), Point(x=1.0, y=2.0))
True
>>> engine.run(Point(x=1.0, y=2.0), Point(x=1.0, y=3.0))
False

docs.title: coola.equality.tester.ScalarEqualityTester
docs.text:
Bases: BaseEqualityTester[float]

Implement a scalar equality tester.

This tester handles numeric scalar types (int, float, complex) with support for NaN equality and tolerance-based comparisons. Two NaNs are equal only if equal_nan is True, a bool and an enum member are labels and are compared exactly, and the other numbers are close if |a - b| <= atol + rtol * max(|a|, |b|).

This tester is registered for int, float and complex in the default registry.

Example 
>>> from coola.equality import Tolerance
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.engine import Engine
>>> from coola.equality.tester import ScalarEqualityTester, get_default_registry
>>> registry = get_default_registry()
>>> tester = ScalarEqualityTester()
>>> tester.objects_are_equal(42.0, 42.0, Engine(EqualityConfig()))
True
>>> tester.objects_are_equal(42.0, 1.0, Engine(EqualityConfig()))
False
>>> tester.objects_are_equal(42.0, 42.0001, Engine(EqualityConfig(tolerance=Tolerance(atol=1e-3))))
True

docs.title: coola.equality.tester.SequenceEqualityTester
docs.text:
Bases: BaseEqualityTester['Sequence[Any]']

Implement a sequence equality tester.

This tester handles sequence types (list, tuple, deque, Sequence ABC). The two sequences must have the same length, and the items are compared in order. A sequence of exact scalars (int, str, bytes, bool and None) is compared at once.

Example 
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.engine import Engine
>>> from coola.equality.tester import get_default_registry
>>> engine = Engine(EqualityConfig())
>>> engine.run([1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 3])
True
>>> engine.run([1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 4])
False
>>> engine.run([1, 2, 3], [1, 2])
False

docs.title: coola.equality.tester.SetEqualityTester
docs.text:
Bases: BaseEqualityTester['AbstractSet[Any]']

Implement a set equality tester.

This tester handles set and frozenset. Unlike ==, the elements are matched by hash and type, so equal_nan applies to them (the tolerance does not). The location of a difference is the element of actual that has no match in expected.

Example 
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.engine import Engine
>>> from coola.equality.tester import get_default_registry
>>> engine = Engine(EqualityConfig())
>>> engine.run({1, 2, 3}, {1, 2, 3})
True
>>> engine.run({1, 2, 3}, {1, 2, 4})
False

docs.title: coola.equality.tester.TableEqualityTester
docs.text:
Bases: BaseEqualityTester[Any]

Implement an equality tester for the tables of pandas, polars and pyarrow.

The structure is compared first, then the columns one by one, each by its kind (see Column). The comparison stops at the first column that differs. A table is a leaf for the engine: the difference is reported as a whole, with the name of the first column that differs, and no row. The user finds the row with the tools of the library (DataFrame.compare, polars.testing, Table.equals).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default adapter Callable[[Any], Table]

The function that converts an object to a Table.

required Example 
>>> import pandas as pd
>>> from coola.equality import compare
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.engine import Engine
>>> from coola.equality.tester import TableEqualityTester, get_default_registry
>>> from coola.equality.tester.pandas import pandas_frame
>>> engine = Engine(EqualityConfig())
>>> tester = TableEqualityTester(pandas_frame)
>>> tester.objects_are_equal(
...     pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2]}), pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2]}), engine
... )
True
>>> tester.objects_are_equal(
...     pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2]}), pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 3]}), engine
... )
False
>>> print(compare(pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2]}), pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 3]})).reason)
tables have different values: column 'a' differs

docs.title: coola.equality.tester.TolerantEqualEqualityTester
docs.text:
Bases: BaseEqualityTester[object]

Implement an equality tester for objects that support both allclose and equal methods.

This tester is designed for objects that implement both an allclose(other, rtol, atol, equal_nan) method for tolerance-based comparison and an equal(other, equal_nan) method for exact comparison. The tester calls allclose when a tolerance is not zero, otherwise equal. An object that does not have both methods is different.

Example 
>>> from coola.equality import Tolerance
>>> import math
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.engine import Engine
>>> from coola.equality.tester import TolerantEqualEqualityTester, get_default_registry
>>> class MyFloat:
...     def __init__(self, value: float) -> None:
...         self._value = float(value)
...     def allclose(
...         self,
...         other: object,
...         rtol: float = 1e-5,
...         atol: float = 1e-8,
...         equal_nan: bool = False,
...     ) -> bool:
...         if type(other) is not type(self):
...             return False
...         if equal_nan and math.isnan(self._value) and math.isnan(other._value):
...             return True
...         return math.isclose(self._value, other._value, rel_tol=rtol, abs_tol=atol)
...     def equal(self, other: object, equal_nan: bool = False) -> bool:
...         if type(other) is not type(self):
...             return False
...         if equal_nan and math.isnan(self._value) and math.isnan(other._value):
...             return True
...         return self._value == other._value
...
>>> registry = get_default_registry()
>>> tester = TolerantEqualEqualityTester()
>>> tester.objects_are_equal(MyFloat(42), MyFloat(42), Engine(EqualityConfig()))
True
>>> tester.objects_are_equal(MyFloat(1.0), MyFloat(1.4), Engine(EqualityConfig()))
False
>>> tester.objects_are_equal(
...     MyFloat(1.0), MyFloat(1.4), Engine(EqualityConfig(tolerance=Tolerance(atol=0.5)))
... )
True

docs.title: coola.equality.tester.TorchPackedSequenceEqualityTester
docs.text:
Bases: BaseEqualityTester[PackedSequence]

Implement an equality tester for torch.nn.utils.rnn.PackedSequence.

This tester compares the data tensor and the metadata of two packed sequences: batch_sizes, sorted_indices and unsorted_indices. The location of a difference is the name of the attribute.

Example 
>>> import torch
>>> from torch.nn.utils.rnn import pack_padded_sequence
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.engine import Engine
>>> from coola.equality.tester import get_default_registry
>>> engine = Engine(EqualityConfig())
>>> def make(value):
...     return pack_padded_sequence(
...         torch.tensor([[1.0, value], [3.0, 4.0]]),
...         lengths=torch.tensor([2, 1]),
...         batch_first=True,
...         enforce_sorted=False,
...     )
...
>>> engine.run(make(2.0), make(2.0))
True
>>> engine.run(make(2.0), make(5.0))
False

docs.title: coola.equality.tester.TorchTensorEqualityTester
docs.text:
Bases: BaseEqualityTester[Tensor]

Implement an equality tester for torch.Tensor.

Two tensors are equal if they have the same data type, shape, device, layout and equal elements. The numbers are compared with the tolerance and equal_nan of the comparison, and a boolean tensor is exact. The tensors on the meta device have no data: only the metadata is compared. The location of a difference is the index of the first element that differs.

Example 
>>> import torch
>>> from coola.equality import compare
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.engine import Engine
>>> from coola.equality.tester import TorchTensorEqualityTester, get_default_registry
>>> engine = Engine(EqualityConfig())
>>> tester = TorchTensorEqualityTester()
>>> tester.objects_are_equal(torch.ones(2, 3), torch.ones(2, 3), engine)
True
>>> tester.objects_are_equal(torch.ones(2, 3), torch.zeros(2, 3), engine)
False
>>> compare(torch.ones(2, 3), torch.zeros(2, 3)).path
(0, 0)

docs.title: coola.equality.tester.XarrayDataArrayEqualityTester
docs.text:
Bases: BaseEqualityTester[DataArray]

Implement an equality tester for xarray.DataArray.

This tester compares the variable (data, dimensions and attributes), the name and the coordinate variables of two DataArrays. The location of a difference is the name of the attribute.

Example 
>>> import numpy as np
>>> import xarray as xr
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.engine import Engine
>>> from coola.equality.tester import get_default_registry
>>> engine = Engine(EqualityConfig())
>>> engine.run(xr.DataArray(np.arange(6), dims=["z"]), xr.DataArray(np.arange(6), dims=["z"]))
True
>>> engine.run(xr.DataArray(np.ones(6), dims=["z"]), xr.DataArray(np.zeros(6), dims=["z"]))
False
