docs.title: coola.equality.tester.get_default_registry
docs.text:
get_default_registry() -> EqualityTesterRegistry

Get or create the default global registry with common Python types.

Returns a singleton registry instance that is pre-configured with equality testers for Python's built-in types including sequences (list, tuple), mappings (dict), and scalar types (int, float).

This function uses a singleton pattern to ensure the same registry instance is returned on subsequent calls, which is efficient and maintains consistency across an application.

Returns:

Type Description EqualityTesterRegistry

A EqualityTesterRegistry instance with equality testers registered for: - Scalar types (int, float) - Sequences (list, tuple, deque, array.array, Sequence ABC) - Mappings (dict, OrderedDict, MappingProxyType, Mapping ABC) - Third-party library types (numpy, torch, pandas, polars, jax, xarray, pyarrow)

Notes

The singleton pattern means modifications to the returned registry affect all future calls to this function. If you need an isolated registry, create a new EqualityTesterRegistry instance directly.

Example 
>>> from coola.equality.tester import get_default_registry
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> registry = get_default_registry()
>>> # Registry is ready to use with common Python types
>>> config = EqualityConfig()
>>> registry.objects_are_equal([1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 3], config)
True
>>> registry.objects_are_equal([1, 2, 3], [1, 1], config)
False

docs.title: coola.equality.tester.register_equality_testers
docs.text:
register_equality_testers(
    mapping: Mapping[type, BaseEqualityTester[Any]],
    *,
    exist_ok: bool = False,
) -> None

Register custom equality testers to the default global registry.

This allows users to add support for custom types without modifying global state directly.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default mapping Mapping[type, BaseEqualityTester[Any]]

Dictionary mapping types to equality tester instances

required exist_ok bool

If False, raises error if any type already registered

False Example 
>>> from coola.equality.tester import register_equality_testers, BaseEqualityTester
>>> class MyType:
...     def __init__(self, value):
...         self.value = value
...
>>> class MyEqualityTester(BaseEqualityTester[MyType]):
...     def objects_are_equal(self, actual: MyType, expected: MyType, ctx) -> bool:
...         return actual.value == expected.value or ctx.fail("values differ")
...
>>> register_equality_testers({MyType: MyEqualityTester()})

docs.title: coola.factory
docs.text: Contain factory utilities.

docs.title: coola.factory.factory
docs.text:
factory(
    _target_: str,
    *args: Any,
    _init_: str = "__init__",
    _allowed_prefixes_: Sequence[str] | None = None,
    **kwargs: Any,
) -> Any

Instantiate dynamically an object given its configuration.

This function provides a universal factory that can instantiate any class or call any function by its fully qualified name. Unlike the AbstractFactory or Registry approaches, this function does not require prior registration of classes.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default _target_ str

The fully qualified name of the object (class or function) to instantiate, e.g., "collections.Counter" or "math.isclose".

required *args Any

Positional arguments to pass to the class constructor or function.

() _init_ str

The function or method used to create the object. If "__init__" (default), the object is created by calling the constructor. Can also be the name of a public class method or static method that returns an instance of the class (a name that starts with _, such as "__new__", is refused).

'__init__' _allowed_prefixes_ Sequence[str] | None

An optional allow-list of module prefixes that _target_ must match (see import_object). It is keyword-only, and it is the choice of the code that calls this function: whoever unpacks untrusted data into factory owns it. When it is set, an argument that is a configuration is refused.

None **kwargs Any

Keyword arguments to pass to the class constructor or function. Any name is accepted, including obj and cls.

{}

Returns:

Type Description Any

The instantiated object with the given parameters.

Raises:

Type Description ImportError

if the target cannot be found, is not allowed by _allowed_prefixes_, or if importing its module fails (the original error is then raised unchanged).

TypeError

if _target_ is not a string.

ValueError

if _allowed_prefixes_ is set and an argument is a dict with a _target_ key (a nested configuration): the target could resolve it without the allow-list. Resolve it first, with the same list.

Note

_target_ is resolved at the top level only: a nested dictionary with a _target_ key is passed to the target unchanged, it is not instantiated. Resolve the nested configurations with resolve_object and pass the results.

Security

_target_ is imported and called with no allowlist or restriction on which module or class it may reference: this function will import arbitrary module code and instantiate or call arbitrary objects from a dotted path string. Only pass a _target_ that comes from a trusted source (e.g. code you wrote, or a configuration file you control). Never resolve a _target_ derived from untrusted input, such as a third-party-uploaded config file or a network payload, as this is a remote-code-execution vector. _allowed_prefixes_ is a filter on a path, not a sandbox: it limits what is called, not the arguments. A prefix that contains a function that imports or resolves objects from its arguments (any resolve_*, import_object, importlib, pickle, eval, os.system, ...) makes the list worthless: never allow "coola" or "coola.factory". The path is checked, not the module that defines the object, so a re-export is allowed by the prefix of the re-exporting module.

Example 
>>> from coola.factory import factory
>>> factory("collections.Counter", [1, 2, 1, 3])
Counter({1: 2, 2: 1, 3: 1})

docs.title: coola.factory.import_object
docs.text:
import_object(
    object_path: object,
    *,
    allowed_prefixes: Sequence[str] | None = None,
) -> Any

Import an object given its path.

This function dynamically imports a class, function, or other Python object using its fully qualified name. The object path should have the structure module_path.object_name (e.g., "collections.Counter" or "math.isclose").

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default object_path object

The fully qualified path of the object to import. Must be a string in the format "module.path.ObjectName".

required allowed_prefixes Sequence[str] | None

An optional allow-list of module prefixes. If provided, object_path must be equal to a prefix or start with prefix + ".", otherwise an ImportError is raised before anything is imported. A string is treated as a single prefix.

None

Returns:

Type Description Any

The imported object.

Raises:

Type Description TypeError

if object_path is not a string.

ImportError

if object_path is empty or has an empty module name ("", ".Counter"), is not allowed by allowed_prefixes, or if its module or attribute does not exist ("The target object does not exist: ..."). A dependency of the target module that is not installed keeps its own ModuleNotFoundError.

Note

coola.utils.imports.import_object is a different function: it takes a path with a colon ("package.module:name") and is used by the lazy registries. This function takes a dotted path ("package.module.name"), checks allowed_prefixes and reports a missing target with one ImportError.

Security

By default, this function imports arbitrary module code with no restriction on which module or attribute it may reference: importing a module executes its top-level code. Use allowed_prefixes to restrict it. Only pass an object_path that comes from a trusted source. Never resolve an object_path derived from untrusted input, such as a third-party-uploaded config file or a network payload, as this is a remote-code-execution vector.

Example 
>>> from coola.factory import import_object
>>> cls = import_object("collections.Counter")
>>> cls()
Counter()
>>> fn = import_object("math.isclose")
>>> fn(1, 1)
True
>>> pi = import_object("math.pi")
>>> pi
3.141592653589793
>>> pkg = import_object("math")
>>> pkg
<module 'math' (built-in)>

docs.title: coola.factory.instantiate_object
docs.text:
instantiate_object(
    obj: Callable[..., Any] | type,
    /,
    *args: Any,
    _init_: str = "__init__",
    **kwargs: Any,
) -> Any

Instantiate dynamically an object from its configuration.

This function creates an instance of a class or calls a callable with the provided arguments. For classes, it supports different instantiation methods (constructor or public class methods). For any other callable (function, builtin, functools.partial, or an object implementing __call__), it simply calls it with the given arguments.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default obj Callable[..., Any] | type

The class to instantiate or the callable to call. Must be a class or a callable object.

required *args Any

Positional arguments to pass to the class constructor or callable.

() _init_ str

The function or method to use to create the object. This parameter is ignored if obj is not a class. For classes, if "__init__" (default), the object is created by calling the constructor (__new__ and __init__). Can also be the name of a public class method or static method that returns an instance of the class. A name that starts with _ is refused.

'__init__' **kwargs Any

Keyword arguments to pass to the class constructor or callable. Any name is accepted, including obj and cls: obj is positional-only.

{}

Returns:

Type Description Any

The instantiated object if obj is a class, otherwise the returned value of the callable.

Raises:

Type Description TypeError

if obj is not a class or a callable, if it is an abstract class, if _init_ is not a public method name (it is not a string or it starts with _), if the class does not have a callable _init_ attribute, or if _init_ does not return an instance of obj.

Security

obj is instantiated or called with the given arguments with no allowlist or restriction on what it may do: an arbitrary class or callable will be invoked as-is. Only pass an obj (and _init_) that come from a trusted source. Never instantiate an object whose class/callable or arguments are derived from untrusted input, as this is a remote-code-execution vector.

Example 
>>> from collections import Counter
>>> from coola.factory import instantiate_object
>>> instantiate_object(Counter, [1, 2, 1])
Counter({1: 2, 2: 1})
>>> instantiate_object(list, [1, 2, 1])
[1, 2, 1]

docs.title: coola.factory.is_object_config
docs.text:
is_object_config(
    config: dict[str, Any],
    cls: type,
    *,
    allowed_prefixes: Sequence[str] | None = None,
    import_target: bool = False,
) -> bool

Indicate if the input configuration is a configuration for a given class.

This function only checks if the value of the key _target_ is valid. It does not check the other values. If _target_ indicates a function, the returned type hint is used to check the class. A function whose return type hint cannot be resolved (e.g. a forward reference to an undefined name, or a string annotation that is not valid Python) is not a configuration for cls. A config that is not a dict, or whose _target_ is not a string, is not a configuration for cls.

The module of _target_ is not imported to answer: if it is not imported yet, the configuration is not a configuration for cls (importing a module runs its top-level code). Use allowed_prefixes to restrict the modules that can be imported, or import_target=True to import the module of any _target_.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default config dict[str, Any]

The configuration to check.

required cls type

The object class.

required allowed_prefixes Sequence[str] | None

An optional allow-list of module prefixes that _target_ must match (see import_object). If None (default), any _target_ is allowed, but its module is imported only if import_target is True. If it is set, the module of a _target_ that matches is imported when needed.

None import_target bool

If True, the module of _target_ is imported if it is not imported yet, even without allowed_prefixes. If False (default), a _target_ whose module is not imported yet and that is not restricted by allowed_prefixes is not a configuration for cls.

False

Returns:

Type Description bool

True if the input configuration is a configuration for the given class.

Raises:

Type Description ImportError

if _target_ does not match allowed_prefixes, or if it cannot be imported.

Security

By default, the module of the _target_ is not imported, so a configuration from an untrusted source cannot run the top-level code of an arbitrary module. With allowed_prefixes or import_target=True, the module is imported to check the class, and importing a module runs its top-level code: do not use them with a _target_ that comes from an untrusted source, unless allowed_prefixes restricts the modules that can be imported.

Example 
>>> from coola.factory import is_object_config
>>> from collections import Counter
>>> is_object_config({"_target_": "collections.Counter", "iterable": [1, 2, 1, 3]}, Counter)
True

docs.text:
resolve_object(
    obj: T | dict[str, Any],
    *,
    allowed_prefixes: Sequence[str] | None = None,
    strict: bool = False,
) -> T

resolve_object(
    obj: T | dict[str, Any],
    cls: type[T],
    *,
    allowed_prefixes: Sequence[str] | None = None,
    strict: bool = False,
) -> T

resolve_object(
    obj: Any,
    cls: tuple[type, ...],
    *,
    allowed_prefixes: Sequence[str] | None = None,
    strict: bool = False,
) -> Any

resolve_object(
    obj: Any,
    cls: type | tuple[type, ...] = object,
    *,
    allowed_prefixes: Sequence[str] | None = None,
    strict: bool = False,
) -> Any

Resolve an instance of cls from an existing object or a configuration dictionary.

A dict with the key "_target_" is always a factory configuration: it is built, and the result is checked against cls. Any other object, including a dict without "_target_", is returned as-is if it is an instance of cls. The key "_target_" is reserved: a dict that has it (for example Counter({"_target_": 2})) cannot be passed through as data.

Note

"_target_" is resolved at the top level only: a nested dictionary with a "_target_" key is passed to the target unchanged, it is not instantiated. With allowed_prefixes it is refused with a ValueError. Resolve the nested configurations with resolve_object (with the same allowed_prefixes) and pass the results.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default obj Any

Either a fully configured instance of cls, or a dict containing a factory specification (with a "_target_" key pointing to the fully-qualified class name). The other keys are passed to the target by keyword, except "_init_" and "_allowed_prefixes_".

required cls type | tuple[type, ...]

The expected type, or a tuple of types (as accepted by isinstance). Used to validate the resolved object, whether obj was already an instance or was built from a configuration dictionary. Defaults to object, which accepts any resolved value without validation.

object allowed_prefixes Sequence[str] | None

An optional allow-list of module prefixes that the "_target_" of the configuration must match (see import_object): "mypackage" allows "mypackage" and "mypackage.sub.Class" but not "mypackage2.Class". If None (default), any "_target_" is allowed. The "_allowed_prefixes_" key of a configuration is ignored: the data cannot set, widen or narrow the list. When it is set, an argument that is a configuration is refused.

None strict bool

If True, a "_target_" that is not a class and has no usable return type hint (a function without annotation, a built-in function) is refused before it is called, because the type of its result cannot be checked beforehand. If False (default), it is called and the result is checked afterwards.

False

Returns:

Type Description Any

A configured instance of cls.

Raises:

Type Description TypeError

If the "_target_" is a class (or a function whose return type hint is a class) that is not a subclass of cls -- it is then not called --, or if the resolved object (including a dict without "_target_") is not an instance of cls.

ImportError

If the "_target_" does not match allowed_prefixes, or if it cannot be found.

ValueError

If allowed_prefixes is set and an argument of the configuration is itself a configuration (a dict with a "_target_" key).

Security

When obj is a dict with a "_target_" key, its value is imported and the target is called: this imports and instantiates arbitrary objects from a dotted path string with no allowlist by default. Only call this function with a configuration dictionary that comes from a trusted source; never resolve a _target_ derived from untrusted input, as this is a remote-code-execution vector. If the configuration cannot be fully trusted, pass allowed_prefixes to restrict the "_target_" to the modules you expect, and check the arguments of the allowed objects too: an allow-list limits what can be called, not the arguments it is called with, and a prefix that contains a function that resolves its arguments (any resolve_*, import_object, pickle, eval, ...) makes it worthless: never allow "coola" or "coola.factory".

Example 
>>> from datetime import date
>>> from coola.factory import resolve_object
>>> # From an existing instance:
>>> d = resolve_object(date(2020, 1, 1), cls=date)
>>> # From a configuration dictionary:
>>> d = resolve_object(
...     {"_target_": "datetime.date", "year": 2020, "month": 1, "day": 1}, cls=date
... )

docs.title: coola.hashing
docs.text:
Provide deterministic hashing functions.

These are content hashes for identity and caching, not for security: do not use them for passwords, signatures or integrity against an attacker.

Hashes are deterministic across calls, processes and machines, and follow these rules:

  • Every hash is domain-separated by a type tag, so values of different types never share a hash even if their text form is the same (1, 1.0, True and "1" are all distinct).
  • Ordered containers (list, tuple, OrderedDict) are order-sensitive and unordered containers (dict, set) are not, like in coola equality. Each container family has its own tag, so a list and a tuple with the same items hash differently.
  • Container hashes are built only from the hashes of their children, resolved through a HasherRegistry.
  • Unsupported types raise TypeNotRegisteredError (a KeyError) unless ignore_unhashable is set.
  • A container that contains itself raises ValueError.
  • The output is a lowercase hex string of length characters (an even number from 2 to 128, default 64).

docs.title: coola.hashing.BaseHasher
docs.text:
Bases: ABC, Generic[T]

Base class for type-specific hashers.

A hasher describes the content of a type, it does not hash. The rules of the contract are:

  1. encode is pure and cheap: it does not call the registry, does not recurse, does not modify data and does not depend on id(), on hash() or on the iteration order of a set or of a mapping (an unordered Node says so instead).
  2. It returns bytes (a leaf, see tagged) or a Node.
  3. The children of a Node are encoded by their own hasher.
  4. The tag is a constant of the hasher, except for the user-defined classes whose qualified name is the identity. A subclass therefore hashes like its base.
  5. An exception propagates unchanged.
Example 
>>> from coola.hashing import BaseHasher, Node, hash_object, register_hashers
>>> class Point:
...     def __init__(self, x, y):
...         self.x, self.y = x, y
...
>>> class PointHasher(BaseHasher[Point]):
...     def encode(self, data):
...         return Node("Point", [data.x, data.y])
...
>>> register_hashers({Point: PointHasher()})
>>> hash_object(Point(1, 2)) == hash_object(Point(1, 2))
True
>>> hash_object(Point(1, 2)) == hash_object(Point(2, 1))
False

docs.title: coola.hashing.ContentHasher
docs.text:
Bases: InlineDisplayMixin, BaseHasher[SupportsCoolaHash]

Hasher for objects that implement __coola_hash__.

The object is described by the tag custom:module.Class and the value of __coola_hash__, which the engine hashes through the registry. The qualified class name is part of the tag, so two classes with the same content hash differently. The default registry uses it as a fallback for every class that defines the method and has no hasher of its own.

Example 
>>> from coola.hashing import ContentHasher, hash_object
>>> class Point:
...     def __init__(self, x, y):
...         self.x, self.y = x, y
...     def __coola_hash__(self):
...         return (self.x, self.y)
...
>>> hasher = ContentHasher()
>>> hasher
ContentHasher()
>>> hasher.encode(Point(1, 2)).children
[(1, 2)]
>>> hash_object(Point(1, 2)) == hash_object(Point(1, 2))
True

docs.title: coola.hashing.DataclassHasher
docs.text:
Bases: InlineDisplayMixin, BaseHasher[Any]

Hasher for dataclass instances.

The hash combines the qualified class name with a mapping from field name to field value, with every value hashed through the registry. Only the fields with compare=True are hashed, like in objects_are_equal, so two equal dataclasses have the same hash. Because dataclasses have no common base class, it cannot be registered for a type: the default registry uses it as a fallback (see HasherRegistry.register_fallback) for every dataclass that has no hasher of its own.

Example 
>>> from dataclasses import dataclass
>>> from coola.hashing import DataclassHasher
>>> @dataclass
... class Point:
...     x: int
...     y: int
...
>>> hasher = DataclassHasher()
>>> hasher
DataclassHasher()
>>> hasher.encode(Point(1, 2)).ordered
False

docs.title: coola.hashing.DatetimeHasher
docs.text:
Bases: InlineDisplayMixin, BaseHasher[date | time]

Hasher for datetime.date, datetime.datetime and datetime.time objects.

This hasher converts the object to its ISO 8601 string representation via isoformat() and hashes that string under a tag made of the concrete class name.

Since datetime.datetime is a subclass of datetime.date, both types are handled by this hasher. The class name is part of the tag, so a date and a datetime never produce the same hash, even for the same calendar day.

Aware datetimes are converted to UTC first, so equal instants in different time zones hash the same, like they compare equal. Naive and aware datetimes differ. An aware time is normalised the same way, like time.__eq__ does: the offset is subtracted from the time of day (without wrapping around midnight) and the payload is the resulting number of microseconds. A naive time uses its ISO string.

Example 
>>> from datetime import date
>>> from coola.hashing import DatetimeHasher
>>> hasher = DatetimeHasher()
>>> hasher
DatetimeHasher()
>>> hasher.encode(date(2021, 1, 1))
b'date\x002021-01-01'

docs.title: coola.hashing.HasherRegistry
docs.text:
Bases: TypeRegistry[Hasher[Any]]

Registry that manages and dispatches hashers based on data type.

This registry maintains a mapping from Python types to hasher instances and uses the Method Resolution Order (MRO) for type lookup. When hashing data, it automatically selects the most specific registered hasher for the data's type, falling back to parent types or a default hasher if needed.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default initial_state dict[type, T] | None

Optional initial mapping of types to hashers. If provided, the state is copied to prevent external mutations.

None Example

Basic usage with a sequence hasher:

>>> from coola.hashing import HasherRegistry, SequenceHasher, StrHasher
>>> registry = HasherRegistry({object: StrHasher(), list: SequenceHasher()})
>>> registry
HasherRegistry(
  (<class 'object'>): StrHasher()
  (<class 'list'>): SequenceHasher(tag='sequence')
)
>>> len(registry.hash([1, 2, 3]))
64

Registering custom hashers:

>>> from coola.hashing import HasherRegistry, SequenceHasher, StrHasher
>>> registry = HasherRegistry({object: StrHasher()})
>>> registry.register(list, SequenceHasher())
>>> len(registry.hash([1, 2, 3]))
64

Working with nested structures:

>>> from coola.hashing import get_default_registry
>>> registry = get_default_registry()
>>> data = {"a": [1, 2], "b": [3, 4]}
>>> len(registry.hash(data))
64

docs.title: coola.hashing.HasherRegistry.find_hasher
docs.text:
find_hasher(data_type: type) -> Hasher[Any]

Type-specific alias for find: find the appropriate hasher for a given type.

See TypeRegistry.resolve for the full behavior description (MRO resolution, caching, and the KeyError on no match). If no hasher is registered for the type or its parent types, the fallbacks (see register_fallback) are tried.

A subclass of Enum resolves to the hasher of Enum unless a hasher is registered for the enum class itself (or for a parent that is not a builtin base of the mixin). A member of class C(bytes, Enum) would otherwise hash as the plain value, like a member of a different enum with the same value.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default data_type type

The Python type to find a hasher for.

required

Returns:

Type Description Hasher[Any]

The most specific registered hasher for this type, resolved

Hasher[Any]

via MRO, or the hasher of the first matching fallback.

Raises:

Type Description TypeNotRegisteredError

If no hasher is found.

Example 
>>> from collections.abc import Sequence
>>> from coola.hashing import HasherRegistry, SequenceHasher, StrHasher
>>> registry = HasherRegistry({object: StrHasher()})
>>> registry.register(Sequence, SequenceHasher())
>>> hasher = registry.find_hasher(list)
>>> hasher
StrHasher()

docs.title: coola.hashing.HasherRegistry.hash
docs.text:
hash(
    data: object,
    *,
    length: int = 64,
    ignore_unhashable: bool = False,
) -> str

Hash the given data.

This is the registry-level entry point for hashing. It finds the hasher of each object with find_hasher and walks the nested structure with the engine (see coola.hashing.engine). The hash is the first length characters of the 128-character hex digest, so a hash is the start of the longer ones.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default data object

The data to hash. Can be a nested structure such as a list, dict, or tuple.

required length int

The length of the returned hex string: an even int between 2 and 128 inclusive.

64 ignore_unhashable bool

If True, objects for which no hasher is registered (including their parent types via MRO) are replaced by a deterministic placeholder hash instead of raising a TypeNotRegisteredError. This also applies to nested objects. The placeholder only depends on the type, so any two unsupported objects of the same type hash the same; a UserWarning is emitted once per type. Defaults to False, which raises an error.

False

Returns:

Type Description str

A string representing the hash of the input data.

Raises:

Type Description TypeNotRegisteredError

If no hasher is registered for the type of data or of a nested object (or any of their parent types) and ignore_unhashable is False. It is a subclass of KeyError.

ValueError

If length is not valid, or if data contains itself (a self-referencing container).

Example 
>>> from coola.hashing import get_default_registry
>>> registry = get_default_registry()
>>> len(registry.hash({"scores": [95, 87, 92], "name": "test"}))
64

docs.title: coola.hashing.MappingHasher
docs.text:
Bases: InlineDisplayMixin, BaseHasher[Mapping[Any, Any]]

Hasher for mapping types.

This hasher describes a mapping as a Node whose children are the keys and the values, which the engine hashes through the registry. The entries (a key and its value) are sorted by digest, not by key, so mappings with the same key-value pairs but different insertion orders produce the same hash, without requiring keys to be orderable. This matches coola equality, which ignores the order of the keys of a dict. Register the hasher with ordered=True for a mapping type whose order is meaningful, like OrderedDict: its equality is order-sensitive too.

The tag identifies the mapping family, so a dict and an OrderedDict with the same items hash differently.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default tag str

The type tag mixed into the hash. Defaults to "mapping".

'mapping' ordered bool

If True, items are hashed in iteration order instead of being sorted. Defaults to False.

False Example 
>>> from coola.hashing import MappingHasher
>>> hasher = MappingHasher()
>>> hasher
MappingHasher(tag='mapping', ordered=False)
>>> hasher.encode({"a": 1}).tag
'mapping'

Describe a container: a tag and the children to hash.

Each child is encoded by its own hasher, found by the registry, so the children can be any value, including values built on the spot (a list of field names, a NumPy array, a str dtype).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default tag str

The constant tag of the hasher.

required children Iterable[Any]

The values to hash. They are consumed once, lazily.

required ordered bool

If True, the position of a child matters. If False, the groups of children are sorted by digest, so the hash does not depend on the iteration order.

True group int

The number of consecutive children that form one entry of an unordered node (a mapping uses 2: key, value).

Bases: InlineDisplayMixin, BaseHasher[PurePath]

Hasher for pathlib.PurePath and pathlib.Path objects.

This hasher describes the POSIX string representation of the path as written. It never touches the filesystem and does not depend on the current working directory, so hashes are portable across machines. A relative path and the absolute path of the same location therefore hash differently; use ResolvedPathHasher to hash the real location instead.

Example 
>>> from pathlib import Path
>>> from coola.hashing import PathHasher
>>> hasher = PathHasher()
>>> hasher
PathHasher()
>>> hasher.encode(Path("/tmp/file.txt"))
b'Path\x00/tmp/file.txt'

docs.title: coola.hashing.ReprHasher
docs.text:
Bases: InlineDisplayMixin, BaseHasher[Any]

Hasher for objects whose repr() is a reliable canonical representation.

This hasher converts the object to its repr() string and hashes it under a type tag. Instances of bool, int, float and complex (including subclasses) and the NumPy scalars use the builtin repr and the builtin type name as tag, so they hash like the equivalent builtin value (np.float32(1.5) hashes like 1.5, np.int64(3) like 3). Negative zero is normalised to zero, since -0.0 == 0.0. It is preferable to StrHasher for numeric types (int, float, complex, bool) because repr() guarantees round-trip accuracy for floating point values, whereas str() may lose precision on some platforms.

For the other types, the tag is the module and the qualified name of the class by default, so a user class never shares the tag of another class with the same name. Pass tag to register a constant tag for a type (ReprHasher("timedelta")): a subclass then hashes like its base.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default tag str | None

The type tag used for the values that are not a bool, an int, a float or a complex. If None, the tag is derived from the class of the hashed object. Defaults to None.

None Example 
>>> from coola.hashing import ReprHasher
>>> hasher = ReprHasher()
>>> hasher
ReprHasher()
>>> hasher.encode(1234)
b'int\x001234'

docs.text:
Bases: InlineDisplayMixin, BaseHasher[Path]

Hasher for pathlib.Path objects that hashes the resolved location.

The path is resolved (following symlinks, collapsing ./.. segments, making it absolute) before hashing, so that two differently written but logically equivalent paths hash the same. The result depends on the filesystem and on the current working directory, so it is not portable across machines. If resolution fails, the unresolved path is hashed instead.

Example 
>>> from pathlib import Path
>>> from coola.hashing import ResolvedPathHasher
>>> hasher = ResolvedPathHasher()
>>> hasher
ResolvedPathHasher()
>>> hasher.encode(Path("file.txt")).startswith(b"Path")
True

A secret is a value with a hasher, so the policy is the one of the registry and applies wherever the secret is (in a model, a dict, a list, a dataclass...).

What to do with a secret:

  • "error": raise a ValueError. The message never contains the secret. It forces an explicit decision instead of hashing, or silently ignoring, secret data by accident.
  • "reveal": hash the real value (get_secret_value()). Use it only when the hash itself is treated as sensitive.
  • "exclude": hash a constant, so the value is never hashed and two objects that differ only by a secret have the same hash. The position of the secret is kept: it is part of the schema of the class.

Defaults to "error".

'error' Example 
>>> from pydantic import SecretStr
>>> from coola.hashing import SecretHasher
>>> hasher = SecretHasher("exclude")
>>> hasher
SecretHasher(on_secret='exclude')
>>> hasher.encode(SecretStr("a")) == hasher.encode(SecretStr("b"))
True

Bases: InlineDisplayMixin, BaseHasher[Any]

Hasher for objects whose str() is a reliable canonical representation.

This hasher converts the object to its str() string and then computes the hash of that string. Unlike ReprHasher, which uses repr(), this hasher uses str(), which is more human-readable but does not guarantee round-trip accuracy for floating point values.

docs.title: coola.hashing.hash_object
docs.text:
hash_object(
    data: object,
    *,
    registry: HasherRegistry | None = None,
    length: int = 64,
    ignore_unhashable: bool = False,
) -> str

Compute a hash of a nested data structure.

The hash is deterministic and depends on the type of every value, on the order of ordered containers, and not on the order of unordered ones. For example [1, 2], (1, 2) and {1, 2} all hash differently, while {"a": 1, "b": 2} and {"b": 2, "a": 1} hash the same. An OrderedDict is the exception among mappings: the order of its keys matters, so two OrderedDict with the same items in a different order hash differently.

Note

The hash of a dataclass, a pydantic model, an enum member or an object with a __coola_hash__ method includes the module and the qualified name of its class. The hash changes when the class is renamed or moved to another module, and a class defined in a script run as __main__ hashes differently from the same class imported. Do not persist these hashes (or the IDs derived from them, such as generate_stable_uuid5) across such a change.

The options are keyword-only: it was easy to write hash_object(data, 32) and pass 32 as the registry.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default data object

The data to hash. Can be a nested structure such as a list, dict, or tuple.

required registry HasherRegistry | None

The registry used to resolve hashers for each data type. If None, the default registry is used.

None length int

The desired length of the returned hex string. Must be an even number between 2 and 128 inclusive. Defaults to 64.

64 ignore_unhashable bool

If True, objects for which no hasher is registered (including nested objects found while hashing sequences or mappings) are replaced by a deterministic placeholder hash instead of raising an error. The placeholder only depends on the type, so it is lossy, and a UserWarning is emitted each time one is used. Defaults to False, which raises a TypeNotRegisteredError (a KeyError) when an unhashable object is encountered.

False

Returns:

Type Description str

A string representing the hash of the input data.

Raises:

Type Description TypeNotRegisteredError

If data (or a nested object within it) has a type for which no hasher is registered and ignore_unhashable is False. It is a subclass of KeyError.

ValueError

If length is not an even number between 2 and 128, or if data contains itself (a self-referencing container).

Example 
>>> from coola.hashing import hash_object
>>> len(hash_object({"a": 1, "b": "abc"}))
64
>>> len(hash_object({"a": 1, "b": "abc"}, length=16))
16

docs.title: coola.identifier
docs.text:
Provide identifiers: content-derived, time-ordered and human-friendly.

The stable identifiers (generate_stable_content_id, generate_stable_uuid5) are derived from nested data through coola.hashing. The others are generated: time-ordered (ULID, UUIDv7, Snowflake, ObjectId) or checksummed.

Every generator returns a str identifier except generate_snowflake_id/SnowflakeIdGenerator.generate, which return a plain int (a Snowflake ID is defined as a 64-bit integer, e.g. for use as a database BIGINT primary key).

docs.title: coola.identifier.ObjectIdGenerator
docs.text:
Generate MongoDB ObjectId style 12-byte identifiers.

All the state needed to mint IDs (the per-instance random value and the counter) lives on the instance rather than at module scope, so each generator is independent: create one per process/test instead of sharing mutable global state. Use generate_object_id for the common case of a single, shared, process-wide generator.

Note

After a fork (os.fork, or multiprocessing with the fork start method), the child process receives a copy of the generator. To prevent the parent and its children from producing the same identifiers, the random per-process value and the counter are regenerated in the child process, and its lock is recreated.

Example 
>>> from coola.identifier import ObjectIdGenerator
>>> generator = ObjectIdGenerator()
>>> object_id = generator.generate()
>>> len(object_id)
24

docs.title: coola.identifier.ObjectIdGenerator.generate
docs.text:
generate(timestamp: int | None = None) -> str

Generate a MongoDB ObjectId style 12-byte identifier.

The returned value packs a 4-byte Unix timestamp (seconds), a 5-byte value fixed once per generator instance, and a 3-byte counter that increments (and silently wraps modulo 2**24) on every call, into a 24-character lowercase hex string. Because the timestamp is the most significant part, IDs generated in a later second sort (as plain strings) after IDs generated in an earlier one.

Note

Unlike SnowflakeIdGenerator.generate, this never raises or blocks: if more than 2**24 IDs are requested within the same second, the counter wraps around silently, at the cost of no longer guaranteeing strict ordering (or, in the extreme, uniqueness) for IDs minted within that second.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default timestamp int | None

The Unix timestamp in seconds to encode. If None (default), the current time is used. Exposed mainly for deterministic testing.

None

Returns:

Type Description str

A 24-character lowercase hex string.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If timestamp does not fit in 32 bits (i.e. is negative or exceeds 2**32 - 1).

Example 
>>> from coola.identifier import ObjectIdGenerator
>>> generator = ObjectIdGenerator()
>>> object_id = generator.generate()
>>> len(object_id)
24

docs.title: coola.identifier.SnowflakeIdGenerator
docs.text:
Generate Snowflake-style 64-bit identifiers.

All the state needed to mint monotonically increasing IDs (the last timestamp seen and the current sequence number) lives on the instance rather than at module scope, so each generator is independent: create one per worker/shard/test instead of sharing mutable global state.

Warning

The uniqueness of the IDs across processes comes from the worker_id passed to generate, not from random values. Two processes that use the same worker_id (the default is 0) can generate the same ID in the same millisecond. This includes the children of a fork, which inherit the state of the generator of their parent: give each process or worker a distinct worker_id.

Note

If the system clock moves backward, generate raises a RuntimeError instead of waiting for the clock to catch up (the wait could be unbounded). The state of the generator is not modified by the failed call.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default last_timestamp_ms int

The millisecond timestamp of the last ID minted by this generator, or -1 (default) if none has been minted yet. Pass the value persisted from a previous instance (e.g. across a process restart) together with sequence to preserve the monotonically increasing guarantee; leave at the default for a fresh generator.

-1 sequence int

The sequence number of the last ID minted for last_timestamp_ms. Ignored (treated as 0) when last_timestamp_ms is -1.

0

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If last_timestamp_ms is not -1 and does not fit in 41 bits, or if sequence does not fit in 12 bits.

Example 
>>> from coola.identifier import SnowflakeIdGenerator
>>> generator = SnowflakeIdGenerator()
>>> snowflake_id = generator.generate()
>>> isinstance(snowflake_id, int)
True

docs.title: coola.identifier.SnowflakeIdGenerator.generate
docs.text:
generate(
    worker_id: int = 0, timestamp_ms: int | None = None
) -> int

Generate a Snowflake-style 64-bit identifier.

The returned integer is composed of a 41-bit millisecond timestamp (relative to a fixed epoch), a 10-bit worker_id, and a 12-bit sequence number that increments for IDs minted within the same millisecond by this generator. Because the timestamp is the most significant part, IDs generated later are numerically greater than IDs generated earlier (from the same, or an earlier, millisecond).

Note

The sequence counter is local to this generator instance: it guarantees uniqueness for calls made on this instance for a given worker_id, not across other instances or processes. Assign each concurrently running generator (one per process or shard, typically) a distinct worker_id to avoid collisions between them.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default worker_id int

An identifier for the process or shard minting the ID, used to avoid collisions between concurrent generators. Must fit in 10 bits (0 to 1023). Defaults to 0, which is fine for a single-process use case.

0 timestamp_ms int | None

The Unix timestamp in milliseconds to encode. If None (default), the current time is used. Exposed mainly for deterministic testing. An explicit timestamp does not update the state of the generator, and the sequence number is random instead of incrementing, so such IDs are neither monotonic nor guaranteed to be unique.

None

Returns:

Type Description int

A 64-bit non-negative integer, monotonically increasing

int

for successive calls with the same worker_id (as long

int

as the system clock does not move backward).

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If worker_id does not fit in 10 bits, or if timestamp_ms (relative to the fixed epoch) does not fit in 41 bits.

RuntimeError

If the system clock moved backward relative to the last call, which would otherwise risk generating a duplicate or decreasing ID.

Example 
>>> from coola.identifier import SnowflakeIdGenerator
>>> generator = SnowflakeIdGenerator()
>>> snowflake_id = generator.generate(worker_id=3)
>>> isinstance(snowflake_id, int)
True

generate_checksummed_id(
    length: int = _DEFAULT_LENGTH,
    group_size: int = _DEFAULT_GROUP_SIZE,
    sep: str = "-",
) -> str

Generate a random identifier with a trailing check symbol.

Draws length random Crockford Base32 characters, appends one check symbol computed from them (a mod-37 checksum, per the Crockford Base32 spec), and groups the result into chunks of group_size characters separated by sep for readability.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default length int

The number of random (non-check) characters to generate. Must be positive.

_DEFAULT_LENGTH group_size int

The number of characters per group in the formatted output. Must be positive. Pass a number greater than or equal to length + 1 (or sep="") to disable grouping.

_DEFAULT_GROUP_SIZE sep str

The separator inserted between groups. Must not contain a character from the extended Crockford Base32 alphabet, or verify_checksummed_id would not be able to tell a separator character apart from a payload/check one.

'-'

Returns:

Type Description str

A string of length random characters plus one check

str

symbol, grouped by group_size and joined by sep.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If length or group_size is not positive, if length exceeds 1024, or if sep contains a character from the extended Crockford Base32 alphabet.

Example 
>>> from coola.identifier import generate_checksummed_id, verify_checksummed_id
>>> checksummed_id = generate_checksummed_id()

docs.title: coola.identifier.generate_stable_content_id
docs.text:
generate_stable_content_id(
    data: object,
    *,
    registry: HasherRegistry | None = None,
    length: int = 64,
    ignore_unhashable: bool = False,
) -> str

Compute a content-addressed identifier for a nested data structure.

Unlike generate_stable_uuid5, the returned identifier is the raw hash_object digest: it is not reshaped into a UUID, so its collision resistance and length are exactly those of the underlying hash rather than being bounded by uuid.uuid5's SHA-1 pass.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default data object

The data to derive an identifier from. Can be a nested structure such as a list, dict, or tuple.

required registry HasherRegistry | None

The registry used to resolve hashers for each data type, forwarded to hash_object. If None, the stable registry (get_stable_registry) is used: it has only the built-in hashers, so the identifier does not depend on the installed plugins or on register_hashers. Passing another registry opts out of this stability.

None length int

The desired length of the returned hex string, forwarded to hash_object. Must be an even number between 2 and 128 inclusive. Defaults to 64.

64 ignore_unhashable bool

Forwarded to hash_object. If True, objects for which no hasher is registered are replaced by a deterministic placeholder hash instead of raising an error. Defaults to False, which raises a KeyError when an unhashable object is encountered.

False

Returns:

Type Description str

A lowercase hex string identifier of the requested length.

Raises:

Type Description KeyError

If data (or a nested object within it) has a type for which no hasher is registered and ignore_unhashable is False.

Example 
>>> from coola.identifier import generate_stable_content_id
>>> generate_stable_content_id({"source": "cats.txt", "page": 1})  # doctest: +ELLIPSIS
'...'
>>> generate_stable_content_id(
...     {"page": 1, "source": "cats.txt"}
... ) == generate_stable_content_id({"source": "cats.txt", "page": 1})
True

docs.title: coola.identifier.generate_stable_uuid5
docs.text:
generate_stable_uuid5(
    data: object,
    *,
    registry: HasherRegistry | None = None,
    namespace: UUID = _NAMESPACE,
    ignore_unhashable: bool = False,
) -> str

Compute a stable, reproducible UUID for a nested data structure.

Hashes data via hash_object (at its maximum, 128-hex-digit length, so the identifier gets the full benefit of the underlying hash's collision resistance) to guarantee a consistent digest regardless of e.g. mapping insertion order, then derives a deterministic UUID from that digest using uuid.uuid5 under a fixed namespace.

Note

uuid.uuid5 always returns a 128-bit value regardless of the strength of the digest fed into it, so generate_stable_uuid5(a) == generate_stable_uuid5(b) if and only if hash_object(a) == hash_object(b) (modulo the astronomically unlikely case of a uuid.uuid5 collision on two different digests). Note also that uuid.uuid5 hashes its input with SHA-1 internally, so the final UUID's collision resistance is bounded by SHA-1 regardless of how strong hash_object's own digest is.

Warning

The value returned by generate_stable_uuid5 for a given data is stable only as long as hash_object (and the hashers resolved by registry for the types in data) keep producing the same digest for that data. A change to the hashing algorithms of coola in a future release would silently change the UUIDs produced here. Do not rely on cross-version stability for UUIDs persisted long-term (e.g. as database primary keys) unless you pin coola and pass an explicit, version-controlled registry.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default data object

The data to derive a UUID from. Can be a nested structure such as a list, dict, or tuple.

required registry HasherRegistry | None

The registry used to resolve hashers for each data type, forwarded to hash_object. If None, the stable registry (get_stable_registry) is used: it has only the built-in hashers, so the identifier does not depend on the installed plugins or on register_hashers. Passing another registry opts out of this stability.

None namespace UUID

The UUID namespace passed to uuid.uuid5. Defaults to a namespace fixed for this module; pass a different one to derive UUIDs in a separate identifier space (e.g. to avoid collisions with UUIDs minted by another system for unrelated data).

_NAMESPACE ignore_unhashable bool

Forwarded to hash_object. If True, objects for which no hasher is registered are replaced by a deterministic placeholder hash instead of raising an error. Defaults to False, which raises a KeyError when an unhashable object is encountered.

False

Returns:

Type Description str

A lowercase UUID string of the form

str

'xxxxxxxx-xxxx-5xxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx'.

Raises:

Type Description KeyError

If data (or a nested object within it) has a type for which no hasher is registered and ignore_unhashable is False.

Example 
>>> from coola.identifier import generate_stable_uuid5
>>> generate_stable_uuid5({"source": "cats.txt", "page": 1})  # doctest: +ELLIPSIS
'...'
>>> generate_stable_uuid5({"page": 1, "source": "cats.txt"}) == generate_stable_uuid5(
...     {"source": "cats.txt", "page": 1}
... )
True

docs.title: coola.identifier.generate_ulid
docs.text:
generate_ulid(timestamp_ms: int | None = None) -> str

Generate a ULID (Universally Unique Lexicographically Sortable Identifier).

A ULID packs a 48-bit millisecond timestamp followed by 80 bits of randomness into a 26-character Crockford Base32 string. Because the timestamp is the most significant part, ULIDs generated later sort (lexicographically, as plain strings) after ULIDs generated earlier, unlike uuid.uuid4 which sorts randomly.

Note

When the current time is used (timestamp_ms=None), ULIDs are monotonic within a process, as recommended by the ULID specification: ULIDs generated in the same millisecond (or after the clock moved backward) keep the timestamp and increment the random part by one, so they still sort in the order of generation. The state is per process, protected by a lock, and reset in the child process of a fork. Across processes, ULIDs generated in the same millisecond are not ordered. When timestamp_ms is given, the random part is always random: two ULIDs with the same timestamp are not ordered.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default timestamp_ms int | None

The Unix timestamp in milliseconds to encode. If None (default), the current time is used and the ULIDs are monotonic (see below). Exposed mainly for deterministic testing and for backfilling.

None

Returns:

Type Description str

A 26-character uppercase Crockford Base32 ULID string.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If timestamp_ms does not fit in 48 bits (i.e. is negative or exceeds 2**48 - 1).

Example 
>>> from coola.identifier import generate_ulid
>>> ulid = generate_ulid()
>>> len(ulid)
26

docs.title: coola.identifier.generate_uuid7
docs.text:
generate_uuid7(timestamp_ms: int | None = None) -> str

Generate a UUIDv7 (RFC 9562) identifier.

A UUIDv7 packs a 48-bit millisecond timestamp, followed by the 4-bit version, 12 bits of randomness, the 2-bit variant, and 62 more bits of randomness, into a standard 128-bit UUID layout. Because the timestamp is the most significant part, UUIDv7 values generated later sort (lexicographically, as canonical UUID strings) after UUIDv7 values generated earlier, unlike uuid.uuid4 which sorts randomly.

Note

When the current time is used (timestamp_ms=None), UUIDv7 values are monotonic within a process (the "method 1" counter of RFC 9562): values generated in the same millisecond (or after the clock moved backward) keep the timestamp and increment the 74 random bits by one, so they still sort in the order of generation, which keeps database indexes append-only. The state is per process, protected by a lock, and reset in the child process of a fork. Across processes, values generated in the same millisecond are not ordered. When timestamp_ms is given, the random bits are always random: two values with the same timestamp are not ordered.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default timestamp_ms int | None

The Unix timestamp in milliseconds to encode. If None (default), the current time is used and the UUIDs are monotonic (see below). Exposed mainly for deterministic testing and for backfilling.

None

Returns:

Type Description str

A lowercase UUID string of the form

str

'xxxxxxxx-xxxx-7xxx-yxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx'.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If timestamp_ms does not fit in 48 bits (i.e. is negative or exceeds 2**48 - 1).

Example 
>>> from coola.identifier import generate_uuid7
>>> uuid7 = generate_uuid7()
>>> len(uuid7)
36

verify_checksummed_id(
    identifier: str, sep: str = "-"
) -> bool

Verify the check symbol of an identifier from generate_checksummed_id.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default identifier str

The identifier to verify, in the grouped form returned by generate_checksummed_id.

required sep str

The group separator used when identifier was generated.

'-'

Per the Crockford Base32 spec, decoding is case-insensitive and normalizes the characters most often confused when an identifier is hand-transcribed: 'O' with '0', and 'I'/'L' with '1'. identifier is normalized this way before its check symbol is verified, so e.g. a lowercase retype or an 'O' typed for a '0' still verifies correctly.

Returns:

Type Description bool

True if the trailing character is a valid check symbol for

bool

the characters preceding it, False otherwise (including

bool

when identifier contains a character outside the extended

bool

Crockford Base32 alphabet, or is too short to contain a

bool

payload and a check symbol, is not a str, or contains a non-ASCII character).

Example 
>>> from coola.identifier import generate_checksummed_id, verify_checksummed_id
>>> verify_checksummed_id(generate_checksummed_id())
True
>>> verify_checksummed_id("not-a-valid-id")
False
>>> verify_checksummed_id(generate_checksummed_id().lower())
True

docs.title: coola.io.BaseFileSaver.save
docs.text:
save(
    to_save: T,
    path: str | PathLike[str],
    *,
    exist_ok: bool = False,
    fsync: bool = False,
) -> None

Save the data into the given path.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default to_save T

The data to save. The data should be compatible with the saving engine.

required path str | PathLike[str]

The path where to save the data. A str or any path-like object is converted to a Path.

required exist_ok bool

If exist_ok is False (the default), FileExistsError is raised if the target file already exists. If exist_ok is True, FileExistsError will not be raised unless the given path already exists in the file system and is not a file.

Note: the exist_ok=False guarantee holds against a concurrent creation of path between the initial existence check and the commit step (the commit uses os.link which atomically fails with FileExistsError in that case).

Note: concurrent save calls targeting the same path, from this process or from other processes, never produce a mixed file: each writes its own hidden temporary file (.<name>-<uuid><ext>) and commits it atomically, so the file is the complete content of one of them. With exist_ok=True which one is unspecified (the last commit wins); with exist_ok=False exactly one wins and the others raise FileExistsError. save takes no lock: a caller that needs mutual exclusion around a read-modify-write of one file uses its own lock.

False fsync bool

If True, the data is flushed to the disk before the file is committed, and the directory is flushed after, so the file is not empty or missing after a power failure or a system crash. It is slower. If False (the default), the data is only written to the operating system cache: the file is still replaced atomically (a reader never sees a partially written file), but its content can be lost if the machine crashes right after the call. This is fine for caches and most logs.

False Note

The caller needs write access to the directory of path, not only to the file: the data is first written to a hidden temporary file next to path. A process killed between the write and the commit leaves this file; it is safe to delete. The saved file is committed with a hard link, or with a rename if the filesystem does not support hard links (e.g. FAT/exFAT, and some network and container volumes); in that case two processes that create the same file at the same instant can both succeed (the last one wins, no file is torn).

Raises:

Type Description FileExistsError

if the file already exists and exist_ok is False.

IsADirectoryError

If path is a directory.

NotADirectoryError

If the parent of path is a file.

Example 
>>> import tempfile
>>> from pathlib import Path
>>> from coola.io import JsonSaver, JsonLoader
>>> with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmpdir:
...     path = Path(tmpdir).joinpath("data.json")
...     JsonSaver().save({"key1": [1, 2, 3], "key2": "abc"}, path)
...     data = JsonLoader().load(path)
...     data
...
{'key1': [1, 2, 3], 'key2': 'abc'}

save_json(
    to_save: Any,
    path: str | PathLike[str],
    *,
    encoding: str = DEFAULT_ENCODING,
    exist_ok: bool = False,
    fsync: bool = False,
    **kwargs: Any,
) -> None

Save the given data in a JSON file.

The file is what json.dump writes, so the output follows the Python json module and is not strict JSON by default: NaN and infinite floats are written as the non-standard tokens NaN and Infinity, and the keys that are not strings (for example int) are written as strings, so they are strings after load_json. Pass allow_nan=False to raise an error for NaN and infinite floats. The data is not converted: use coola.nested.convert_to_jsonable first for the objects that json does not support.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default to_save Any

Anyhe data to write in a JSON file.

required path str | PathLike[str]

The path where to write the JSON file. A str or any path-like object is converted to a Path.

required encoding str

The file encoding to use when writing the file. Defaults to "utf-8".

DEFAULT_ENCODING exist_ok bool

If exist_ok is False (the default), FileExistsError is raised if the target file already exists. If exist_ok is True, FileExistsError will not be raised unless the given path already exists in the file system and is not a file.

False fsync bool

If True, flush the data to the disk before committing the file, so it survives a power failure or a system crash. It is slower. Defaults to False: the file is replaced atomically, but its content may be lost if the machine crashes right after the call.

False **kwargs Any

Additional arguments passed to json.dump, e.g. indent or sort_keys.

{}

Raises:

Type Description FileExistsError

if the file already exists.

Example 
>>> import tempfile
>>> from pathlib import Path
>>> from coola.io import save_json, load_json
>>> with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmpdir:
...     path = Path(tmpdir).joinpath("data.json")
...     save_json({"key1": [1, 2, 3], "key2": "abc"}, path)
...     data = load_json(path)
...     data
...
{'key1': [1, 2, 3], 'key2': 'abc'}

docs.title: coola.io.base.BaseFileSaver.save
docs.text:
save(
    to_save: T,
    path: str | PathLike[str],
    *,
    exist_ok: bool = False,
    fsync: bool = False,
) -> None

Save the data into the given path.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default to_save T

The data to save. The data should be compatible with the saving engine.

required path str | PathLike[str]

The path where to save the data. A str or any path-like object is converted to a Path.

required exist_ok bool

If exist_ok is False (the default), FileExistsError is raised if the target file already exists. If exist_ok is True, FileExistsError will not be raised unless the given path already exists in the file system and is not a file.

Note: the exist_ok=False guarantee holds against a concurrent creation of path between the initial existence check and the commit step (the commit uses os.link which atomically fails with FileExistsError in that case).

Note: concurrent save calls targeting the same path, from this process or from other processes, never produce a mixed file: each writes its own hidden temporary file (.<name>-<uuid><ext>) and commits it atomically, so the file is the complete content of one of them. With exist_ok=True which one is unspecified (the last commit wins); with exist_ok=False exactly one wins and the others raise FileExistsError. save takes no lock: a caller that needs mutual exclusion around a read-modify-write of one file uses its own lock.

False fsync bool

If True, the data is flushed to the disk before the file is committed, and the directory is flushed after, so the file is not empty or missing after a power failure or a system crash. It is slower. If False (the default), the data is only written to the operating system cache: the file is still replaced atomically (a reader never sees a partially written file), but its content can be lost if the machine crashes right after the call. This is fine for caches and most logs.

False Note

The caller needs write access to the directory of path, not only to the file: the data is first written to a hidden temporary file next to path. A process killed between the write and the commit leaves this file; it is safe to delete. The saved file is committed with a hard link, or with a rename if the filesystem does not support hard links (e.g. FAT/exFAT, and some network and container volumes); in that case two processes that create the same file at the same instant can both succeed (the last one wins, no file is torn).

Raises:

Type Description FileExistsError

if the file already exists and exist_ok is False.

IsADirectoryError

If path is a directory.

NotADirectoryError

If the parent of path is a file.

Example 
>>> import tempfile
>>> from pathlib import Path
>>> from coola.io import JsonSaver, JsonLoader
>>> with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmpdir:
...     path = Path(tmpdir).joinpath("data.json")
...     JsonSaver().save({"key1": [1, 2, 3], "key2": "abc"}, path)
...     data = JsonLoader().load(path)
...     data
...
{'key1': [1, 2, 3], 'key2': 'abc'}

docs.title: coola.iterator
docs.text:
Utilities to traverse and filter nested data structures.

dfs_iterate and bfs_iterate are lazy generators that yield the leaves of a nested structure, once per occurrence and never a container, in depth-first (pre-order) or breadth-first (level order) order. The child finder of an object is chosen from its type along the Method Resolution Order, and one child finder serves both orders. Keys are never yielded, the input is never modified, iterators and generators are leaves (never consumed), and a container that contains itself raises a ValueError. Both orders yield the same leaves; only the order differs, and neither is limited by the depth of the data.

docs.title: coola.iterator.BaseChildFinder
docs.text:
Bases: ABC, Generic[T]

Abstract base class for the child finders.

A child finder describes the shape of the values of a type. It is registered in a ChildFinderRegistry and is used by dfs_iterate and bfs_iterate. The generic type parameter T indicates the type of data this child finder handles.

Notes
  • Subclasses must implement the find_children method.
  • find_children is pure and cheap: it does not call the registry, does not recurse, does not modify the data and does not consume the children (it returns them).
  • The result is consumed once, lazily, in order. It can be the container itself, a view (data.values()) or a generator.
  • A leaf returns None: the traversal yields the value itself. A container with no child returns an empty iterable: it is not a leaf and yields nothing.
  • The children are the values to visit: a child finder never returns the keys of a mapping.
Example 
>>> from coola.iterator import BaseChildFinder, dfs_iterate, register_child_finders
>>> class Node:
...     def __init__(self, left, right):
...         self.left, self.right = left, right
...
>>> class NodeChildFinder(BaseChildFinder[Node]):
...     def find_children(self, data):
...         return [data.left, data.right]
...
>>> register_child_finders({Node: NodeChildFinder()})
>>> list(dfs_iterate(Node(1, Node(2, 3))))
[1, 2, 3]

>>> print(DefaultChildFinder().find_children(42))
None
>>> IterableChildFinder().find_children([1, 2])

docs.title: coola.iterator.ChildFinderRegistry
docs.text:
Bases: TypeRegistry[BaseChildFinder[Any]]

Registry that maps Python types to child finders.

During a traversal, the registry selects the most specific child finder for the type of an object using the Method Resolution Order (MRO). The registry is only a dispatcher: the traversal is done by dfs_iterate and bfs_iterate, so one registry serves both orders. The resolved child finders are cached.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default initial_state dict[type, T] | None

An optional dictionary mapping Python types to BaseChildFinder instances. If provided, the registry is initialized with this mapping.

None

Attributes:

Name Type Description _state dict[K, V]

Mapping of registered data types to child finders.

Example 
>>> from coola.iterator import (
...     ChildFinderRegistry,
...     DefaultChildFinder,
...     IterableChildFinder,
...     bfs_iterate,
...     dfs_iterate,
... )
>>> registry = ChildFinderRegistry(
...     {object: DefaultChildFinder(), list: IterableChildFinder()}
... )
>>> list(dfs_iterate([1, [2, 3], 4], registry=registry))
[1, 2, 3, 4]
>>> list(bfs_iterate([1, [2, 3], 4], registry=registry))
[1, 4, 2, 3]

docs.title: coola.iterator.DataclassChildFinder
docs.text:
Bases: InlineDisplayMixin, BaseChildFinder[Any]

Child finder for dataclass instances.

The children of a dataclass instance are the values of its fields, in the order of the definition of the fields. It is registered as a fallback for dataclasses.is_dataclass in the default registry. A child finder registered for the type of the dataclass has priority; register DefaultChildFinder to keep a dataclass as a leaf.

Example 
>>> from dataclasses import dataclass
>>> from coola.iterator import DataclassChildFinder
>>> @dataclass
... class Config:
...     lr: float
...     layers: list
...
>>> list(DataclassChildFinder().find_children(Config(0.1, [1, 2])))
[0.1, [1, 2]]

docs.title: coola.iterator.DefaultChildFinder
docs.text:
Bases: InlineDisplayMixin, BaseChildFinder[Any]

Default child finder: the data is a leaf.

This child finder is the fallback for the objects that do not have a specialized child finder registered. It is used for the primitive types (int, float, str, bool, ...), the iterators and every object without a structure to traverse.

Example 
>>> from coola.iterator import DefaultChildFinder
>>> child_finder = DefaultChildFinder()
>>> print(child_finder.find_children(42))
None
>>> print(child_finder.find_children("hello"))
None

docs.title: coola.iterator.IterableChildFinder
docs.text:
Bases: InlineDisplayMixin, BaseChildFinder[Iterable[Any]]

Child finder for the iterable containers.

The container is its own iterable of children: its elements are visited in the order of its iteration. It works with lists, tuples, sets and any object implementing the Iterable protocol.

Example 
>>> from coola.iterator import IterableChildFinder
>>> child_finder = IterableChildFinder()
>>> list(child_finder.find_children((4, 2, 1)))
[4, 2, 1]
>>> list(child_finder.find_children([]))

docs.title: coola.iterator.MappingChildFinder
docs.text:
Bases: InlineDisplayMixin, BaseChildFinder[Mapping[Any, Any]]

Child finder for the mappings.

The children of a mapping are its values, in the order of its iteration. The keys are never visited. It works with dictionaries and any object implementing the Mapping protocol.

Example 
>>> from coola.iterator import MappingChildFinder
>>> child_finder = MappingChildFinder()
>>> list(child_finder.find_children({"a": 1, "b": 2}))
[1, 2]
>>> list(child_finder.find_children({"a": {"b": 1, "c": 2}, "d": 3}))
[{'b': 1, 'c': 2}, 3]

docs.title: coola.iterator.bfs_iterate
docs.text:
bfs_iterate(
    data: object,
    *,
    registry: ChildFinderRegistry | None = None,
) -> Iterator[Any]

Iterate over the leaves of nested data in breadth-first order.

The traversal is level order, left to right inside a level. It visits the same leaves as dfs_iterate; only the order differs. The child finder of each object is chosen from its type with registry. Only the leaves are yielded, never a container.

The function is a generator: the leaves are produced on demand. It uses an explicit queue, so there is no limit on the depth of the data. The memory is proportional to the width of a level.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default data object

The nested data to traverse.

required registry ChildFinderRegistry | None

The registry used to resolve the child finders. If None, the default registry is used.

None

Yields:

Type Description Any

The leaves of data in breadth-first order.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If a container contains itself, when the traversal reaches it (the leaves before it are already yielded).

Example 
>>> from coola.iterator import bfs_iterate
>>> list(bfs_iterate({"a": 1, "b": "abc"}))
[1, 'abc']
>>> list(bfs_iterate([1, [2, [3]], 4]))
[1, 4, 2, 3]

docs.title: coola.iterator.dfs_iterate
docs.text:
dfs_iterate(
    data: object,
    *,
    registry: ChildFinderRegistry | None = None,
) -> Iterator[Any]

Iterate over the leaves of nested data in depth-first order.

The traversal is pre-order, left to right. The child finder of each object is chosen from its type with registry. Only the leaves are yielded, once per occurrence, never a container (an empty container yields nothing). The keys of a mapping are never yielded. Iterators and generators are leaves: they are never consumed.

The function is a generator: the leaves are produced on demand and nothing is walked before the first next. It uses an explicit stack, so there is no limit on the depth of the data.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default data object

The nested data to traverse.

required registry ChildFinderRegistry | None

The registry used to resolve the child finders. If None, the default registry is used.

None

Yields:

Type Description Any

The leaves of data in depth-first order.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If a container contains itself, when the traversal reaches it (the leaves before it are already yielded).

Example 
>>> from coola.iterator import dfs_iterate
>>> list(dfs_iterate({"a": 1, "b": "abc"}))
[1, 'abc']
>>> list(dfs_iterate([1, [2, 3], {"x": 4}]))
[1, 2, 3, 4]

docs.title: coola.iterator.filter_by_type
docs.text:
filter_by_type(
    iterator: Iterable[Any],
    types: type[T] | tuple[type[T], ...],
) -> Iterator[T]

Filter an iterator to yield only values of specified types.

This function acts as a type-safe filter that passes through only values matching the specified type(s). It's particularly useful when working with heterogeneous collections where you need to extract elements of specific types.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default iterator Iterable[Any]

An iterator or iterable to filter. Can contain values of any type.

required types type[T] | tuple[type[T], ...]

A single type or tuple of types to filter for. Only values that are instances of these types will be yielded. Follows the same semantics as the built-in isinstance() function.

required

Yields:

Type Description T

Values from the input iterator that are instances of any of the specified

T

types, preserving the original order of elements.

Example

Filter mixed-type list to get only integers:

>>> from coola.iterator import filter_by_type
>>> list(filter_by_type([1, "hello", 2, 3.14, "world", 4], int))
[1, 2, 4]

Filter for multiple types:

>>> from coola.iterator import filter_by_type
>>> # Note: bool is a subclass of int
>>> list(filter_by_type([1, "hello", 2.5, True, None, [1, 2]], (int, float)))
[1, 2.5, True]
Notes
  • This function uses isinstance() internally, so subclass relationships are respected (e.g., bool values will match int type).
  • With a tuple of types, the type checker infers the union of the types (Iterator[int | float] for (int, float)).
  • The input iterator is consumed as items are yielded.
  • For empty iterators or when no items match, the generator yields nothing.

get_default_registry() -> ChildFinderRegistry

Get or create the default global registry for child finders.

This function returns a singleton instance of the ChildFinderRegistry, which is pre-configured with child finders for the common Python types: the sequences, the sets, the mappings and the dataclasses are entered, the scalars and the other objects are leaves.

Returns:

Type Description ChildFinderRegistry

An ChildFinderRegistry instance with child finders registered for common Python types.

Notes

The singleton pattern means any changes to the returned registry affect all future calls to this function. If an isolated registry is needed, create a new ChildFinderRegistry instance directly.

Example 
>>> from coola.iterator import get_default_registry
>>> registry = get_default_registry()
>>> registry.has_child_finder(list)
True

'' suffix str

docs.title: coola.nested.convert_to_jsonable
docs.text:
convert_to_jsonable(data: Any) -> Any

Recursively convert a nested data structure to a JSON-compatible representation.

This function walks through nested containers (e.g. list, tuple, dict) and applies coola.utils.conversion.to_jsonable to every object, converting pydantic.BaseModel and dataclass objects found at any depth (see to_jsonable for the supported types and the limits: keys are not converted, NaN is kept). Sets are converted to sorted lists. Use to_jsonable directly if the data is a single, non-nested object.

The contract is "accepted by the Python json module", not "strict JSON": the keys of the dictionaries are not converted (json.dumps raises a TypeError for a key such as a tuple, and turns an int key into a string), and NaN and infinite floats are kept (json.dumps(..., allow_nan=False) raises a ValueError). coola.utils.conversion.to_jsonable converts one object and leaves the containers unchanged; this function applies it to every object of a nested structure.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default data Any

The nested data structure to convert.

required

Returns:

Type Description Any

The converted data, with the same structure as the input.

Example 
>>> from dataclasses import dataclass
>>> from coola.nested import convert_to_jsonable
>>> @dataclass
... class Point:
...     x: int
...     y: int
...
>>> convert_to_jsonable([Point(x=1, y=2), {"key": Point(x=3, y=4)}])
[{'x': 1, 'y': 2}, {'key': {'x': 3, 'y': 4}}]

Convert a mapping of sequences to a list of dictionaries.

All the sequences must have the same length. A string (or bytes) is not accepted as a sequence, because it would be split per character. An empty mapping gives an empty list, so a list of empty dictionaries ([{}, {}]) does not round trip with convert_to_dict_of_lists.
