docs.title: Equality Testers
docs.text:
An equality tester is responsible for comparing objects of a specific type. Each tester:

  1. Checks if it can handle the given type
  2. Returns True if the objects are equal, False if they are different (ctx.fail(reason)), or the child pairs that must all be equal
>>> from coola.equality import objects_are_equal
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.engine import Engine
>>> from coola.equality.tester import SequenceEqualityTester, get_default_registry
>>> engine = Engine(EqualityConfig())
>>> tester = SequenceEqualityTester()
>>> list(tester.objects_are_equal([1.0, 2.0], [1.0, 3.0], engine))
[(1.0, 1.0, 0), (2.0, 3.0, 1)]
>>> engine.run([1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 3])
True
>>> engine.run([1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 4])
False

docs.title: Registry System
docs.text:
!!! tip "Import collisions"

`get_default_registry` exists in several `coola` subpackages with different return types. Import it
from `coola.equality.tester`, or import the module and call `tester.get_default_registry()`.

The registry maintains a mapping from types to testers and automatically selects the right tester:

>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.tester import get_default_registry
>>> registry = get_default_registry()
>>> config = EqualityConfig()
>>> # Registry automatically selects SequenceEqualityTester for lists
>>> registry.objects_are_equal([1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 3], config)
True
>>> # Registry automatically selects MappingEqualityTester for dicts
>>> registry.objects_are_equal({"a": 1}, {"a": 1}, config)
True

The registry uses Python's Method Resolution Order (MRO) to find the most specific tester for a given type, which means it can handle inheritance correctly.

docs.title: SequenceEqualityTester
docs.text:
Handles sequence types like list, tuple, and deque:

>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.engine import Engine
>>> from coola.equality.tester import get_default_registry
>>> config = EqualityConfig()
>>> engine = Engine(config)
>>> engine.run([1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 3])
True
>>> engine.run([1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 4])
False
>>> # Works with nested structures
>>> engine.run(
...     [1, {"a": 2}, [3, 4]],
...     [1, {"a": 2}, [3, 4]],
... )
True

The tester recursively compares elements using the registry, so nested structures are handled correctly.

docs.title: SetEqualityTester
docs.text:
Handles set and frozenset. Unlike ==, the elements are matched by hash and type, so equal_nan applies to them (the tolerance does not):

>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.engine import Engine
>>> from coola.equality.tester import get_default_registry
>>> config = EqualityConfig(equal_nan=True)
>>> engine = Engine(config)
>>> engine.run({1.0, float("nan")}, {1.0, float("nan")})
True
>>> engine.run({1.0, 2.0}, {1.0, 3.0})
False

docs.title: MappingEqualityTester
docs.text:
Handles mapping types like dict:

>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.engine import Engine
>>> from coola.equality.tester import get_default_registry
>>> config = EqualityConfig()
>>> engine = Engine(config)
>>> engine.run({"a": 1, "b": 2}, {"a": 1, "b": 2})
True
>>> engine.run({"a": 1, "b": 2}, {"a": 1, "b": 3})
False
>>> # Works with nested structures
>>> engine.run(
...     {"x": [1, 2], "y": {"z": 3}},
...     {"x": [1, 2], "y": {"z": 3}},
... )
True

docs.title: OrderedMappingEqualityTester
docs.text:
Like MappingEqualityTester, and it also requires the keys to be in the same order. It is registered for collections.OrderedDict, whose order is meaningful (Python's == also compares it between two OrderedDicts). The other mappings ignore the order of the keys:

>>> from collections import OrderedDict
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.engine import Engine
>>> from coola.equality.tester import get_default_registry
>>> config = EqualityConfig()
>>> engine = Engine(config)
>>> engine.run(OrderedDict(a=1, b=2), OrderedDict(a=1, b=2))
True
>>> engine.run(OrderedDict(a=1, b=2), OrderedDict(b=2, a=1))
False

docs.title: ScalarEqualityTester
docs.text:
Handles scalar types like int, float, and bool:

>>> from coola.equality import Tolerance
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.engine import Engine
>>> from coola.equality.tester import get_default_registry, ScalarEqualityTester
>>> config = EqualityConfig()
>>> engine = Engine(config)
>>> tester = ScalarEqualityTester()
>>> tester.objects_are_equal(42, 42, engine)
True
>>> tester.objects_are_equal(3.14, 3.14, engine)
True
>>> # With tolerance
>>> engine_tol = Engine(EqualityConfig(tolerance=Tolerance(atol=0.01)))
>>> tester.objects_are_equal(1.0, 1.005, engine_tol)
True

docs.title: EqualEqualityTester
docs.text:
Generic tester that uses Python's == operator:

>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.tester import EqualEqualityTester
>>> class MyList(list):
...     def equal(self, other: object) -> bool:
...         return self == other
>>> config = EqualityConfig()
>>> engine = Engine(config)
>>> tester = EqualEqualityTester()
>>> tester.objects_are_equal(MyList([1, 2, 3]), MyList([1, 2, 3]), engine)
True
>>> tester.objects_are_equal(MyList([1, 2, 3]), MyList([1, 2, 4]), engine)
False

docs.title: NumpyArrayEqualityTester
docs.text:
Handles NumPy arrays:

>>> from coola.equality import Tolerance
>>> import numpy as np
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.engine import Engine
>>> from coola.equality.tester import get_default_registry, NumpyArrayEqualityTester
>>> config = EqualityConfig()
>>> engine = Engine(config)
>>> tester = NumpyArrayEqualityTester()
>>> tester.objects_are_equal(
...     np.array([1, 2, 3]),
...     np.array([1, 2, 3]),
...     engine,
... )
True
>>> tester.objects_are_equal(
...     np.array([1, 2, 3]),
...     np.array([1, 2, 4]),
...     engine,
... )
False
>>> # With tolerance
>>> engine_tol = Engine(EqualityConfig(tolerance=Tolerance(atol=0.01)))
>>> tester.objects_are_equal(
...     np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0]),
...     np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.001]),
...     engine_tol,
... )
True

docs.title: NumpyMaskedArrayEqualityTester
docs.text:
Handles NumPy masked arrays:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.engine import Engine
>>> from coola.equality.tester import get_default_registry, NumpyMaskedArrayEqualityTester
>>> config = EqualityConfig()
>>> engine = Engine(config)
>>> tester = NumpyMaskedArrayEqualityTester()
>>> arr1 = np.ma.array([1, 2, 3], mask=[0, 0, 1])
>>> arr2 = np.ma.array([1, 2, 99], mask=[0, 0, 1])  # Masked value differs
>>> engine.run(arr1, arr2)
False

docs.title: TorchTensorEqualityTester
docs.text:
Handles PyTorch tensors:

>>> from coola.equality import Tolerance
>>> import torch
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.engine import Engine
>>> from coola.equality.tester import get_default_registry, TorchTensorEqualityTester
>>> config = EqualityConfig()
>>> engine = Engine(config)
>>> tester = TorchTensorEqualityTester()
>>> tester.objects_are_equal(
...     torch.tensor([1, 2, 3]),
...     torch.tensor([1, 2, 3]),
...     engine,
... )
True
>>> # With tolerance
>>> engine_tol = Engine(EqualityConfig(tolerance=Tolerance(atol=0.01)))
>>> tester.objects_are_equal(
...     torch.tensor([1.0, 2.0, 3.0]),
...     torch.tensor([1.0, 2.0, 3.001]),
...     engine_tol,
... )
True

docs.title: TorchPackedSequenceEqualityTester
docs.text:
Handles PyTorch PackedSequence objects:

>>> import torch
>>> from torch.nn.utils.rnn import pack_padded_sequence
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.engine import Engine
>>> from coola.equality.tester import get_default_registry, TorchPackedSequenceEqualityTester
>>> config = EqualityConfig()
>>> engine = Engine(config)
>>> tester = TorchPackedSequenceEqualityTester()
>>> ps1 = pack_padded_sequence(
...     torch.arange(10).view(2, 5).float(),
...     torch.tensor([5, 3], dtype=torch.long),
...     batch_first=True,
... )
>>> ps2 = pack_padded_sequence(
...     torch.arange(10).view(2, 5).float(),
...     torch.tensor([5, 3], dtype=torch.long),
...     batch_first=True,
... )
>>> engine.run(ps1, ps2)
True

docs.title: Table Testers
docs.text:
pandas, polars and PyArrow run the same algorithm, written once in TableEqualityTester: the structure is compared first (shape, names, data types, index), then the columns one by one, each by its kind, and the comparison stops at the first column that differs. An adapter converts an object of a library to a table. The default registry registers one TableEqualityTester per type:

Library Types pandas DataFrame, Series, Index (also MultiIndex), extension arrays polars DataFrame, LazyFrame, Series PyArrow Array, ChunkedArray, RecordBatch, Table

The numbers (integers, floats, durations) go through the numeric kernel: the tolerance and equal_nan apply and the null values must be at the same positions. The other columns (booleans, strings, categories, instants, decimals, nested values and object columns) are compared by the library (equals), which never sees the tolerance or equal_nan.

A table is one leaf for the engine: compare reports it as different, with the name of the first column that differs and no row. Use the tools of the library to find the row.

>>> import pandas as pd
>>> from coola.equality import compare
>>> df1 = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3], "b": [4, 5, 6]})
>>> df2 = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3], "b": [4, 5, 7]})
>>> result = compare({"prices": df1}, {"prices": df2})
>>> result.path
('prices',)
>>> print(result.reason)
tables have different values: column 'b' differs

To support another library, write an adapter: a function that returns an object with a kind_name (the plural word used in the reasons), a same_structure(other, ctx) method and a columns() method that yields Columns, and register TableEqualityTester(adapter) for the type.

docs.title: Testers for Objects with Methods
docs.text:
• DataclassEqualityTester: Compare two instances of the same dataclass. The fields are compared through the registry, so they support the tolerance and equal_nan
  • EqualNanEqualityTester: Compare objects that have an equal(other, equal_nan) method
  • TolerantEqualEqualityTester: Compare objects that have both an allclose method and an equal method. allclose is used when atol or rtol is not zero, otherwise equal

docs.title: Other Library Testers
docs.text:
• JaxArrayEqualityTester: Compare JAX arrays
  • XarrayDataArrayEqualityTester: Compare xarray DataArrays
  • XarrayDatasetEqualityTester: Compare xarray Datasets
  • XarrayVariableEqualityTester: Compare xarray Variables

docs.title: Tester for Objects Without Value Semantics
ObjectAttributesEqualityTester
docs.text:
A plain class that does not define __eq__, an exception such as ValueError("a"), and a functools.partial are compared by identity: two equal-looking instances are different, unlike a dataclass or a pydantic model, which are compared field by field. This is the rule of "equal means ==", so the tester is not registered by default. Register it for the classes that must be compared by their attributes. It compares the entries of vars(obj), the slots of the class and of its parent classes, the args of an exception and the func, args and keywords of a partial, through the registry (so the tolerance and equal_nan apply), and reports the attribute that differs:

>>> from coola.equality import objects_are_equal
>>> from coola.equality.tester import (
...     DefaultEqualityTester,
...     EqualityTesterRegistry,
...     ObjectAttributesEqualityTester,
... )
>>> class Point:
...     def __init__(self, x):
...         self.x = x
>>> registry = EqualityTesterRegistry({object: DefaultEqualityTester()})
>>> objects_are_equal(Point(1), Point(1), registry=registry)
False
>>> registry.register(Point, ObjectAttributesEqualityTester())
>>> objects_are_equal(Point(1), Point(1), registry=registry)
True

To change the default registry, use register_equality_testers, for example register_equality_testers({BaseException: ObjectAttributesEqualityTester()}) to compare all the exceptions by their args.

docs.title: DefaultEqualityTester
docs.text:
The fallback tester used when no type-specific tester is registered:

>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from coola.equality.tester import DefaultEqualityTester
>>> config = EqualityConfig()
>>> tester = DefaultEqualityTester()
>>> # Works with any type using == comparison
>>> tester.objects_are_equal("hello", "hello", config)
True
>>> tester.objects_are_equal(42, 42, config)
True

docs.title: Default Registry
docs.text:
Get the default pre-configured registry:

>>> from coola.equality.tester import get_default_registry
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> registry = get_default_registry()
>>> config = EqualityConfig()
>>> # Use the registry to compare objects
>>> registry.objects_are_equal([1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 3], config)
True

The default registry includes testers for all supported types.

docs.title: Registering Custom Testers
docs.text:
You can register custom testers for your own types:

>>> from coola.equality.tester import register_equality_testers, DefaultEqualityTester
>>> # Create a custom class
>>> class MyClass:
...     def __init__(self, value):
...         self.value = value
>>> # Register a tester for MyClass (modifies the global default registry)
>>> # Note: This is skipped in doctests to avoid side effects on the global state
>>> register_equality_testers({MyClass: DefaultEqualityTester()})  # doctest: +SKIP

For more complex types, you would create a custom tester class (see "Creating Custom Testers" section below).

docs.title: Creating Custom Registries
docs.text:
You can create a custom registry with specific testers:

>>> from coola.equality.tester import (
...     EqualityTesterRegistry,
...     SequenceEqualityTester,
...     MappingEqualityTester,
...     DefaultEqualityTester,
... )
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> registry = EqualityTesterRegistry(
...     {
...         list: SequenceEqualityTester(),
...         dict: MappingEqualityTester(),
...         object: DefaultEqualityTester(),
...     }
... )
>>> config = EqualityConfig(registry=registry)
>>> registry.objects_are_equal([1, 2], [1, 2], config)
True

docs.title: Creating Custom Testers
docs.text:
To create a custom tester, inherit from BaseEqualityTester and implement objects_are_equal. It receives two objects of the same type and the Engine (ctx). For a leaf, return a verdict:

>>> from coola.equality import objects_are_equal
>>> from coola.equality.tester import BaseEqualityTester, register_equality_testers
>>> class Version:
...     def __init__(self, major: int, minor: int) -> None:
...         self.major = major
...         self.minor = minor
>>> class VersionEqualityTester(BaseEqualityTester[Version]):
...     def objects_are_equal(self, actual: Version, expected: Version, ctx) -> bool:
...         return (actual.major, actual.minor) == (expected.major, expected.minor) or ctx.fail(
...             lambda: (
...                 f"versions differ: {actual.major}.{actual.minor} vs {expected.major}.{expected.minor}"
...             )
...         )

ctx.fail(reason, *path) records the reason and returns False. A reason can be a callable: it is called only when the difference is explained (compare, assert_*), so objects_are_equal formats nothing. For a container, return the child pairs (actual, expected, path part); they are produced lazily and in the order the first difference is wanted. The engine compares them, applies the tolerance, detects the cycles and locates the difference:

>>> from coola.equality import AttributeName, compare
>>> class Point:
...     def __init__(self, x: float, y: float) -> None:
...         self.x = x
...         self.y = y
>>> class PointEqualityTester(BaseEqualityTester[Point]):
...     def objects_are_equal(self, actual: Point, expected: Point, ctx):
...         return (
...             (actual.x, expected.x, AttributeName("x")),
...             (actual.y, expected.y, AttributeName("y")),
...         )
>>> register_equality_testers({Point: PointEqualityTester()})  # doctest: +SKIP

Two testers are equal if they have the same type and the same attributes (==); a tester has no state but its configuration.

docs.title: Type Resolution with MRO
docs.text:
The registry uses Python's Method Resolution Order (MRO) to find testers:

>>> from coola.equality.tester import get_default_registry
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> from collections import OrderedDict
>>> registry = get_default_registry()
>>> config = EqualityConfig()
>>> # OrderedDict inherits from dict, but it has its own, more specific tester
>>> # And the tester checks that both objects have the same type
>>> od = OrderedDict([("a", 1), ("b", 2)])
>>> registry.objects_are_equal(od, {"a": 1, "b": 2}, config)
False
>>> # Comparing two OrderedDicts works (same type, same order)
>>> registry.objects_are_equal(od, OrderedDict([("a", 1), ("b", 2)]), config)
True
>>> registry.objects_are_equal(od, OrderedDict([("b", 2), ("a", 1)]), config)
False

This means you can register a tester for a base class and it will work for all subclasses.

docs.title: Recursive Comparison
docs.text:
Testers that handle collections (sequences, mappings) recursively use the registry to compare nested values:

>>> from coola.equality.tester import get_default_registry
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> registry = get_default_registry()
>>> config = EqualityConfig()
>>> # Nested structure: list containing dict containing list
>>> nested1 = [1, {"a": [2, 3]}, 4]
>>> nested2 = [1, {"a": [2, 3]}, 4]
>>> registry.objects_are_equal(nested1, nested2, config)
True

The recursion depth is controlled by the max_depth parameter in EqualityConfig.

docs.title: Performance Considerations
docs.text:
The registry includes an LRU cache for type lookups to optimize performance:

>>> from coola.equality.tester import get_default_registry
>>> registry = get_default_registry()
>>> # First lookup for a type will cache the result
>>> # Subsequent lookups for the same type will be faster
>>> # This is automatically managed internally

docs.title: Testing Framework Integration
docs.text:
Testers are commonly used in testing frameworks:

>>> from coola.equality.tester import get_default_registry
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> def assert_equal(actual, expected):
...     registry = get_default_registry()
...     config = EqualityConfig()
...     if not registry.objects_are_equal(actual, expected, config):
...         raise AssertionError(f"{actual} != {expected}")
>>> assert_equal([1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 3])  # Passes
>>> # assert_equal([1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 4])  # Would raise AssertionError

docs.title: Custom Type Support
docs.text:
Add support for your custom types:

>>> from coola.equality.tester import BaseEqualityTester, register_equality_testers
>>> class Point:
...     def __init__(self, x, y):
...         self.x = x
...         self.y = y
>>> class PointEqualityTester(BaseEqualityTester[Point]):
...     def objects_are_equal(self, actual, expected, ctx):
...         return ((actual.x, expected.x, 0), (actual.y, expected.y, 1))
>>> # Register the tester (modifies global state, so skipped in doctests)
>>> register_equality_testers({Point: PointEqualityTester()})  # doctest: +SKIP

docs.title: Tolerance-Based Comparisons
docs.text:
Use testers with tolerance configurations:

>>> from coola.equality import Tolerance
>>> import numpy as np
>>> from coola.equality.tester import get_default_registry
>>> from coola.equality.config import EqualityConfig
>>> registry = get_default_registry()
>>> config = EqualityConfig(tolerance=Tolerance(atol=1e-5, rtol=1e-5))
>>> registry.objects_are_equal(
...     np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0]),
...     np.array([1.00001, 2.00001, 3.00001]),
...     config,
... )
True

docs.title: Design Principles
docs.text:
The tester system is designed around several key principles:

  1. Type-based dispatch: Automatically selects the right tester based on object type

  2. Extensibility: Easy to add support for new types by registering custom testers

  3. One extension point: A tester is a class with one method, and it never recurses

  4. Iterative comparison: Nested structures are compared with an explicit stack, so there is no RecursionError

  5. Performance: LRU caching of type lookups for efficient repeated comparisons

  6. Configurability: EqualityConfig provides fine-grained control over comparison behavior

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• coola.equality: Main equality comparison functions
  • coola.registry: General registry pattern used by the tester system

docs.title: How to Add Support for a New Type
docs.text:
This tutorial walks through teaching coola about one custom class by registering an equality tester, a summarizer, and a hasher. Each one is registered in the default registry of its package, so the top-level functions (objects_are_equal, summarize, hash_object) pick it up automatically.

Prerequisites: You'll need to know a bit of Python.

docs.title: The custom class
docs.text:
>>> class Point:
...     def __init__(self, x: float, y: float) -> None:
...         self.x = x
...         self.y = y

docs.title: 1. Equality
docs.text:
Subclass BaseEqualityTester, implement objects_are_equal, then register it. A tester never recurses: it returns a verdict (True, or ctx.fail(reason) which returns False), or the (actual, expected, path part) pairs that must all be equal. The engine checks the identity and the type, applies the tolerance, detects the cycles and locates the difference.

>>> from coola.equality import objects_are_equal
>>> from coola.equality import AttributeName
>>> from coola.equality.tester import BaseEqualityTester, register_equality_testers
>>> class PointEqualityTester(BaseEqualityTester[Point]):
...     def objects_are_equal(self, actual: Point, expected: Point, ctx):
...         return (
...             (actual.x, expected.x, AttributeName("x")),
...             (actual.y, expected.y, AttributeName("y")),
...         )
>>> register_equality_testers({Point: PointEqualityTester()})
>>> objects_are_equal(Point(1, 2), Point(1, 2))
True
>>> objects_are_equal(Point(1, 2), Point(1, 3))
False

docs.title: 2. Summary
docs.text:
Subclass BaseSummarizer and describe one type: return a str for a leaf, or a Node (a header and the children) for a container. The summarizer does not recurse: the engine summarizes the children with the summarizer of their own type.

>>> from coola.summary import BaseSummarizer, SummaryConfig, register_summarizers, summarize
>>> class PointSummarizer(BaseSummarizer[Point]):
...     def summarize(self, data: Point, config: SummaryConfig, *, compact: bool) -> str:
...         return f"Point(x={data.x}, y={data.y})"
>>> register_summarizers({Point: PointSummarizer()})
>>> print(summarize(Point(1, 2)))
Point(x=1, y=2)

docs.title: 3. Hashing
docs.text:
Subclass BaseHasher. A hasher only describes the content of a type: encode returns a Node (a tag and the children to hash) or, for a leaf, tagged(tag, payload). The engine hashes the children with the hasher of their own type, so the hasher never receives the registry or the options of hash_object. A hasher must be consistent with equality: objects that compare equal must produce the same hash.

>>> from coola.hashing import BaseHasher, Node, hash_object, register_hashers
>>> class PointHasher(BaseHasher[Point]):
...     def encode(self, data: Point) -> Node:
...         return Node("Point", [data.x, data.y])
>>> register_hashers({Point: PointHasher()})
>>> hash_object(Point(1, 2)) == hash_object(Point(1, 2))
True

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Registries resolve by type using the MRO, so a tester registered for a base class also handles its subclasses unless a more specific one is registered.
  • Registering an already-registered type raises an error unless exist_ok=True.
  • Custom types nested in lists or dicts work out of the box once registered.

docs.title: Registering types from a third-party package
docs.text:
A package can add support for its own types without users calling register_* by hand. Expose a function that takes the registry and registers types on it, then declare it as an entry point in one of these groups:

Group Registry coola.equality.testers equality testers coola.summary.summarizers summarizers coola.hashing.hashers hashers coola.recursive.transformers recursive transformers coola.iterator.child_finders Iterator child finders coola.random.managers random managers 
# pyproject.toml of the plugin package
[project.entry-points."coola.summary.summarizers"]
mypkg = "mypkg.coola_plugin:register"

# mypkg/coola_plugin.py
def register(registry):
    registry.register_many({MyType: MySummarizer()})

Plugins run once, when the default registry is first built, after the built-in entries. A plugin that raises is skipped with a RuntimeWarning, and the failure is logged with its traceback. Set the COOLA_STRICT_PLUGINS=1 environment variable (e.g. in CI) to raise the failures instead, so a broken plugin is not missed: every plugin is still attempted, and all the failures are raised together as an ExceptionGroup, each annotated with the name and the group of the plugin.

Set COOLA_DISABLE_PLUGINS=1 to load no plugin at all (a reproducible run, or to check whether a plugin causes a conflict). To find out which plugins were loaded in the process, for example when objects_are_equal or a hash is not what you expect, call get_loaded_plugins():

>>> from coola.equality.tester import get_default_registry
>>> from coola.utils.singleton import get_loaded_plugins
>>> get_default_registry()  # doctest: +SKIP
>>> [(plugin.group, plugin.name, plugin.value) for plugin in get_loaded_plugins()]  # doctest: +SKIP
[('coola.equality.testers', 'mypkg', 'mypkg.coola_plugin:register')]

A plugin is listed after it was applied to a default registry, which loads its plugins the first time it is built.

docs.title: Factory Utilities
docs.text:
This page describes the coola.factory package, which provides utilities to dynamically import and instantiate Python objects from configuration dictionaries.

Prerequisites: You'll need to know a bit of Python. For a refresher, see the Python tutorial.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The coola.factory package makes it possible to build objects (classes or functions) from plain data, such as a dictionary loaded from JSON or YAML. This is a common pattern for configuration- driven code: instead of hard-coding which class to instantiate, you describe it with a fully-qualified name and a set of keyword arguments.

The package provides:

  • import_object: import an object (class, function, ...) from its fully qualified name
  • instantiate_object: instantiate an object given a target and its arguments
  • factory: a universal factory function that imports and instantiates an object from a fully qualified name, without requiring prior registration
  • resolve_object: return an object as-is, or build it from a factory configuration
  • is_object_config: check if a configuration dictionary targets a given class
  • OBJECT_TARGET / OBJECT_INIT: the configuration keys used by the functions above

Unlike coola.registry, which requires classes to be registered under a key before they can be looked up, coola.factory resolves objects directly from their fully qualified Python path, so any importable object can be used without registration.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
These rules hold for every function of the package. Each one is enforced in a single place, not by the discipline of each entry point.

Property Statement Explicit target The object to import or call is named only by the _target_ string. Every other key is an argument, passed unchanged, by keyword. The reserved keys are _target_, _init_ and _allowed_prefixes_. No collision No parameter of the API can shadow an argument of the target: the target receives every key that is not reserved, whatever its name (obj, cls, config, ...). Top level only _target_ is resolved once per call, at the top level. A nested dictionary is data and is passed unchanged. Import once, call once The target is imported once per call and called once. Nothing else is imported or called. Fails loudly A target that does not exist raises ImportError with one message, whichever function is used. A wrong type raises TypeError. A default is never substituted for a missing object. Check before call When cls is given, a target that is known not to build a cls is refused before it is called. The result is checked again after the call. With strict=True, a target whose result type is unknown is refused too. Opt-in restriction allowed_prefixes is checked against the string before the module is imported. An empty list allows nothing. Without it, any importable object can be called. Policy comes from code The allow-list is an argument of the caller. resolve_object ignores the _allowed_prefixes_ key of a configuration, so the data cannot set, widen or narrow the list. No nested configuration under an allow-list With allowed_prefixes, an argument that is itself a configuration (a dict with _target_) is refused. Resolve it first, with the same list. Public constructors only _init_ is "__init__" (default) or the name of a public class method or static method that returns an instance of the class. A name that starts with _ is refused. Predicates do not import is_object_config imports nothing by default. allowed_prefixes or import_target=True opt in. A malformed configuration is False; a violation of the allow-list raises. Pure, stateless The configuration is never modified. The package keeps no registry, cache or lock, so it is safe to call from any thread and after a fork. Lazy Nothing is imported at import time except the standard library. A target is imported when it is named. Keyword-only options allowed_prefixes, import_target, strict, _init_ and _allowed_prefixes_ are keyword-only.

docs.title: Importing an object by name
docs.text:
import_object dynamically imports a class, function, or other object using its fully qualified name (module_path.object_name):

>>> from coola.factory import import_object
>>> cls = import_object("collections.Counter")
>>> cls()
Counter()
>>> fn = import_object("math.isclose")
>>> fn(1.0, 1.0)
True

It raises a TypeError if object_path is not a string, and an ImportError if the path cannot be resolved.

docs.title: Instantiating an object from a configuration
docs.text:
factory combines import_object with instantiation. It takes a _target_ key with the fully qualified name of a class or function, and forwards the remaining arguments to it:

>>> from coola.factory import factory
>>> factory("collections.Counter", [1, 2, 1, 3])
Counter({1: 2, 2: 1, 3: 1})

Because configurations are often expressed as dictionaries (e.g. parsed from JSON or YAML), it is common to unpack the configuration into factory. The OBJECT_TARGET constant ("_target_") is provided so that code does not need to hard-code the literal key name:

>>> from coola.factory import factory, OBJECT_TARGET
>>> config = {OBJECT_TARGET: "collections.Counter", "a": 4, "b": 2}
>>> factory(**config)
Counter({'a': 4, 'b': 2})

docs.title: Controlling how the object is created
docs.text:
By default, factory calls the class, which runs __new__ and __init__. The special OBJECT_INIT key ("_init_") names a public class method or static method to call instead, for example an alternative constructor. The method must return an instance of the class. A name that starts with _ (such as "__new__") is refused. _init_ is ignored when the target is a function:

>>> from coola.factory import factory, OBJECT_INIT
>>> factory("collections.OrderedDict", ["a", "b"], _init_="fromkeys")
OrderedDict({'a': None, 'b': None})
>>> factory("collections.OrderedDict", a=1)
OrderedDict({'a': 1})

docs.title: Resolving an object or a configuration
docs.text:
resolve_object is convenient in code that accepts either an already-built instance or a configuration dictionary. If the input is already an instance of the expected type, it is returned unchanged; if it is a dict with a _target_ key, it is built:

>>> from datetime import date
>>> from coola.factory import resolve_object
>>> resolve_object(date(2020, 1, 1), cls=date)
datetime.date(2020, 1, 1)
>>> resolve_object({"_target_": "datetime.date", "year": 2020, "month": 1, "day": 1}, cls=date)
datetime.date(2020, 1, 1)

A dict that has the key _target_ is always a configuration, whatever cls is: the key is reserved, so such a dict cannot be passed through resolve_object as data. Any other object, including a dict without _target_, is returned as is if it is an instance of cls.

docs.title: Nested configurations
docs.text:
_target_ is resolved at the top level only. A nested dictionary that has a _target_ key is passed to the target as a plain dict, it is not instantiated (unlike Hydra, which instantiates the nested configurations):

>>> from coola.factory import resolve_object
>>> config = {
...     "_target_": "collections.OrderedDict",
...     "when": {"_target_": "datetime.date", "year": 2020, "month": 1, "day": 1},
... }
>>> resolve_object(config)
OrderedDict({'when': {'_target_': 'datetime.date', 'year': 2020, 'month': 1, 'day': 1}})

This is deliberate: allowed_prefixes (and _allowed_prefixes_) applies to the one _target_ of the call, so a configuration cannot make coola import more modules by nesting targets. With an allow-list, a nested configuration (a top-level argument that is a dict with _target_) is refused with a ValueError, because the target could resolve it without the list. To build the nested object, resolve it yourself, with the same restrictions, and pass the result:

>>> from datetime import date
>>> when = resolve_object(
...     {"_target_": "datetime.date", "year": 2020, "month": 1, "day": 1},
...     cls=date,
...     allowed_prefixes=["datetime"],
... )
>>> resolve_object({"_target_": "collections.OrderedDict", "when": when})
OrderedDict({'when': datetime.date(2020, 1, 1)})

docs.title: Security: restricting the targets
docs.text:
!!! danger "Only resolve configurations that you trust"

`import_object`, `factory` and `resolve_object` import and call whatever the `_target_` names
(for example `"os.system"`). Never resolve a configuration that comes from untrusted input.

If a configuration cannot be fully trusted (for example, a file edited by users), restrict the modules that _target_ may reference with allowed_prefixes. A target is allowed if it is equal to a prefix, or starts with the prefix followed by a dot:

>>> from coola.factory import resolve_object
>>> config = {"_target_": "collections.Counter", "a": 2}
>>> resolve_object(config, allowed_prefixes=["collections"])
Counter({'a': 2})
>>> resolve_object({"_target_": "os.getcwd"}, allowed_prefixes=["collections"])
Traceback (most recent call last):
    ...
ImportError: Object path 'os.getcwd' is not allowed. Allowed prefixes: ['collections']

allowed_prefixes is checked before the module is imported. resolve_object ignores the _allowed_prefixes_ key of a configuration: the list always comes from the code of the caller, so the data cannot set, widen or narrow it. It is also available in resolve_loader, resolve_saver, is_object_config, is_loader_config and is_saver_config. For factory, use the _allowed_prefixes_ key.

This is a mitigation, not a sandbox: it limits what can be called, not the arguments it is called with. Only allow objects that are safe to call with arbitrary arguments.

!!! danger "Never allow a prefix that contains a function that resolves its arguments"

A prefix that contains a function that imports or resolves objects from its arguments (any
`resolve_*`, `import_object`, `importlib`, `pickle`, `eval`, `os.system`, ...) makes the list
worthless. In particular, `"coola"` and `"coola.factory"` must never be allowed prefixes.
For example, `coola.io.resolve_loader` resolves its `loader` argument without the allow-list:

```python
factory(
    "coola.io.resolve_loader",
    loader={"_target_": "os.getcwd"},
    _allowed_prefixes_=["coola.io"],
)  # calls os.getcwd
```

The same holds for a path that is checked but not the module that defines the object: a
re-export (`mypkg.helper` defined elsewhere) is allowed by `"mypkg"`.

Allow the narrowest prefix, and resolve nested configurations yourself, with the same list.

docs.title: Checking if a configuration targets a class
docs.text:
is_object_config checks whether the _target_ of a configuration resolves to (or returns, for functions with a type-hinted return value) a given class. The module of the target is not imported to answer: if it is not imported yet, the configuration is not a configuration for the class (importing a module runs its top-level code). Pass allowed_prefixes (a matching target is imported if needed) or import_target=True (any target is imported) to import it; do this only for a trusted configuration. A function whose return type hint cannot be resolved is not a configuration for the class:

>>> from coola.factory import is_object_config
>>> from collections import Counter
>>> is_object_config({"_target_": "collections.Counter", "iterable": [1, 2, 1, 3]}, Counter)
True

See the reference for the complete API.

docs.title: Hashing Objects
docs.text:
This page describes the coola.hashing package, which provides deterministic hashing of Python objects, including nested data structures.

Prerequisites: You'll need to know a bit of Python. For a refresher, see the Python tutorial.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The coola.hashing package computes a stable hash string for arbitrary objects, including nested containers. Unlike Python's built-in hash(), which is randomized across processes for strings by default and is not guaranteed to be stable across Python versions, coola.hashing always returns the same hash for equivalent data. The hashes are content fingerprints for identity, caching and deduplication: they are not cryptographic guarantees, so do not use them for passwords, signatures or integrity against an attacker. It offers:

  1. Deterministic hashes - the same input always produces the same output
  2. Recursive hashing - nested list, dict, tuple, and other containers are hashed element by element
  3. Type-specific hashers - each Python type is handled by a hasher tailored to it
  4. Extensibility - register hashers for custom types

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
The default registry is designed around the following properties.

Property Statement Equality-consistent Objects that are equal for objects_are_equal have the same hash. The reverse can fail for a few types that share a hash on purpose, e.g. a list subclass and a list, or a NumPy float64 and a float. Deterministic The same value gives the same hash across calls, processes, machines and operating systems. It does not depend on PYTHONHASHSEED, on object addresses or on the iteration order of a set. Type-sensitive Values of different types hash differently, even when their text looks the same: 1, 1.0, True, "1", b"1", memoryview(b"1") and [1] are all distinct. Structure-sensitive Nesting and item boundaries matter: [[1], 2], [1, [2]] and [1, 2] are distinct, and so are ["ab", "c"] and ["a", "bc"]. Order rules Ordered containers are order-sensitive ([1, 2] differs from [2, 1]). Unordered containers are not ({1, 2} equals {2, 1}). OrderedDict is ordered, like in objects_are_equal. Composable A container hash is built only from the digests of its children, resolved through the registry, so each type can be extended independently. Fixed width, user-chosen The output is a lowercase hex string of length characters (an even number between 2 and 128, default 64). It is the first length characters of the full 128-character hash. No silent false equality An unsupported type fails loudly by default. The ignore_unhashable placeholder is an explicit, documented opt-out that warns once per type. Cycle-safe A container that contains itself raises ValueError, whichever hasher is registered for it. Any depth No RecursionError, whatever the nesting or the caller's stack: the engine uses an explicit stack. The depth is bounded by memory only. Linear cost The cost is linear in the number of objects, not of paths: a container reachable by several paths (a DAG) is hashed once per call. Pure, thread-safe Hashing has no side effect and keeps no global state (no thread-local, no lock), so a registry and a hasher can be shared by threads. Reading the filesystem is an explicit opt-in (ResolvedPathHasher). Errors propagate An exception of a hasher propagates unchanged. An invalid length raises ValueError before any traversal. A secret is never hashed unless asked for, wherever it is. Cross-library scalars Subclasses of bool, int, float and complex (such as np.float64) hash like the equivalent builtin, independently of the library version. Consistent with siblings Dataclasses and pydantic models are entered, only their compare=True fields count (like objects_are_equal); options are keyword-only; one extension point (encode).

Not guaranteed:

  • Stability across versions of coola. The format can change in a major release (the format version is part of every digest, so two formats are never confused). get_stable_registry() makes the stable identifiers independent of the installed plugins.
  • Stability across versions of a library when the library changes what an object means (the dtype names of pandas, for example).
  • Hashes of classes that are renamed or moved. A dataclass, a model, an enum and a custom object hash with their qualified class name.
  • Cycles. A cyclic structure raises ValueError, although objects_are_equal accepts it.
  • Resistance to an adversary. Do not use a hash as a security boundary.

docs.title: The encoding
docs.text:
Every hash is derived from one rule. A hasher describes a value as a leaf (tag, a NUL byte and a payload) or as a node (a tag and the children to hash). The engine computes

digest(x)  = BLAKE2b-512(preimage, person = b"coola-hash-2")          # 64 bytes
leaf       : preimage = 0x00 + tag + 0x00 + payload
node       : preimage = 0x01 + tag + 0x00 + e1 + e2 + ... + en         # one entry per child
entry      : 0xFF + 64-byte digest of the child, or, if the child is a leaf of at most 64 bytes,
             its size (one byte) + the leaf itself ("inlined leaf")
unordered  : the entries (a key and its value) are sorted
hash_object(x, length=n) = digest(x).hex()[:n]

The entries are self-delimiting (a marker 0xFF and a fixed width, or a size), which makes the concatenation unambiguous without other delimiters. A short leaf (a number, a short string) is part of the preimage of its parent instead of a BLAKE2b call of its own, which is what makes the flat containers fast. The leading 0x00/0x01 byte makes a leaf and a node with the same tag different. The registry dispatches on type(data) along the Method Resolution Order, so the most specific registered type wins. A scalar and a standard-library container have a constant tag, so a subclass hashes like its base; a user-defined class (dataclass, model, enum, custom object) uses its qualified name.

docs.title: Choices that may surprise you
docs.text:
Question Answer [1, 2] vs (1, 2) Different. They are different types, and each sequence family has its own tag. list vs deque Different, for the same reason. 1 vs 1.0 vs True All different. 1 == 1.0 in Python, but the identity of a hash is the type and the value. {"a": 1, "b": 2} vs {"b": 2, "a": 1} Same. Insertion order is not semantic for mappings. dict vs OrderedDict Different, like in objects_are_equal. OrderedDict with the same items in another order Different. Order is the point of an OrderedDict, and objects_are_equal also says they are different. set vs frozenset Different. Both are order-insensitive. set vs list with the same items Different. str vs bytes Different. IntEnum / StrEnum member vs its value Different. Enum members are not collapsed into int or str. Subclass instance vs base instance Same for scalars normalised to the builtin (e.g. NumPy floats), and for subclasses that dispatch to the same hasher and tag (e.g. a list subclass). 
>>> from coola.hashing import hash_object
>>> hash_object([1, 2]) != hash_object((1, 2))
True
>>> hash_object(1) != hash_object(1.0)
True
>>> hash_object({"a": 1, "b": 2}) == hash_object({"b": 2, "a": 1})
True
>>> hash_object({1, 2, 3}) == hash_object({3, 2, 1})
True

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
The simplest way to hash an object is hash_object:

>>> from coola.hashing import hash_object
>>> len(hash_object({"a": 1, "b": "abc"}))
64

hash_object uses the default global registry, which is pre-configured with hashers for common built-in types (str, bytes, int, float, bool, complex, list, tuple, dict, set, date, datetime, Path, ...). The same input always returns the same hash:

>>> from coola.hashing import hash_object
>>> hash_object([1, 2, 3]) == hash_object([1, 2, 3])
True

The options (registry, length and ignore_unhashable) are keyword-only, because hash_object(data, 32) would pass 32 as the registry.

docs.title: Controlling the Hash Length
docs.text:
The length argument controls the length of the returned hex string (an even number between 2 and 128, defaults to 64). A bool or a float is rejected like an odd number. Hashes of different lengths are prefixes of one another: hash_object(x, length=16) is the first 16 characters of hash_object(x, length=128). A short identifier can therefore be matched against a stored longer hash with startswith, and changing the length later does not change the start of the hashes you already have.

>>> from coola.hashing import hash_object
>>> len(hash_object("hello", length=16))
16
>>> hash_object([1, 2], length=128).startswith(hash_object([1, 2], length=16))
True

docs.title: Handling Unhashable Types
docs.text:
By default, hash_object raises a KeyError if it encounters an object (including a nested one) for which no hasher is registered:

>>> from coola.hashing import hash_object
>>> try:
...     hash_object(object())
... except KeyError as e:
...     print("Error")
Error

Pass ignore_unhashable=True to replace unhashable objects with a deterministic placeholder hash instead of raising an error. The placeholder only depends on the type, so it is lossy: any two unsupported objects of the same type hash the same. A UserWarning is emitted once per type in each call, so a silent false equality does not hide in a cache key.

>>> import warnings
>>> from coola.hashing import hash_object
>>> with warnings.catch_warnings():
...     warnings.simplefilter("ignore")
...     print(len(hash_object(object(), ignore_unhashable=True)))
64

Self-referencing containers (e.g. a list that contains itself) raise a ValueError. There is no limit on the nesting depth and no RecursionError, and a container that is reachable by several paths is hashed once, so a structure with 2**60 paths takes a linear time:

>>> from coola.hashing import hash_object
>>> data = []
>>> for _ in range(60):
...     data = [data, data]
>>> len(hash_object(data))
64

docs.title: Supported Types
docs.text:
The default registry hashes only the following types (and their subclasses):

Type Notes str UTF-8 text, no Unicode normalisation bytes, bytearray A bytes and a bytearray with the same content hash differently int, float, complex, bool, None The repr of the builtin value, so a NumPy scalar that is a float hashes like the same float Enum (including IntEnum, StrEnum) The qualified class name and the member name, not the value list, tuple, deque, other Sequence Order matters. One tag per family: a list and a tuple with the same items hash differently NamedTuple Tagged with the class and field names, so it differs from a plain tuple dict, other Mapping Independent of the order of the keys OrderedDict Own tag. The order of the keys matters, like in objects_are_equal set, frozenset Independent of the iteration order. A set and a frozenset hash differently date, datetime, time ISO 8601 form; aware datetime and time are normalised to UTC timedelta, timezone The repr of the value uuid.UUID, zoneinfo.ZoneInfo The string form (the UUID text, the zone key) decimal.Decimal The normalised value: Decimal('1.0') and Decimal('1.00') have the same hash fractions.Fraction The numerator and the denominator in lowest terms range The items, not the arguments: range(0) and range(5, 5) have the same hash, in constant time NumPy scalars (np.float32, np.int64...) Like the equivalent builtin value: np.float32(1.5) hashes like 1.5 dataclass instances The qualified class name and the fields, hashed through the registry objects with a __coola_hash__() method The value of their __coola_hash__() (see SupportsCoolaHash), tagged with the class name pathlib.PurePath, pathlib.Path The POSIX form of the path as written, without touching the filesystem pydantic BaseModel (if pydantic installed) The qualified class name and the fields, hashed through the registry numpy.ndarray, torch.Tensor, jax.Array The dtype, the shape and the values (not the memory layout, the device or requires_grad); -0.0 hashes like 0.0 pandas, polars data frames and series The names, the dtypes, the index (pandas) and the values pyarrow arrays and tables The names, the types and the values; the chunk layout is ignored xarray DataArray, Dataset, Variable The dimensions, the values, the coordinates, the attributes and the name

The array libraries are only imported if they are installed. A NumPy array and a PyTorch tensor with the same content hash differently. Your own classes still need a registered hasher (a class with a __coola_hash__() method and a dataclass work without registration, see below). Otherwise hash_object raises a TypeNotRegisteredError that lists the remedies (or hashes a placeholder with ignore_unhashable=True). To change what is part of the hash, register your own hasher, for example for NumPy arrays:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> from coola.hashing import BaseHasher, digest, hash_object, register_hashers, tagged
>>> class NumpyHasher(BaseHasher[np.ndarray]):
...     def encode(self, data):
...         header = f"{data.dtype}|{data.shape}|".encode()
...         return tagged("array", header + digest(np.ascontiguousarray(data).tobytes()))
>>> register_hashers({np.ndarray: NumpyHasher()}, exist_ok=True)
>>> hash_object({"a": np.arange(3)}) == hash_object({"a": np.arange(3)})
True
>>> hash_object(np.arange(3)) == hash_object(np.arange(3).astype(float))
False

The hash values can change between versions of coola: do not persist them as a stable identifier across upgrades without checking. The unit tests keep one golden vector per hasher family (tests/unit/hashing/test_golden.py), so a change of the format is a deliberate edit.

hash_object uses the default registry, which changes when code calls register_hashers or when an installed package declares a coola.hashing.hashers entry point. The identifiers generate_stable_content_id and generate_stable_uuid5 use get_stable_registry() instead (the built-in hashers only) when no registry is given, so they do not depend on the installed packages. Passing another registry opts out of this stability.

docs.title: Behavior per Type
docs.text:
• str: tag str, UTF-8 payload. There is no Unicode normalisation, so a precomposed é and e followed by a combining accent are different strings. A lone surrogate (for example in a file name from os.fsdecode) is encoded with surrogatepass, which never collides with a valid string.
  • bytes, bytearray: tagged with their type name, payload is the raw content.
  • bool, int, float, complex, None: tag is the type name, payload is the builtin repr, which round-trips exactly. bool is checked before int, so True and 1 differ. -0.0 hashes like 0.0 (they are equal), and all NaNs hash the same.
  • Enum: the qualified class name and the member name, not the member value.
  • list, tuple, deque, other Sequence: the tag is the sequence family, the payload is the child hashes in order. A named tuple also includes its class name and field names, so Point(1, 2) differs from (1, 2). Strings and bytes are never iterated as sequences.
  • dict, other Mapping: each item is key_hash + value_hash, and items are sorted by the key hash, not by the key. Keys do not need to be orderable and can have mixed types. OrderedDict is the exception: its items are hashed in order, so two OrderedDicts with the same items in a different order hash differently, like objects_are_equal says they are different. Register MappingHasher(tag, ordered=True) for another mapping type whose order is meaningful.
  • set, frozenset: the sorted item hashes under the set or frozenset tag.
  • date, datetime, time: tagged with the concrete class name, payload is the ISO 8601 string. Aware datetimes are converted to UTC first, so the same instant in two time zones hashes the same, while a naive and an aware datetime differ. An aware time is normalised the same way (the offset is subtracted from the time of day), so equal aware times hash the same. timedelta and timezone use their repr.
  • Path, PurePath: the POSIX form of the path as written, with no filesystem access, so the hash is portable across machines. A relative and an absolute path to the same location differ. Register ResolvedPathHasher to resolve symlinks, .. and relative paths first; the result then depends on the filesystem and on the current working directory. Hashing the content of a file is a different operation that is not provided by a hasher.
  • pydantic BaseModel: the qualified model class name plus the fields, hashed as a mapping through the registry (extra fields included). Two different model classes with the same values therefore differ. A secret (SecretStr, SecretBytes) is a value with a hasher, so the policy is the one of the registry and applies wherever the secret is (in a model, a dict, a dataclass...). The default registry raises a ValueError (the message never contains the secret). To change the policy, build a registry with get_secret_hashers:
  • "error" (default) raises a ValueError,
  • "reveal" hashes the real secret value,
  • "exclude" hashes a constant, so objects that differ only by a secret hash the same (the position of the secret is kept).
>>> from pydantic import BaseModel, SecretStr
>>> from coola.hashing import get_default_registry, get_secret_hashers
>>> class Creds(BaseModel):
...     user: str
...     password: SecretStr
>>> registry = get_default_registry().copy()
>>> registry.register_many(get_secret_hashers("exclude"), exist_ok=True)
>>> registry.hash(Creds(user="a", password="x")) == registry.hash(Creds(user="a", password="y"))
True
  • Dataclasses: the qualified class name plus the field values. The default registry hashes every dataclass with DataclassHasher (a fallback, see Fallbacks), without registration.
  • Objects with their own hash method: the result of hash, tagged with the qualified class name (see Custom Objects).
>>> from dataclasses import dataclass
>>> from coola.hashing import hash_object
>>> @dataclass
... class Point:
...     x: int
...     y: int
>>> hash_object(Point(1, 2)) == hash_object(Point(1, 2))
True
>>> hash_object(Point(1, 2)) != hash_object({"x": 1, "y": 2})
True

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: Situation Behavior length is odd or outside 2 to 128 ValueError No hasher for the type TypeNotRegisteredError (a KeyError) naming the type, or a lossy placeholder with ignore_unhashable=True Self-referencing container ValueError("Cannot hash a self-referencing <type>.") Deep nesting Works: the only limit is the memory An exception of a hasher Propagates unchanged Secret with the default registry ValueError, without leaking the value

docs.title: Type-Specific Hashers
docs.text:
Each hasher implements the BaseHasher interface and describes one kind of object with encode; the engine hashes the children of a Node with the hasher of their own type. The built-in hashers include:

  • StringHasher - hashes str objects, namespaced by the str type tag
  • BytesHasher - hashes bytes and bytearray objects, namespaced by the type tag
  • EnumHasher - hashes Enum members by class name and member name
  • ReprHasher - hashes an object's repr(); used for numeric types (int, float, complex, bool) because repr() preserves floating point precision
  • StrHasher - hashes an object's str(); more human-readable but does not guarantee round-trip accuracy for floats
  • DatetimeHasher - hashes date/datetime/time objects via their ISO 8601 representation
  • PathHasher - hashes pathlib.Path objects via their POSIX form as written, so hashes do not depend on the filesystem or the working directory
  • ResolvedPathHasher - opt-in hasher that resolves the path first (symlinks, .., relative paths), so logically equivalent paths hash the same. The result depends on the filesystem and the current working directory
  • SequenceHasher - hashes list, tuple and the other Sequence types element by element, under a configurable type tag
  • MappingHasher - hashes dict and other Mapping types, sorted by key hash so that insertion order does not affect the result (unless ordered=True)
  • SetHasher - hashes set and frozenset, sorted by item hash
  • DataclassHasher - hashes dataclass instances from the class name and the field values (used for every dataclass by the default registry)
  • PydanticModelHasher - hashes pydantic BaseModel objects from the class name and the fields
  • SecretHasher / get_secret_hashers - the policy ("error", "reveal", "exclude") for SecretStr and SecretBytes, wherever they are
  • ContentHasher - hashes objects that implement the SupportsCoolaHash protocol (i.e. that define a __coola_hash__() method that returns their content), namespaced by the class name
  • NumpyArrayHasher, TorchTensorHasher, JaxArrayHasher - hash the dtype, the shape and the values of an array or of a tensor (require the corresponding package)
  • PandasSeriesHasher, PandasDataFrameHasher, PolarsSeriesHasher, PolarsDataFrameHasher - hash the names, the dtypes and the values of a series or of a data frame (require the corresponding package)
  • PyarrowArrayHasher, PyarrowTableHasher - hash the types and the values of a PyArrow array or table (require pyarrow)
  • XarrayHasher - hashes the dimensions, the values, the coordinates, the attributes and the name of an xarray DataArray, Dataset or Variable (requires xarray)

A hasher describes the content of a type with encode; the engine does the hashing. Each hasher can be used directly to see that description:

>>> from coola.hashing import SequenceHasher, StrHasher
>>> StrHasher().encode(1)
b'str:int\x001'
>>> SequenceHasher("list").encode([1, 2, 3])
Node(tag='list', children=[1, 2, 3], ordered=True, group=1)

docs.title: The Hasher Registry
docs.text:
HasherRegistry maps Python types to hasher instances and dispatches to the most specific registered hasher for an object's type, using the Method Resolution Order (MRO):

>>> from coola.hashing import HasherRegistry, SequenceHasher, StrHasher
>>> from collections.abc import Sequence
>>> registry = HasherRegistry({object: StrHasher(), Sequence: SequenceHasher()})
>>> len(registry.hash([1, 2, 3]))
64

docs.title: The Default Registry
docs.text:
!!! tip "Unambiguous alias"

`get_default_registry` exists in several `coola` subpackages with different return types.
`get_default_hasher_registry` is an alias of the same function with a more explicit name, which avoids
import collisions.

get_default_registry returns the singleton registry used internally by hash_object. Because it is a singleton, any modification made via register_hashers affects every subsequent call:

>>> from coola.hashing import register_hashers, StrHasher
>>> class Point:
...     def __init__(self, x, y):
...         self.x, self.y = x, y
...
...     def __str__(self):
...         return f"Point({self.x}, {self.y})"
>>> register_hashers({Point: StrHasher()})

register_hashers raises an AlreadyRegisteredError if a type is already registered, unless exist_ok=True is passed to overwrite the existing registration.

If you need an isolated registry instead of mutating the shared singleton, create a HasherRegistry instance directly, as shown above.

docs.title: Fallbacks
docs.text:
A registry maps types to hashers, so it cannot say "every dataclass" or "every class with a __coola_hash__() method". HasherRegistry.register_fallback(predicate, hasher) registers a hasher for the types that satisfy a predicate. A fallback is only used if no hasher is registered for the type or for one of its parent types (object excluded), so a hasher registered for a type always wins. The default registry has two fallbacks: dataclasses (DataclassHasher) and the classes with a __coola_hash__() method (ContentHasher). A dataclass that also defines __coola_hash__() uses the dataclass hasher.

>>> from coola.hashing import HasherRegistry, SequenceHasher, DataclassHasher
>>> from dataclasses import dataclass, is_dataclass
>>> registry = HasherRegistry({list: SequenceHasher()})
>>> registry.register_fallback(is_dataclass, DataclassHasher())
>>> @dataclass
... class Point:
...     x: int
>>> registry.find_hasher(Point)
DataclassHasher()

The hasher registered for object is the last resort: the fallbacks are tried before it. A predicate can only be registered once (AlreadyRegisteredError, unless exist_ok=True, which keeps its position); if several predicates match, the first registered one wins.

HasherRegistry.unregister_fallback(predicate) removes a fallback and returns its hasher, clear() removes the hashers and the fallbacks, and equal() compares the fallbacks (predicates, in order, and hashers) as well as the hashers.

docs.title: Custom Objects
docs.text:
For a class that cannot be a dataclass, define a __coola_hash__() method that returns the content of the object (any value that can be hashed). ContentHasher hashes that value through the registry, with the qualified class name as tag, so two classes with the same content hash differently and the object cannot bypass the protections of the engine (cycles, depth, length):

>>> from coola.hashing import hash_object
>>> class Point:
...     def __init__(self, x, y):
...         self.x, self.y = x, y
...
...     def __coola_hash__(self):
...         return (self.x, self.y)
>>> hash_object(Point(1, 2)) == hash_object(Point(1, 2))
True
>>> hash_object(Point(1, 2)) == hash_object((1, 2))
False

docs.title: Writing a Hasher
docs.text:
A hasher only describes the content of a type: encode(data) returns the bytes of a leaf (tagged(tag, payload)) or a Node(tag, children). The engine hashes the children with the hasher of their own type, handles the cycles, the shared containers and the depth, and applies length and ignore_unhashable. When you add a hasher, follow these rules so that it keeps the guarantees above:

  1. Pick a unique, stable tag, and never reuse the tag of another type family. The tag is a constant of the hasher, except for user-defined classes, whose qualified name is the identity.
  2. Return tagged(...) for a leaf, or a Node for a container. Reduce a big buffer with digest(buffer) before it enters tagged.
  3. Do not call the registry and do not recurse: put the children in the Node. Use ordered=False (and group=2 for a key and a value) when the order is not meaningful.
  4. Do not depend on object addresses, id(), hash(), the iteration order of dicts or sets, the locale, the time zone or the clock.
  5. Register the hasher for the most general type whose semantics are identical, and for the exact type where they are not.
  6. Test stability, equality-consistency, type-sensitivity, item boundaries and order.

docs.title: Identifiers
docs.text:
This page describes the coola.identifier package, which provides functions to generate identifiers for nested data structures and for time-ordered records.

Prerequisites: You'll need to know a bit of Python. For a refresher, see the Python tutorial.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The coola.identifier package provides several identifier generators, covering two different problems:

Function Same data → same ID? Format Use case generate_stable_uuid5 UUID string Reproducible ID, needs a valid UUID (e.g. UUID DB column) generate_stable_content_id hex string Reproducible ID, full hash strength (dedup, caching) generate_ulid 26-char string Unique, sortable-by-creation-time ID generate_uuid7 UUID string Unique, sortable-by-creation-time ID, needs a valid UUID generate_snowflake_id 64-bit integer Unique, sortable-by-creation-time ID as a single integer generate_object_id 24-char hex string Unique, sortable-by-creation-time ID, never blocks/raises generate_checksummed_id grouped string Random ID with a check symbol, for identifiers humans retype

generate_stable_uuid5 and generate_stable_content_id are content-addressed: they are built on top of coola.hashing's hash_object, so calling them twice with equal data (regardless of e.g. mapping insertion order) always returns the same identifier. generate_ulid, generate_uuid7, generate_snowflake_id and generate_object_id are not derived from data at all: they mint a fresh, unique value every call, ordered by creation time instead.

The four time-ordered generators (generate_ulid, generate_uuid7, generate_snowflake_id, and generate_object_id) each have a matching extract_*_timestamp* function (extract_ulid_timestamp_ms, extract_uuid7_timestamp_ms, extract_snowflake_timestamp_ms, and extract_object_id_timestamp) that recovers the timestamp packed into a previously generated identifier.

docs.title: generate_stable_uuid5
docs.text:
generate_stable_uuid5 computes a stable, reproducible UUID for a nested data structure. It hashes data with hash_object (so mapping key order, for example, does not affect the result), then derives a deterministic uuid.uuid5 from that digest under a fixed namespace:

>>> from coola.identifier import generate_stable_uuid5
>>> generate_stable_uuid5({"source": "cats.txt", "page": 1})  # doctest: +ELLIPSIS
'...'
>>> generate_stable_uuid5({"page": 1, "source": "cats.txt"}) == generate_stable_uuid5(
...     {"source": "cats.txt", "page": 1}
... )
True

Use it when the identifier must be a valid UUID string, e.g. to populate a UUID-typed database column. A UUID has 122 random bits, so its collision resistance is bounded by its width (birthday bound 2^61), regardless of how strong the underlying hash used by hash_object is.

Pass a custom namespace to derive UUIDs in a separate identifier space, e.g. to avoid collisions with UUIDs minted by another system for unrelated data:

>>> import uuid
>>> from coola.identifier import generate_stable_uuid5
>>> namespace = uuid.uuid4()
>>> generate_stable_uuid5({"a": 1}, namespace=namespace)  # doctest: +ELLIPSIS
'...'

!!! warning

The hash format changed in `coola` 2.0 (see the [migration guide](../migration/v1.1_to_v2.0.md)):
every identifier changes, and an identifier stored with an older version must be regenerated.

The UUID `generate_stable_uuid5` returns for a given input is stable only as long as
`hash_object` (and the hashers resolved for the types in the data) keep producing the same
digest. Do not rely on cross-version stability for UUIDs persisted long-term unless you pin
`coola` and pass an explicit, version-controlled hasher registry.

docs.title: generate_stable_content_id
docs.text:
generate_stable_content_id is an alternative to generate_stable_uuid5 that skips the UUID reshaping step: it returns the hash_object digest directly.

>>> from coola.identifier import generate_stable_content_id
>>> generate_stable_content_id({"source": "cats.txt", "page": 1})  # doctest: +ELLIPSIS
'...'
>>> generate_stable_content_id({"page": 1, "source": "cats.txt"}) == generate_stable_content_id(
...     {"source": "cats.txt", "page": 1}
... )
True

This keeps the full collision resistance and configurable length of the underlying hash, at the cost of not being a valid UUID string:

>>> from coola.identifier import generate_stable_content_id
>>> generate_stable_content_id({"a": 1}, length=16)  # doctest: +ELLIPSIS
'...'

Prefer generate_stable_content_id over generate_stable_uuid5 when you don't need UUID format compliance (e.g. internal cache keys, deduplication) and want the strongest possible collision resistance.

docs.title: Custom hasher registry and unhashable data
docs.text:
Both generate_stable_uuid5 and generate_stable_content_id forward registry and ignore_unhashable to hash_object:

>>> from coola.hashing import HasherRegistry, StringHasher
>>> from coola.identifier import generate_stable_content_id
>>> registry = HasherRegistry({object: StringHasher()})
>>> generate_stable_content_id("meow", registry=registry)  # doctest: +ELLIPSIS
'...'
>>> import warnings
>>> with warnings.catch_warnings():
...     warnings.simplefilter("ignore")  # a warning says that the type has no hasher
...     generate_stable_content_id(object(), ignore_unhashable=True)  # doctest: +ELLIPSIS
'...'

By default, a KeyError is raised if data contains a type for which no hasher is registered. See the hashing reference for how to register hashers for custom types.

docs.title: generate_ulid
docs.text:
generate_ulid generates a ULID (Universally Unique Lexicographically Sortable Identifier): a 26-character Crockford Base32 string packing a 48-bit millisecond timestamp followed by 80 bits of randomness. Two calls with the same input never return the same value:

>>> from coola.identifier import generate_ulid
>>> generate_ulid()  # doctest: +ELLIPSIS
'...'
>>> generate_ulid() == generate_ulid()
False

Because the timestamp is the most significant part, ULIDs generated later sort (as plain strings) after ULIDs generated earlier, unlike uuid.uuid4, which sorts randomly. Use it for a unique record ID that should also sort roughly by insertion order.

ULIDs generated with the current time are monotonic within a process, as recommended by the ULID specification: ULIDs generated in the same millisecond (or after the clock moved backward) keep the timestamp and increment the random part by one, so they sort in the order of generation. Across processes, ULIDs generated in the same millisecond are not ordered. A ULID generated with an explicit timestamp_ms always has a random part, so it is not ordered relative to the others.

Use extract_ulid_timestamp_ms to recover the timestamp encoded in a ULID, e.g. to check how old a record is without a separate stored timestamp column:

>>> from coola.identifier import extract_ulid_timestamp_ms, generate_ulid
>>> ulid = generate_ulid(timestamp_ms=1704067200000)
>>> extract_ulid_timestamp_ms(ulid)
1704067200000

docs.title: generate_uuid7
docs.text:
generate_uuid7 generates a UUIDv7 (RFC 9562): like generate_ulid, it packs a 48-bit millisecond timestamp followed by randomness, but into the standard 128-bit UUID layout (version and variant bits included) instead of a Base32 string:

>>> from coola.identifier import generate_uuid7
>>> generate_uuid7()  # doctest: +ELLIPSIS
'...'
>>> generate_uuid7() == generate_uuid7()
False

Like ULIDs, UUIDv7 values sort (as plain strings) in creation-time order, and they are monotonic within a process when the current time is used (the 74 random bits are incremented within the same millisecond), which keeps the inserts in a database index append-only. Prefer generate_uuid7 over generate_ulid when the identifier must be a valid UUID string (e.g. a UUID-typed database column, or an API expecting uuid.UUID formatting); prefer generate_ulid otherwise, since it packs more randomness (80 bits) than UUIDv7 leaves available (74 bits, once the version and variant bits are subtracted).

extract_uuid7_timestamp_ms recovers the timestamp, the same way extract_ulid_timestamp_ms does for a ULID:

>>> from coola.identifier import extract_uuid7_timestamp_ms, generate_uuid7
>>> uuid7 = generate_uuid7(timestamp_ms=1704067200000)
>>> extract_uuid7_timestamp_ms(uuid7)
1704067200000

docs.title: generate_snowflake_id
docs.text:
generate_snowflake_id generates a Snowflake-style 64-bit integer identifier, in the spirit of Twitter's original Snowflake service: a 41-bit millisecond timestamp, a 10-bit worker_id, and a 12-bit per-millisecond sequence number, packed into a single integer:

>>> from coola.identifier import generate_snowflake_id
>>> id1 = generate_snowflake_id()
>>> id2 = generate_snowflake_id(worker_id=3)

Like generate_ulid, successive IDs are monotonically increasing, but the result is a plain 64-bit integer rather than a string, useful when the identifier must fit a BIGINT-style column, or when IDs need to be attributable to the worker/shard that minted them via worker_id.

generate_snowflake_id is a thread-safe convenience wrapper around a shared, process-wide SnowflakeIdGenerator instance: its sequence counter is local to that instance, so it guarantees uniqueness across calls sharing it, not across other instances or processes. Assign each concurrently running generator (typically one per process or shard) a distinct worker_id to avoid collisions between them. This includes the children of a fork (os.fork, or multiprocessing with the fork start method): they inherit the state of the generator of their parent, so they must not keep the default worker_id=0.

If the system clock moves backward (typically a step adjustment by NTP, or a virtual machine that resumes from a pause), the generator raises a RuntimeError instead of minting an ID that could be a duplicate or smaller than a previous one. This is a deliberate choice: waiting for the clock to catch up could block for an unbounded time. The error is raised before the state of the generator is modified, so the next call works once the clock is back to the last timestamp. If your system can see steps of the clock, retry the call after a short delay, or run the time synchronization in slew mode.

Use SnowflakeIdGenerator directly instead of the module-level function when you need several independent generators in the same process, e.g. one per worker thread, or an isolated instance in a test, without them sharing state through a global singleton:

>>> from coola.identifier import SnowflakeIdGenerator
>>> generator = SnowflakeIdGenerator()
>>> id1 = generator.generate()
>>> id2 = generator.generate(worker_id=3)

extract_snowflake_timestamp_ms recovers the timestamp encoded in a Snowflake-style ID:

>>> from coola.identifier import extract_snowflake_timestamp_ms, generate_snowflake_id
>>> snowflake_id = generate_snowflake_id()
>>> isinstance(extract_snowflake_timestamp_ms(snowflake_id), int)
True

docs.title: generate_object_id
docs.text:
generate_object_id generates a MongoDB ObjectId style 24-character hex string: a 4-byte timestamp, a 5-byte per-process value, and a 3-byte counter. Like SnowflakeIdGenerator, later IDs sort after earlier ones, but the counter silently wraps instead of raising or blocking when exhausted within a second, and no worker_id needs to be configured. After a fork, the child process gets its own random per-process value and counter, so the parent and its children do not produce the same identifiers:

>>> from coola.identifier import generate_object_id
>>> generate_object_id()  # doctest: +ELLIPSIS
'...'

extract_object_id_timestamp recovers the (second-resolution) Unix timestamp encoded in an identifier previously returned by generate_object_id or ObjectIdGenerator.generate:

>>> from coola.identifier import extract_object_id_timestamp, generate_object_id
>>> object_id = generate_object_id()
>>> isinstance(extract_object_id_timestamp(object_id), int)
True

docs.title: generate_checksummed_id
docs.text:
generate_checksummed_id adds a Crockford Base32 check symbol to a random identifier, so that a single mistyped or transposed character is caught locally, without needing a lookup. Use it for identifiers a human is expected to read back or retype, e.g. a support code or license key:

>>> from coola.identifier import generate_checksummed_id, verify_checksummed_id
>>> checksummed_id = generate_checksummed_id()
>>> verify_checksummed_id(checksummed_id)
True

verify_checksummed_id follows the Crockford Base32 spec's own transcription rules: it is case-insensitive, and it normalizes 'O' to '0' and 'I'/'L' to '1' before checking the check symbol, so a human who reads back 'O' for '0' (or types in lowercase) still verifies correctly:

>>> verify_checksummed_id(checksummed_id.lower())
True

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
Property Statement Declared shape Every generator returns a str, except SnowflakeIdGenerator.generate and generate_snowflake_id, which return an int of at most 63 bits. Random bits are CSPRNG The random bits of generate_ulid, generate_uuid7, generate_object_id and generate_checksummed_id come from secrets or os.urandom, never random. Identifier, not a secret An identifier is not an access token. The time-ordered ones are guessable (the next value is the previous one plus one) and the content-derived ones are reproducible. Authorize every access explicitly. Stable IDs are content-derived generate_stable_uuid5 and generate_stable_content_id give the same ID for equal data, regardless of the mapping insertion order. Collision resistance generate_stable_uuid5 is bounded by the 122 random bits of a UUID (birthday bound 2^61), whatever the hash. generate_stable_content_id keeps the strength of the underlying hash. Time-ordered IDs sort ULID, UUIDv7 and Snowflake IDs sort in creation order. They are monotonic within a process when the current time is used. generate_object_id sorts by second only. Not ordered across processes Two processes that mint an ID in the same tick (a millisecond, a second for ObjectId) do not give ordered IDs. Snowflake uniqueness It holds for the calls that share a generator. Give each concurrent generator, including each fork, its own worker_id. Thread-safe Every generator can be called from several threads without a lock of the caller. Fork-safe After a fork, generate_ulid, generate_uuid7 and generate_object_id do not repeat the identifiers of the parent. A Snowflake generator does, unless the child uses another worker_id. Recoverable timestamp The four time-ordered generators have a matching extract_* function. Check symbol verify_checksummed_id is True for every identifier of generate_checksummed_id and detects any single wrong character and any swap of two adjacent characters.

The stable IDs inherit the hashing properties, including the fact that they can change between versions of coola.

Not guaranteed:

  • Order across processes. Identifiers minted in the same tick by two processes are ordered by their random part, not by the time of the call.
  • Uniqueness of Snowflake IDs across processes that use the same worker_id: assigning worker numbers is the job of the caller.
  • Stability of the stable IDs across major versions of coola, and across registries other than the stable one.
  • Unguessability of any identifier.

docs.title: Which one should I use?
docs.text:
• Need the same identifier every time for the same data? Use generate_stable_uuid5 (valid UUID format) or generate_stable_content_id (raw hash, stronger collision resistance, configurable length).
  • Need a unique identifier per call, sortable by creation time? Use generate_ulid (string, more randomness), generate_uuid7 (string, valid UUID format), generate_snowflake_id (64-bit integer) or generate_object_id (24-character hex string, sorts by second).
