  • Need a code that a human retypes (support code, license key)? Use generate_checksummed_id and verify_checksummed_id.
  • Need a plain random UUID, a short random string, a prefixed identifier or an opaque public identifier? Use the standard library or a dedicated library: str(uuid.uuid4()), secrets.token_urlsafe(16), f"cus_{generate_ulid()}", or a library such as sqids.
  • Need an unpredictable token (session, API key, password reset link)? None of these: use secrets.token_urlsafe.

docs.title: Data Loaders and Savers
docs.text:
This page describes the coola.io package, which provides a small set of loaders and savers to read and write data to files, with a consistent, format-agnostic API.

Prerequisites: You'll need to know a bit of Python. For a refresher, see the Python tutorial.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The coola.io package provides:

  1. Base classes - BaseLoader, BaseSaver, and BaseFileSaver to define custom loaders and savers
  2. Format-specific loaders and savers - JSON, pickle, text, and PyTorch
  3. Functional shortcuts - load_*/save_* functions for one-off usage without instantiating a loader or saver
  4. Configuration utilities - resolve_loader/resolve_saver to instantiate a loader or saver from a configuration, and is_loader_config/is_saver_config to check configurations

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
coola.io reads and writes one value to one file through a small, format-agnostic interface, and a write either happens completely or leaves the target as it was. The built-in loaders and savers are designed around the following properties.

Property Statement Atomic write A file saver writes to a hidden temporary file next to the target and commits it with one atomic operation. A reader sees the old file or the new file, never a partial one, and an interrupted save leaves the target as it was. No silent overwrite save raises FileExistsError if the target exists, unless exist_ok=True. This holds when the file is created concurrently, because the commit is a hard link. No torn file Concurrent saves of the same path, in one process or in several, never produce a mix: the file is the complete content of one of them. Which one is unspecified. With exist_ok=False, exactly one wins and the others raise FileExistsError. Clean failure If writing fails, the temporary file is removed and the original exception is raised, even if the cleanup itself fails. An existing target is left untouched. Opt-in durability By default the data only reaches the operating system cache. fsync=True flushes the file before the commit and the directory after it, so the file survives a power failure. It is slower. Directory safety A path that is a directory raises IsADirectoryError, a parent that is a file raises NotADirectoryError, missing parents are created. A symbolic link target is overwritten through the link, and the mode of an overwritten file is kept. Path-like input Every method takes a str or any os.PathLike; ~ and file:// URIs are expanded. Format-agnostic API Every loader has load(path) and every saver has save(data, path, exist_ok=...). Formats can be swapped without changing the calling code. Comparable Two loaders (or two savers) are equal (equal()) if they have the same type and the same configuration (encoding, keyword arguments). Safe by default for load TorchLoader uses weights_only=True unless told otherwise. PickleLoader cannot be made safe: only load pickle files that you trust. Extensible A format is added by subclassing BaseLoader or BaseFileSaver. The atomic write, exist_ok and fsync come with the base class. A backend that is not a file subclasses BaseSaver. Errors propagate The OSError of the file system and the exceptions of the format library (JSONDecodeError, UnpicklingError, ...) are raised unchanged. Only the cases listed above (exists, directory, parent is a file) are translated. Lazy optional libraries import coola.io imports no optional library. TorchLoader and TorchSaver import torch the first time they are used. Configurable resolve_loader / resolve_saver build an object from a _target_ configuration, with allowed_prefixes for configurations that are not trusted.

Not guaranteed:

  • Round trip beyond the format: JSON turns tuples into lists and non-string keys into strings and writes NaN as a non-standard token, and save_text writes str(data) for non-string data.
  • Durability without fsync=True, and which of several concurrent saves wins.
  • A hidden .<name>-<uuid><ext> file after a crash: a process killed (SIGKILL, power loss) between the write and the commit leaves its temporary file. It is hidden, never taken for the target, and safe to delete.
  • exist_ok=False on a file system without hard links (FAT/exFAT, some network and container volumes): the commit falls back on "check, then rename", so two processes that create the same file at the same instant can both succeed. The last one wins; no file is torn.
  • Replacing a file that another process has open on Windows: os.replace raises PermissionError, which propagates.
  • Streaming, compression and remote storage: one value per call, local files only.

docs.title: Loading and Saving Data
docs.text: Each supported format has a loader class, a saver class, and two convenience functions.

docs.title: JSON
docs.text:
>>> import tempfile
>>> from pathlib import Path
>>> from coola.io import save_json, load_json
>>> with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmpdir:
...     path = Path(tmpdir).joinpath("data.json")
...     save_json({"key1": [1, 2, 3], "key2": "abc"}, path)
...     data = load_json(path)
...     data
{'key1': [1, 2, 3], 'key2': 'abc'}

The class-based equivalent is JsonLoader and JsonSaver:

>>> import tempfile
>>> from pathlib import Path
>>> from coola.io import JsonSaver, JsonLoader
>>> with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmpdir:
...     path = Path(tmpdir).joinpath("data.json")
...     JsonSaver().save({"key1": [1, 2, 3], "key2": "abc"}, path)
...     data = JsonLoader().load(path)
...     data
{'key1': [1, 2, 3], 'key2': 'abc'}

JsonSaver forwards extra keyword arguments to json.dump, e.g. indent or sort_keys:

>>> import tempfile
>>> from pathlib import Path
>>> from coola.io import JsonSaver
>>> with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmpdir:
...     path = Path(tmpdir).joinpath("data.json")
...     JsonSaver(indent=2, sort_keys=True).save({"b": 1, "a": 2}, path)

docs.title: Pickle
docs.text:
>>> import tempfile
>>> from pathlib import Path
>>> from coola.io import save_pickle, load_pickle
>>> with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmpdir:
...     path = Path(tmpdir).joinpath("data.pkl")
...     save_pickle({"key1": [1, 2, 3], "key2": "abc"}, path)
...     data = load_pickle(path)
...     data
{'key1': [1, 2, 3], 'key2': 'abc'}

PickleLoader/PickleSaver are the class-based equivalents, and PickleSaver forwards extra keyword arguments to pickle.dump.

!!! danger "Only load pickle files that you trust"

Unpickling can execute arbitrary code. Never call `load_pickle` or `PickleLoader.load` on a file
that comes from an untrusted or unauthenticated source. For PyTorch files, `load_torch` and
`TorchLoader` use `weights_only=True` by default, which only loads tensors and simple containers.
Pass `weights_only=False` only for trusted files.

docs.title: Text
docs.text:
>>> import tempfile
>>> from pathlib import Path
>>> from coola.io import save_text, load_text
>>> with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmpdir:
...     path = Path(tmpdir).joinpath("data.txt")
...     save_text("hello", path)
...     data = load_text(path)
...     data
'hello'

TextLoader/TextSaver accept an encoding argument (defaults to "utf-8"). save_text and TextSaver accept a str only and raise a TypeError for any other object: call str on the data to write its text representation.

docs.title: PyTorch
docs.text:
>>> import tempfile
>>> from pathlib import Path
>>> from coola.io import save_torch, load_torch  # doctest: +SKIP
>>> with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmpdir:  # doctest: +SKIP
...     path = Path(tmpdir).joinpath("data.pt")
...     save_torch({"key1": [1, 2, 3], "key2": "abc"}, path)
...     data = load_torch(path)
...     data
{'key1': [1, 2, 3], 'key2': 'abc'}

TorchLoader/TorchSaver forward extra keyword arguments to torch.load/torch.save respectively, and require PyTorch to be installed.

docs.title: Overwrite Behavior
docs.text:
By default, every saver raises FileExistsError if the target path already exists. Pass exist_ok=True to overwrite it:

>>> import tempfile
>>> from pathlib import Path
>>> from coola.io import save_text
>>> with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmpdir:
...     path = Path(tmpdir).joinpath("data.txt")
...     save_text("hello", path)
...     save_text("world", path, exist_ok=True)

File savers (BaseFileSaver subclasses, i.e. all the built-in savers) write to a temporary file first and then atomically move it into place, so a job interrupted while writing never leaves a partially written file at the target path.

To build a file name that does not collide with an existing file, without exist_ok=True, see add_uuid_suffix() in coola.utils.

docs.title: Durability
docs.text:
The move is atomic, but by default the data is only written to the operating system cache: if the machine crashes right after save, the file can be missing or empty even though a reader never saw a partial file. This is fine for caches and most logs. For data that must survive a power failure, pass fsync=True: the data is flushed to the disk before the file is moved into place, and the directory is flushed afterward. It is slower.

>>> import tempfile
>>> from pathlib import Path
>>> from coola.io import save_json
>>> with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmpdir:
...     save_json({"key": "value"}, Path(tmpdir).joinpath("data.json"), fsync=True)

docs.title: Requirements on the directory
docs.text:
save needs write access to the directory of the target path, not only to the file: the data is written to a hidden temporary file next to the target, and then committed with one atomic operation. save takes no lock and creates no lock file. A temporary file left by a process killed between the write and the commit is not removed: it is hidden, named .<name>-<uuid><ext>, and safe to delete.

Concurrent saves of the same path never produce a mix. A caller that needs mutual exclusion (a read-modify-write of one file) uses a lock of its own around the read and the write.

When exist_ok=False, the file is committed with a hard link, so a file created concurrently is never overwritten. On filesystems without hard link support (FAT/exFAT, some network and container volumes), save falls back to checking that the target does not exist and renaming the temporary file.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
The built-in loaders and savers are designed around the following properties.

Property Statement Atomic write A file saver writes to a temporary file next to the target and then moves it into place, so a reader never sees a partially written file, and an interrupted save leaves no partial file. No silent overwrite save raises FileExistsError if the target exists, unless exist_ok=True. This also holds if the file is created concurrently, because the commit uses a hard link. No torn file Concurrent saves of the same path, in one process or in several, never produce a mix: the file is the complete content of one of them. Which one is unspecified. With exist_ok=False, exactly one wins and the others raise FileExistsError. Opt-in durability By default the data only reaches the operating system cache. fsync=True flushes the file and the directory, so the file survives a power failure. It is slower. Clean failure If writing fails, the temporary file is removed and the original exception is raised, even if the cleanup itself fails. An existing target file is left untouched. Directory safety A path that is a directory raises IsADirectoryError. Missing parent directories are created. Format-agnostic API Every loader has load(path) and every saver has save(data, path, exist_ok=...), so formats can be swapped without changing the calling code. Comparable Loaders and savers implement equal(): two of them are equal if they have the same type and the same configuration (e.g. encoding or keyword arguments). Safe by default for load TorchLoader uses weights_only=True unless told otherwise. PickleLoader cannot be made safe: only load pickle files that you trust. Extensible A loader or saver for another format is added by subclassing BaseLoader or BaseFileSaver, which reuses the atomic write and exist_ok handling.

Not guaranteed:

  • Round trip beyond the format: JSON turns tuples into lists and non-string keys into strings, and text files store str(data) for non-string data.
  • Durability without fsync=True.
  • Which of several concurrent saves wins.
  • exist_ok=False on a file system without hard links: two processes that create the same file at the same instant can both succeed (the last one wins, no file is torn).

docs.title: Comparing Loaders and Savers
docs.text:
Loaders and savers implement equal() so they can be compared, including with coola.equality:

>>> from coola.io import JsonLoader, TextLoader
>>> JsonLoader().equal(JsonLoader())
True
>>> JsonLoader().equal(TextLoader())
False

docs.title: Configuration-Based Instantiation
docs.text:
Loaders and savers can be instantiated from a configuration dictionary, which is convenient when the format is only known at runtime (e.g. read from a config file):

>>> from coola.io import resolve_loader, resolve_saver
>>> loader = resolve_loader({"_target_": "coola.io.JsonLoader"})
>>> loader
JsonLoader(encoding=None)
>>> saver = resolve_saver({"_target_": "coola.io.JsonSaver"})
>>> saver
JsonSaver(encoding='utf-8')

Use is_loader_config/is_saver_config to check if a configuration targets a BaseLoader or BaseSaver:

>>> from coola.io import is_loader_config, is_saver_config
>>> is_loader_config({"_target_": "coola.io.JsonLoader"})
True
>>> is_saver_config({"_target_": "coola.io.JsonLoader"})
False

docs.title: Implementing a Custom Loader or Saver
docs.text:
Subclass BaseLoader and implement _load to implement a custom loader. load is provided by the base class: it converts a str, a file:// URI or any os.PathLike to a Path and calls _load with it. equal(), repr and str also come with the base class and use the fields returned by _display_fields() (none by default); override it in a loader that has options:

>>> from pathlib import Path
>>> from coola.io import BaseLoader
>>> class UpperTextLoader(BaseLoader[str]):
...     def _load(self, path: Path) -> str:
...         return path.read_text().upper()

For a saver that writes to a file, subclass BaseFileSaver and implement _save_file instead of save directly - this reuses the atomic write and exist_ok handling described above:

>>> from pathlib import Path
>>> from coola.io import BaseFileSaver
>>> class UpperTextSaver(BaseFileSaver[str]):
...     def _save_file(self, to_save: str, path: Path) -> None:
...         path.write_text(str(to_save).upper())

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• coola.equality: Used internally to compare loader/saver keyword arguments.
  • coola.utils: Used internally to check optional-dependency availability (e.g. PyTorch).

docs.title: Iterating Over Nested Data
docs.text:
This page describes the coola.iterator package, which provides utilities for iterating over nested data structures using different traversal strategies.

Prerequisites: You'll need to know a bit of Python. For a refresher, see the Python tutorial.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The coola.iterator package provides functions to iterate over nested data structures (lists, dicts, tuples, sets, etc.) using two different traversal strategies:

  • Depth-First Search (DFS): Traverses nested structures by going deep into each branch before moving to the next
  • Breadth-First Search (BFS): Traverses nested structures level by level

The package also provides filtering utilities to extract only specific types from heterogeneous collections.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
Property Statement Leaves only A traversal yields the leaves, once per occurrence, never a container. An empty container has no leaf and yields nothing. Type dispatch The iterator (or child finder) is chosen from the type of the data along the Method Resolution Order, so the most specific registered type wins. Deterministic order DFS is pre-order and BFS is level order, both left to right. A mapping gives its values in insertion order (the keys are never yielded) and a dataclass its fields in the order of their definition. The order inside a set is not specified. Same leaves, different order DFS and BFS visit the same leaves. Only the order differs. Lazy Both dfs_iterate and bfs_iterate are generators: leaves are produced one at a time, and nothing is walked before the first next. Read-only The input is never modified. Every leaf is returned A container that appears several times, without containing itself, gives its leaves each time. Cycle-safe A container that contains itself raises ValueError instead of looping forever or hitting the recursion limit. Iterators are leaves The default registries never consume an iterator or a generator, so an infinite iterator cannot hang the traversal. Depth Both functions use an explicit stack or queue: there is no RecursionError, whatever the nesting. The depth is bounded by memory only. Extensible Support for a new container type is added with one child finder (find_children) registered for the type. It serves both orders.

Not guaranteed: the order of a ChainMap (its values follow the lookup order of the maps), a container that is changed during the traversal, and a registry that is modified during a traversal.

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
The dfs_iterate function performs depth-first traversal of nested data structures:

>>> from coola.iterator import dfs_iterate
>>> list(dfs_iterate({"a": 1, "b": "abc"}))
[1, 'abc']
>>> list(dfs_iterate([1, [2, 3], {"x": 4}]))
[1, 2, 3, 4]

The function yields only the leaf values (atomic values that are not containers), excluding the containers themselves even if they're empty.

docs.title: DFS Traversal Examples
docs.text:
Simple nested lists:

>>> from coola.iterator import dfs_iterate
>>> list(dfs_iterate([1, 2, [3, 4, [5, 6]]]))
[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]

Nested dictionaries:

>>> from coola.iterator import dfs_iterate
>>> data = {"level1": {"level2": {"level3": 42}}}
>>> list(dfs_iterate(data))
[42]

Mixed structures:

>>> from coola.iterator import dfs_iterate
>>> data = {
...     "list": [1, 2, 3],
...     "dict": {"a": 4, "b": 5},
...     "set": {6, 7},
...     "value": 8,
... }
>>> sorted(dfs_iterate(data))  # sorted for consistent output
[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]

Sets and tuples:

>>> from coola.iterator import dfs_iterate
>>> list(dfs_iterate((1, (2, 3))))
[1, 2, 3]
>>> list(dfs_iterate((1, (2, (3, 4)))))
[1, 2, 3, 4]

docs.title: Understanding DFS Order
docs.text:
Depth-first search goes deep into each branch before moving to the next branch:

>>> from coola.iterator import dfs_iterate
>>> data = {
...     "branch1": [1, [2, 3]],
...     "branch2": [4, [5, 6]],
... }
>>> # DFS will fully explore branch1 before moving to branch2
>>> list(dfs_iterate(data))
[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
The bfs_iterate function performs breadth-first traversal of nested data structures:

>>> from coola.iterator import bfs_iterate
>>> list(bfs_iterate({"a": 1, "b": "abc"}))
[1, 'abc']
>>> list(bfs_iterate([1, [2, 3], {"x": 4}]))
[1, 2, 3, 4]

Like dfs_iterate, it yields only the leaf values, excluding containers.

docs.title: BFS Traversal Examples
docs.text:
Nested lists:

>>> from coola.iterator import bfs_iterate
>>> list(bfs_iterate([1, [2, [3, [4]]]]))
[1, 2, 3, 4]

Multi-level structure:

>>> from coola.iterator import bfs_iterate
>>> data = {
...     "level1_a": 1,
...     "level1_b": {"level2_a": 2, "level2_b": {"level3": 3}},
... }
>>> # BFS processes level by level: 1 at level 1, then 2 at level 2, then 3 at level 3
>>> list(bfs_iterate(data))
[1, 2, 3]

docs.title: BFS vs DFS
docs.text:
The main difference between BFS and DFS is the order of traversal:

>>> from coola.iterator import bfs_iterate, dfs_iterate
>>> data = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
>>> list(dfs_iterate(data))  # DFS: depth-first
[1, 2, 3, 4]
>>> list(bfs_iterate(data))  # BFS: breadth-first
[1, 2, 3, 4]

For this simple example, the results are the same, but for more complex nested structures, the traversal order can differ significantly. BFS processes all items at each level before moving deeper, while DFS goes as deep as possible before backtracking.

docs.title: Dataclasses
docs.text:
dfs_iterate and bfs_iterate enter the dataclass instances, like objects_are_equal, hash_object, summarize and recursive_apply: they visit the values of the fields, in the order of their definition (DataclassChildFinder):

>>> from dataclasses import dataclass
>>> from coola.iterator import dfs_iterate
>>> @dataclass
... class Config:
...     lr: float
...     layers: list
>>> list(dfs_iterate(Config(0.1, [1, 2])))
[0.1, 1, 2]

A child finder registered for the type of the dataclass has priority over the default one. To keep a dataclass as a leaf, register DefaultChildFinder() for its type:

>>> from coola.iterator import DefaultChildFinder, get_default_registry
>>> registry = get_default_registry().copy()
>>> registry.register(Config, DefaultChildFinder())
>>> list(dfs_iterate(Config(0.1, [1, 2]), registry=registry))
[Config(lr=0.1, layers=[1, 2])]

docs.title: Basic Filtering
docs.text:
The filter_by_type function filters an iterator to yield only values of specified types:

>>> from coola.iterator import filter_by_type
>>> list(filter_by_type([1, "hello", 2, 3.14, "world", 4], int))
[1, 2, 4]

docs.title: Filtering Multiple Types
docs.text:
You can filter for multiple types using a tuple (the type checker infers the union of the types):

>>> from coola.iterator import filter_by_type
>>> # Note: bool is a subclass of int
>>> list(filter_by_type([1, "hello", 2.5, True, None, [1, 2]], (int, float)))
[1, 2.5, True]

docs.title: Combining with Iteration
docs.text:
You can combine type filtering with nested iteration:

>>> from coola.iterator import dfs_iterate, filter_by_type
>>> data = {"a": 1, "b": "hello", "c": [2, "world", 3.14]}
>>> # Get all numeric values (int and float) from nested structure
>>> list(filter_by_type(dfs_iterate(data), (int, float)))
[1, 2, 3.14]

docs.title: Writing a Child Finder
docs.text:
A child finder inherits from BaseChildFinder and implements find_children(data), which returns the direct children of the object in the order they are visited, or None for a leaf. It does not call the registry and does not recurse: dfs_iterate and bfs_iterate walk the children, so one child finder serves both orders. An empty container returns an empty iterable (it yields nothing), a leaf returns None (the value itself is yielded). MappingChildFinder returns the values of a mapping, and IterableChildFinder the container itself:

>>> from coola.iterator import (
...     BaseChildFinder,
...     MappingChildFinder,
...     bfs_iterate,
...     dfs_iterate,
...     register_child_finders,
... )
>>> list(MappingChildFinder().find_children({"a": 1, "b": 2}))
[1, 2]
>>> class Node:
...     def __init__(self, left, right):
...         self.left, self.right = left, right
>>> class NodeChildFinder(BaseChildFinder[Node]):
...     def find_children(self, data):
...         return [data.left, data.right]
>>> register_child_finders({Node: NodeChildFinder()})
>>> tree = Node(Node(1, 2), 3)
>>> list(dfs_iterate(tree))
[1, 2, 3]
>>> list(bfs_iterate(tree))
[3, 1, 2]

docs.title: Default Registry
docs.text: get_default_registry() (alias get_default_child_finder_registry()) returns the process-wide registry used by dfs_iterate and bfs_iterate. register_child_finders() registers types on this registry. The default registry enters list, tuple, deque, Sequence, set, frozenset, dict, Mapping, MappingProxyType and the dataclasses (the containers of recursive_apply); everything else is a leaf.

docs.title: Using Custom Registry
docs.text:
You can create and use a custom registry:

>>> from coola.iterator import (
...     ChildFinderRegistry,
...     DefaultChildFinder,
...     IterableChildFinder,
...     dfs_iterate,
... )
>>> registry = ChildFinderRegistry()
>>> registry.register(list, IterableChildFinder())
>>> registry.register(object, DefaultChildFinder())
>>> list(dfs_iterate([1, 2, 3], registry=registry))
[1, 2, 3]

docs.title: Extracting All Values
docs.text:
Extract all values from a complex configuration:

>>> from coola.iterator import dfs_iterate
>>> config = {
...     "database": {"host": "localhost", "port": 5432},
...     "cache": {"enabled": True, "ttl": 3600},
... }
>>> list(dfs_iterate(config))
['localhost', 5432, True, 3600]

docs.title: Counting Values
docs.text:
Count specific types in a nested structure:

>>> from coola.iterator import dfs_iterate, filter_by_type
>>> data = {
...     "scores": [95, 87, 92],
...     "names": ["Alice", "Bob", "Charlie"],
... }
>>> len(list(filter_by_type(dfs_iterate(data), int)))
3

docs.title: Finding All Strings
docs.text:
Find all string values in a nested structure:

>>> from coola.iterator import dfs_iterate, filter_by_type
>>> data = {
...     "user": {"name": "John", "age": 30},
...     "posts": [{"title": "Post 1", "views": 100}, {"title": "Post 2", "views": 200}],
... }
>>> list(filter_by_type(dfs_iterate(data), str))
['John', 'Post 1', 'Post 2']

docs.title: Validating Data Types
docs.text:
Check if all numeric values in a structure are within a range:

>>> from coola.iterator import dfs_iterate, filter_by_type
>>> data = {"values": [10, 20, 30], "nested": {"more": [40, 50]}}
>>> numbers = list(filter_by_type(dfs_iterate(data), (int, float)))
>>> all(0 <= n <= 100 for n in numbers)
True

docs.title: Iterators and Cycles
docs.text:
The default registry expands the containers (list, tuple, set, dict, ...) but treat iterators and generators as leaves: they are returned as they are and never consumed, so a generator (or an infinite iterator) in the data cannot be exhausted or hang the traversal.

A container that contains itself cannot be traversed. Both dfs_iterate and bfs_iterate raise a ValueError instead of looping forever or hitting the recursion limit. A container that appears several times without containing itself is not a cycle, and its leaves are returned each time:

>>> from coola.iterator import dfs_iterate
>>> shared = [1, 2]
>>> list(dfs_iterate([shared, shared]))
[1, 2, 1, 2]
>>> data = [1]
>>> data.append(data)
>>> list(dfs_iterate(data))
Traceback (most recent call last):
    ...
ValueError: Cycle detected: an object of type <class 'list'> contains itself

A child finder for a leaf type returns None (like DefaultChildFinder), so both functions yield the value instead of expanding it.

docs.title: Containers and Leaves
docs.text:
The default registry gives the same containers as recursive_apply, so the same data gives the same leaves in both packages:

Type Children list, tuple (and named tuples), deque, Sequence, set, frozenset the elements, in iteration order dict, Mapping, MappingProxyType the values (the keys are never yielded) dataclass instances the values of the fields, in field order str, bytes, UserString, numbers, None, iterators, generators, arrays, ... none: the value is a leaf

range, and a user class that only inherits Collection or collections.abc.Set, are leaves until a child finder is registered for them (see Writing a Child Finder). An empty container has no leaf and yields nothing.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
Property Statement Lazy Both dfs_iterate and bfs_iterate are generators: leaves are produced one at a time. Every leaf is returned A container that appears several times, without containing itself, gives its leaves each time. Cycle-safe A container that contains itself raises ValueError instead of looping forever or hitting the recursion limit. Iterators are leaves The default registries never consume an iterator or a generator, so an infinite iterator cannot hang the traversal. Depth Both functions use an explicit stack or queue: there is no RecursionError, whatever the nesting. The depth is bounded by memory only. Same leaves, different order DFS and BFS visit the same leaves. Only the order differs. Extensible Support for a new type is added with one child finder (find_children) registered for the type. It serves both orders.

Not guaranteed:

  • Shared references. A container reachable by several paths (a DAG) gives its leaves once per path, so the cost is proportional to the number of paths, not to the number of objects.
  • The order inside a set, and the order of a ChainMap (its values follow the lookup order of the maps, last map first).
  • Mutation during the traversal. Changing a container while it is walked is the caller's problem, as for any Python iteration.
  • A registry modified during a traversal. The traversal keeps the child finders it already resolved.

docs.title: Design Principles
docs.text:
The coola.iterator package design provides:

  1. Multiple traversal strategies: Choose between DFS and BFS based on your needs
  2. Generator-based: The leaves are produced on demand (a BFS keeps one level in memory)
  3. Type-aware: Built-in support for common Python types with extensibility
  4. Clean API: Simple functions that compose well with other Python tools

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• coola.recursive: For transforming nested data while preserving structure
  • coola.registry: For understanding the registry pattern used internally

docs.title: Working with Nested Data Structures
docs.text:
This page describes the coola.nested package, which provides utilities for manipulating nested data structures like converting between different formats and working with nested mappings.

Prerequisites: You'll need to know a bit of Python. For a refresher, see the Python tutorial.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The coola.nested package provides utilities for working with nested data structures. It offers:

  1. Data conversion functions - Convert between list-of-dicts and dict-of-lists formats
  2. Mapping utilities - Flatten nested dictionaries, extract values, filter keys, rename keys, merge mappings and flatten a mapping of mappings
  3. JSON conversion - Convert a nested structure to JSON-compatible data
  4. Clean and simple API - Easy-to-use functions for common data transformation tasks

This is particularly useful when working with tabular data, configuration files, or any nested data structures that need to be transformed or manipulated.

docs.title: Converting Between Formats
docs.text: The package provides two main conversion functions for transforming between different representations of tabular data:

docs.title: List of Dicts to Dict of Lists
docs.text:
Use convert_to_dict_of_lists() to convert a sequence of dictionaries (rows) into a dictionary of lists (columns):

>>> from coola.nested import convert_to_dict_of_lists
>>> rows = [
...     {"name": "Alice", "age": 30, "city": "NYC"},
...     {"name": "Bob", "age": 25, "city": "LA"},
...     {"name": "Charlie", "age": 35, "city": "Chicago"},
... ]
>>> convert_to_dict_of_lists(rows)
{'name': ['Alice', 'Bob', 'Charlie'], 'age': [30, 25, 35], 'city': ['NYC', 'LA', 'Chicago']}

This is useful when you need to work with columnar data formats or when preparing data for certain libraries that expect column-oriented data.

Important: All dictionaries in the sequence should have the same keys. The function uses the first dictionary's keys to determine which keys to extract.

docs.title: Dict of Lists to List of Dicts
docs.text:
Use convert_to_list_of_dicts() to convert a dictionary of sequences (columns) into a list of dictionaries (rows):

>>> from coola.nested import convert_to_list_of_dicts
>>> columns = {
...     "name": ["Alice", "Bob", "Charlie"],
...     "age": [30, 25, 35],
...     "city": ["NYC", "LA", "Chicago"],
... }
>>> convert_to_list_of_dicts(columns)
[{'name': 'Alice', 'age': 30, 'city': 'NYC'}, {'name': 'Bob', 'age': 25, 'city': 'LA'}, {'name': 'Charlie', 'age': 35, 'city': 'Chicago'}]

This is useful when you have columnar data and need to process it row-by-row, or when interfacing with APIs that expect row-oriented data.

Important: All sequences in the dictionary should have the same length.

docs.title: Round-Trip Conversion
docs.text:
These conversion functions are inverse operations of each other:

>>> from coola.nested import convert_to_dict_of_lists, convert_to_list_of_dicts
>>> original = [{"x": 1, "y": 2}, {"x": 3, "y": 4}]
>>> columns = convert_to_dict_of_lists(original)
>>> columns
{'x': [1, 3], 'y': [2, 4]}
>>> rows = convert_to_list_of_dicts(columns)
>>> rows
[{'x': 1, 'y': 2}, {'x': 3, 'y': 4}]

docs.title: Getting the First Value
docs.text:
Use get_first_value() to extract the first value from a mapping:

>>> from coola.nested import get_first_value
>>> data = {"first": 10, "second": 20, "third": 30}
>>> get_first_value(data)
10

This is useful when you need to extract a representative value from a dictionary, or when you know the mapping should have at least one value but don't know the key.

Note: If the mapping is empty, this function raises a ValueError.

>>> from coola.nested import get_first_value
>>> get_first_value({})
Traceback (most recent call last):
    ...
ValueError: First value cannot be returned because the mapping is empty

docs.title: Flattening Nested Dictionaries
docs.text:
Use to_flat_dict() to convert nested dictionaries into a flat dictionary with dot-separated keys:

>>> from coola.nested import to_flat_dict
>>> nested = {
...     "database": {
...         "host": "localhost",
...         "port": 5432,
...         "credentials": {
...             "username": "admin",
...             "password": "secret",
...         },
...     },
...     "debug": True,
... }
>>> to_flat_dict(nested)
{'database.host': 'localhost', 'database.port': 5432, 'database.credentials.username': 'admin', 'database.credentials.password': 'secret', 'debug': True}

This is particularly useful for:

  • Configuration management
  • Logging hierarchical data
  • Creating command-line arguments from nested configurations
  • Storing nested data in flat storage systems

docs.title: Customizing the Separator
docs.text:
You can change the separator used to join keys:

>>> from coola.nested import to_flat_dict
>>> nested = {"a": {"b": {"c": 1}}}
>>> to_flat_dict(nested, separator="/")
{'a/b/c': 1}

docs.title: Handling Lists and Tuples
docs.text:
The function also handles lists and tuples by using numeric indices:

>>> from coola.nested import to_flat_dict
>>> data = {
...     "items": [10, 20, 30],
...     "matrix": [[1, 2], [3, 4]],
... }
>>> to_flat_dict(data)
{'items.0': 10, 'items.1': 20, 'items.2': 30, 'matrix.0.0': 1, 'matrix.0.1': 2, 'matrix.1.0': 3, 'matrix.1.1': 4}

docs.title: Mixed Nested Structures
docs.text:
The function works with any combination of dicts, lists, and tuples:

>>> from coola.nested import to_flat_dict
>>> complex_data = {
...     "users": [
...         {"name": "Alice", "scores": [95, 87]},
...         {"name": "Bob", "scores": [78, 92]},
...     ],
... }
>>> to_flat_dict(complex_data)
{'users.0.name': 'Alice', 'users.0.scores.0': 95, 'users.0.scores.1': 87, 'users.1.name': 'Bob', 'users.1.scores.0': 78, 'users.1.scores.1': 92}

str, bytes and bytearray values are leaves: they are never split into characters or bytes.

docs.title: Restoring Lists
docs.text:
from_flat_dict() keeps the integer segments as dictionary keys by default, so a list does not come back as a list. Use restore_lists=True to rebuild the lists. A dictionary whose keys are exactly "0", "1", ..., "n-1" is converted, and the tuples come back as lists:

>>> from coola.nested import from_flat_dict
>>> flat = {"items.0": 10, "items.1": 20, "matrix.0.0": 1, "matrix.1.0": 3}
>>> from_flat_dict(flat)
{'items': {'0': 10, '1': 20}, 'matrix': {'0': {'0': 1}, '1': {'0': 3}}}
>>> from_flat_dict(flat, restore_lists=True)
{'items': [10, 20], 'matrix': [[1], [3]]}

docs.title: Converting Types to Strings
docs.text:
Use the to_str parameter to specify types that should be converted to strings instead of being flattened:

>>> from coola.nested import to_flat_dict
>>> data = {
...     "items": [1, 2, 3],
...     "config": {"values": [4, 5, 6]},
... }
>>> to_flat_dict(data, to_str=(list,))
{'items': '[1, 2, 3]', 'config.values': '[4, 5, 6]'}

This is useful when you want to preserve certain data types as strings in the flattened output.

docs.title: Filtering Keys by Prefix
docs.text:
Use remove_keys_starting_with() to filter out dictionary keys that start with a specific prefix:

>>> from coola.nested import remove_keys_starting_with
>>> data = {
...     "temp_var1": 100,
...     "temp_var2": 200,
...     "result": 42,
...     "temp_cache": [1, 2, 3],
...     "final_output": "done",
... }
>>> remove_keys_starting_with(data, "temp_")
{'result': 42, 'final_output': 'done'}

This is useful for:

  • Removing temporary or internal variables
  • Filtering configuration keys
  • Cleaning up data structures

Note: Only string keys are checked for the prefix. Non-string keys are preserved:

>>> from coola.nested import remove_keys_starting_with
>>> mixed_keys = {
...     "prefix_str": 1,
...     123: 2,
...     ("a", "b"): 3,
... }
>>> remove_keys_starting_with(mixed_keys, "prefix_")
{123: 2, ('a', 'b'): 3}

docs.title: Filtering Keys by Condition
docs.text:
Use remove_keys_containing() to recursively remove the keys that contain a substring, and remove_keys_if() to recursively remove the keys that satisfy any predicate:

>>> from coola.nested import remove_keys_containing, remove_keys_if
>>> remove_keys_containing({"a_tmp": 1, "b": {"c_tmp": 2, "d": 3}}, "tmp")
{'b': {'d': 3}}
>>> remove_keys_if({"a": 1, 2: 2, "b": {"c": 3}}, lambda key: isinstance(key, int))
{'a': 1, 'b': {'c': 3}}

Like remove_keys_starting_with(), they return a new mapping and keep the input unchanged.

docs.title: Adding a Prefix or a Suffix to the Keys
docs.text:
Use add_prefix_suffix_to_keys() to rename the keys of a mapping. By default only the top-level keys are renamed. Use recursive=True to rename the keys of the nested mappings too:

>>> from coola.nested import add_prefix_suffix_to_keys
>>> data = {"a": 1, "b": {"c": 2}}
>>> add_prefix_suffix_to_keys(data, prefix="x_")
{'x_a': 1, 'x_b': {'c': 2}}
>>> add_prefix_suffix_to_keys(data, prefix="x_", suffix="_y", recursive=True)
{'x_a_y': 1, 'x_b_y': {'x_c_y': 2}}

docs.title: Merging Mappings
docs.text:
Use merge_mappings() to merge an iterable of mappings into a single dictionary. The on_duplicate parameter controls what happens when a key appears in several mappings:

on_duplicate Behavior "raise" (default) Raise a DuplicateKeyError, unless the values are equal. "first" Keep the value of the first mapping. "last" Keep the value of the last mapping. "suffix" Keep all the values, adding a numeric suffix to the keys (a, a_1, a_2). 
>>> from coola.nested import merge_mappings
>>> merge_mappings([{"a": 1}, {"b": 2}])
{'a': 1, 'b': 2}
>>> merge_mappings([{"a": 1}, {"a": 2}], on_duplicate="last")
{'a': 2}
>>> merge_mappings([{"a": 1}, {"a": 2}], on_duplicate="suffix")
{'a': 1, 'a_1': 2}
>>> merge_mappings([{"a": 1}, {"a": 2}])
Traceback (most recent call last):
    ...
coola.nested.mapping.DuplicateKeyError: Duplicate key found: 'a'

Use equal_nan=True to consider two NaN values equal when the duplicate keys are compared.

docs.title: Flattening a Mapping of Mappings
docs.text:
Use flatten_mapping() to flatten a mapping whose values are mappings (for example, the metrics of several splits) into a single dictionary. on_duplicate takes "raise" (default), "first", "last" or "prefix". With "prefix", all the values are kept and the duplicated keys are renamed <outer key><separator><inner key>. Use always_prefix=True to rename every key:

>>> from coola.nested import flatten_mapping
>>> metrics = {"train": {"loss": 1, "acc": 2}, "val": {"loss": 3}}
>>> flatten_mapping(metrics, on_duplicate="prefix")
{'acc': 2, 'train.loss': 1, 'val.loss': 3}
>>> flatten_mapping(metrics, always_prefix=True, separator="/")
{'train/loss': 1, 'train/acc': 2, 'val/loss': 3}
>>> flatten_mapping(metrics, on_duplicate="last")
{'loss': 3, 'acc': 2}

With the default on_duplicate="raise", a DuplicateKeyError is raised for the key loss.

docs.title: JSON Conversion
docs.text:
Use convert_to_jsonable() to recursively convert a nested structure to JSON-compatible data. Dataclasses and pydantic models found at any depth are converted to dictionaries, and sets are converted to sorted lists:

>>> from dataclasses import dataclass
>>> from coola.nested import convert_to_jsonable
>>> @dataclass
... class Point:
...     x: int
...     y: int
>>> convert_to_jsonable([Point(x=1, y=2), {"key": Point(x=3, y=4)}, {3, 1, 2}])
[{'x': 1, 'y': 2}, {'key': {'x': 3, 'y': 4}}, [1, 2, 3]]

try_sorted_list() converts an iterable (e.g. a set) to a list. The list is sorted when the values are comparable, so the output is deterministic, otherwise it keeps the iteration order:

>>> from coola.nested import try_sorted_list
>>> try_sorted_list({3, 1, 2})
[1, 2, 3]

docs.title: Working with API Responses
docs.text:
Convert API responses from different formats:

>>> from coola.nested import convert_to_dict_of_lists
>>> # API returns list of user objects
>>> api_response = [
...     {"id": 1, "name": "Alice", "active": True},
...     {"id": 2, "name": "Bob", "active": False},
... ]
>>> # Convert to columnar format for analysis
>>> columns = convert_to_dict_of_lists(api_response)
>>> columns
{'id': [1, 2], 'name': ['Alice', 'Bob'], 'active': [True, False]}

docs.title: Configuration File Processing
docs.text:
Flatten nested configuration for easier access:

>>> from coola.nested import to_flat_dict
>>> config = {
...     "server": {
...         "host": "0.0.0.0",
...         "port": 8080,
...         "ssl": {"enabled": True, "cert": "/path/to/cert"},
...     },
...     "logging": {
...         "level": "INFO",
...         "file": "/var/log/app.log",
...     },
... }
>>> flat_config = to_flat_dict(config)
>>> # Easy to access deeply nested values
>>> flat_config["server.ssl.enabled"]
True
>>> flat_config["logging.level"]
'INFO'

docs.title: Data Cleaning
docs.text:
Remove temporary or internal keys from data:

>>> from coola.nested import remove_keys_starting_with
>>> processed_data = {
...     "result": [1, 2, 3],
...     "_internal_state": {"x": 1},
...     "_cache": [4, 5],
...     "output": "success",
... }
>>> clean_data = remove_keys_starting_with(processed_data, "_")
>>> clean_data
{'result': [1, 2, 3], 'output': 'success'}

docs.title: Batch Processing
docs.text:
Process rows of data individually:

>>> from coola.nested import convert_to_list_of_dicts
>>> # Columnar data from database or CSV
>>> columns = {
...     "id": [1, 2, 3],
...     "value": [10, 20, 30],
... }
>>> # Process each row
>>> for row in convert_to_list_of_dicts(columns):
...     print(f"Processing ID {row['id']} with value {row['value']}")
Processing ID 1 with value 10
Processing ID 2 with value 20
Processing ID 3 with value 30

docs.title: Design Principles
docs.text:
The coola.nested package follows these design principles:

  1. Simple and focused: Each function does one thing well
  2. Type-agnostic: Works with generic Python types (dict, list, tuple)
  3. Non-destructive: All functions return new data structures; original data is unchanged
  4. Predictable: Consistent behavior across different data structures

docs.title: Properties
docs.text: Property Statement Non-destructive The functions return new data structures. The input is not modified. Type-agnostic They work with the generic Python types (dict, list, tuple), not with a specific library. Predictable The same operation behaves the same way on every supported structure. Explicit failure An operation without a defined result raises, e.g. ValueError for the first value of an empty mapping.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• coola.recursive: For recursively transforming nested data
  • coola.iterator: For iterating over nested data structures
  • coola.equality: For comparing nested data structures

docs.title: Nested Data and Leaves
docs.text:
This page explains what kind of data coola works with: nested data, made of containers and leaves. Read it first to understand what the other packages (equality, hashing, summary, recursive, iterator, nested) accept and how they treat each value.

Prerequisites: You'll need to know a bit of Python. For a refresher, see the Python tutorial.

docs.title: What is nested data?
docs.text:
Nested data is a value that contains other values, which may contain other values, and so on. A configuration, the output of a model, a batch of tensors or a JSON document are nested data:

batch = {
    "id": 42,
    "name": "run-1",
    "inputs": [np.zeros((2, 3)), np.ones((2, 3))],
    "metrics": {"loss": 0.25, "tags": ("a", "b")},
}

coola was built to compare, hash, summarize, transform and traverse such objects as a whole, whatever the libraries used inside (Python, NumPy, PyTorch, pandas, ...).

docs.title: Containers and leaves
docs.text:
Every value of a nested structure is one of two things:

  • A container holds other values, called its children: a list, a tuple, a dict, a set, ... coola goes inside a container and looks at its children.
  • A leaf is a value that coola does not open: a number, a string, a NumPy array, a DataFrame, ... The leaf is handled as a whole, by the code that knows its type (for example, the NumPy tester compares two arrays with allclose).
>>> from coola.iterator import dfs_iterate
>>> list(dfs_iterate({"a": 1, "b": [2, 3], "c": {"d": "text"}}))
[1, 2, 3, 'text']

The dictionary and the lists are containers; 1, 2, 3 and 'text' are the leaves. Only the leaves are returned: the containers are never returned, and an empty container has no leaf.

Two rules apply to every package of coola:

  • The type decides. Whether a value is a container or a leaf depends on its type (and its parent classes), not on its content. A list is always a container, even if it is empty; an int is always a leaf.
  • When in doubt, it is a leaf. A type that coola does not know is a leaf. An object is never opened by guessing.

docs.title: The containers
docs.text:
These types are containers in every package:

Type Children list, tuple (and named tuples), collections.deque The elements, in order Other sequences (collections.abc.Sequence, collections.UserList) The elements, in order dict, collections.OrderedDict, defaultdict, Counter The values, in the order of the keys Other mappings (collections.abc.Mapping, MappingProxyType) The values set, frozenset The elements (their order is not specified) Dataclasses The values of the fields, in the order of their definition

The keys of a mapping are not children: they are labels. They are compared by equality, but iterator and recursive never return or transform them.

Containers can be mixed and nested at any depth:

>>> from collections import deque
>>> from dataclasses import dataclass
>>> from coola.iterator import dfs_iterate
>>> @dataclass
... class Config:
...     lr: float
...     layers: list
>>> data = {"config": Config(0.1, [64, 32]), "queue": deque([1, 2]), "seen": (3, (4,))}
>>> list(dfs_iterate(data))
[0.1, 64, 32, 1, 2, 3, 4]

docs.title: The leaves
docs.text:
Everything that is not a container is a leaf. The most common leaves are:

Kind Examples Scalars int, float, complex, bool, None, decimal.Decimal, fractions.Fraction Text and bytes str, bytes (a string is not a container of characters) Dates and identifiers datetime.datetime, datetime.date, pathlib.Path, uuid.UUID, enum.Enum Arrays and tensors numpy.ndarray, torch.Tensor, jax.Array, xarray.DataArray, array.array Tables pandas.DataFrame and Series, polars.DataFrame and Series, pyarrow.Table Iterators Generators and iterators: they are returned as they are and never consumed Other objects Any instance of a class that coola does not know

A NumPy array or a DataFrame holds many values, but coola does not treat it as a container of numbers: it is one leaf, compared, hashed and summarized by a dedicated handler. This is the point of the package: the structure around the arrays is handled by coola, and the arrays are handled by the library that knows them.

>>> import numpy as np
>>> from coola.iterator import dfs_iterate
>>> leaves = list(dfs_iterate({"x": np.zeros(3), "y": [np.ones(2), "text"]}))
>>> [type(leaf).__name__ for leaf in leaves]
['ndarray', 'ndarray', 'str']

Optional libraries (NumPy, PyTorch, pandas, polars, PyArrow, JAX, xarray) are never required: coola uses a library only if it is installed, and importing coola does not import them.

docs.title: What each package does with nested data
docs.text:
The packages share the same idea of container and leaf, and each adds what it does with the leaves:

Package Does what with the leaves equality Compares two nested objects leaf by leaf (objects_are_equal, objects_are_allclose) hashing Computes a stable hash of the whole structure summary Builds a short, readable description, with a depth limit recursive Applies a function to each leaf and rebuilds the same structure iterator Returns the leaves one at a time, depth first or breadth first nested Utilities built on these (flatten, filter keys, convert to JSON-compatible data, ...) 
>>> from coola.equality import objects_are_equal
>>> from coola.recursive import recursive_apply
>>> data = {"a": 1, "b": [2, 3]}
>>> recursive_apply(data, lambda x: x * 10)
{'a': 10, 'b': [20, 30]}
>>> objects_are_equal(data, {"a": 1, "b": [2, 3]})
True

docs.title: Properties shared by all packages
docs.text:
• Any depth. A structure can be nested as deeply as memory allows; recursive and iterator do not hit the Python recursion limit.
  • Cycles are detected. A container that contains itself raises a ValueError instead of looping forever (equality treats the pair as equal).
  • A shared container is visited once per path. [shared, shared] gives the leaves of shared twice.
  • The input is never modified.
  • The same data gives the same leaves in equality, hashing, summary, recursive and iterator.

docs.title: Supporting your own types
docs.text:
If a type is not known, it is a leaf. There are two ways to change that:

  • To handle a leaf type with a specific behaviour (compare two instances of a class, hash them, ...), register a handler for the type in the registry of the package. See Extending coola and the registry guide.
  • To open a custom container, register a handler that returns its children, for example a child finder for iterator or a transformer for recursive.

A handler registered for a type also applies to its subclasses, and the most specific type wins.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• coola.equality: Compare nested data
  • coola.iterator: Iterate over the leaves
  • coola.recursive: Transform the leaves
  • coola.registry: The type dispatch behind all of them

docs.title: Random Number Generator Management
docs.text:
This page describes the coola.random package, which provides a unified interface for managing random number generator (RNG) state across different libraries.

Prerequisites: You'll need to know a bit of Python. For a refresher, see the Python tutorial.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The coola.random package provides a unified interface for controlling random number generators (RNGs) from multiple libraries:

  • Python's built-in random module (always available)
  • NumPy's random module (if NumPy is installed)
  • PyTorch's random module (if PyTorch is installed)

This allows you to set seeds, get and restore RNG states, and manage randomness consistently across different libraries in a single call. A manager knows one library, the registry knows the keys, and the base class knows the scoped context.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
Property Statement One call, all libraries manual_seed seeds random, and NumPy and PyTorch when they are installed. A library that is not installed is skipped, not an error. One seed domain A seed is an int in [0, 2**63) (bool is rejected). Every entry that takes a seed (manual_seed, random_seed, Manager.manual_seed, Manager.seed, get_torch_generator) validates it before any generator is touched. Seed injective For random and NumPy, two different valid seeds give different numbers: a NumPy seed >= 2**32 is split in two 32-bit words, not folded. PyTorch's CPU generator folds the seeds modulo 2**32 itself (see below). Global generators only Only random.seed, numpy.random.seed (the legacy generator) and torch.manual_seed (all the default generators of torch) are managed. random.Random(), default_rng() and torch.Generator() are not. Restorable get_rng_state then set_rng_state brings every managed generator back to where it was. The state is opaque: give it back to the registry that produced it, in the same process. Strict restore set_rng_state raises a ValueError, and changes nothing, if the keys of the state differ from the registered keys. It never silently restores a part of the state. Complete restore If several managers fail to restore, all the others are still restored, then the error is raised (an ExceptionGroup if there are several errors). Scoped seeding random_seed (and Manager.seed) restores the state when the block exits, also when the block raises, and also when the seeding itself raises. Nestable Nested random_seed blocks are independent: the inner block does not change the stream of the outer block. Extensible A manager for another generator is added by registering one BaseRandomManager, in the default registry or through the plugin group coola.random.managers. Lazy Importing coola.random imports no optional library. The first use of the default registry imports the installed ones, so a library imported after the first seed is still seeded. Isolated registries A registry built by the user is independent from the default one; copy() gives an independent registry that shares the managers.

Not guaranteed:

  • Threads. The generators are process-global. Two threads that call random_seed at the same time interleave their saves and restores, and the state at exit is the one of whoever restores last; a thread that draws numbers while another seeds gets numbers of the other's stream. Use one random_seed block at a time, or independent generators (numpy.random.default_rng(seed), get_torch_generator(seed)) in threads.
  • Independent generators. random.Random(), numpy.random.default_rng() and torch.Generator() are not seeded, and their state is not saved or restored. Seed them explicitly.
  • CUDA created inside a scoped block. The CUDA state is saved only if CUDA is already initialized when the state is read (reading it would initialize CUDA, which fails in a forked worker). A CUDA context that the block initializes is seeded by the block and not restored by it.
  • PyTorch seeds. The CPU generator of PyTorch folds the seed modulo 2**32: the seeds 1 and 2**32 + 1 give the same numbers.
  • Equality of states. A state holds NumPy arrays and tensors: compare two states with objects_are_equal, not with ==.
  • Reproducibility across versions. The package seeds the generators; the numbers a library draws from a seed are the library's business. Kernels that are not deterministic (torch.use_deterministic_algorithms) are out of scope.

docs.title: Setting a Random Seed
docs.text:
Use manual_seed() to set the seed for all available random number generators:

>>> from coola.random import manual_seed
>>> manual_seed(42)
>>> # Now all RNGs (random, numpy, torch) are seeded with 42

This sets the seed for:

  • Python's random module
  • NumPy's random generator (if NumPy is available)
  • PyTorch's random generator (if PyTorch is available)

The first call creates the default registry, which imports NumPy and PyTorch when they are installed (about a second). They are imported at that point, and not when they are used later, so that a library that is imported after the call is still seeded. The same applies to random_seed().

docs.title: Validating a Seed
docs.text:
manual_seed() validates the seed before it seeds any library. validate_seed() is available to validate a seed without seeding: it accepts an int in the range [0, 2**63), raises a TypeError for another type and a ValueError for a seed out of range:

>>> from coola.random import validate_seed
>>> validate_seed(42)
>>> validate_seed(-1)
Traceback (most recent call last):
    ...
ValueError: seed must be in the range [0, 2**63), got -1
>>> validate_seed("42")
Traceback (most recent call last):
    ...
TypeError: seed must be an int, got <class 'str'>

docs.title: Using a Random Seed Context
docs.text:
Use the random_seed context manager to temporarily set a seed and automatically restore the previous RNG state afterward:

>>> import numpy
>>> from coola.random import random_seed
>>> with random_seed(42):
...     print(numpy.random.randn(2, 4))
[[...]]
>>> with random_seed(42):
...     print(numpy.random.randn(2, 4))
[[...]]

The context manager ensures that:

  1. The RNG state is saved before setting the seed
  2. The specified seed is applied
  3. The original RNG state is restored after the context exits

This is useful for reproducible code blocks without affecting the global RNG state.

docs.title: Getting and Setting RNG State
docs.text:
You can manually save and restore the entire RNG state:

>>> from coola.random import get_rng_state, set_rng_state
>>> # Save current state
>>> state = get_rng_state()
>>> # ... do some random operations ...
>>> # Restore previous state
>>> set_rng_state(state)

The state is a dictionary containing the state of all registered random managers:

>>> from coola.random import get_rng_state
>>> state = get_rng_state()
>>> state.keys()
dict_keys(['random', 'numpy', 'torch'])

docs.title: Library-Specific Seeds
docs.text: Each manager has a seed context manager, which seeds one library and restores its state when the block exits.

docs.title: Python's Random Module
docs.text:
>>> import random
>>> from coola.random import PythonRandomManager
>>> with PythonRandomManager().seed(42):
...     first = random.random()
>>> with PythonRandomManager().seed(42):
...     second = random.random()
>>> first == second
True

docs.title: NumPy
docs.text:
>>> import numpy as np
>>> from coola.random import NumpyRandomManager
>>> with NumpyRandomManager().seed(42):
...     np.random.rand(3)
array([...])

NumPy's legacy generator only accepts a scalar seed between 0 and 2**32 - 1. NumpyRandomManager gives a seed below 2**32 as is, and splits a larger seed in two 32-bit words, so two different seeds in [0, 2**63) never give the same numbers.

docs.title: PyTorch
docs.text:
>>> import torch
>>> from coola.random import TorchRandomManager
>>> with TorchRandomManager().seed(42):
...     torch.rand(3)
tensor([...])

torch.manual_seed seeds the CPU, CUDA and MPS generators, so one call is enough.

docs.title: Independent Generators
docs.text:
The generators created with random.Random(), numpy.random.default_rng() and torch.Generator() are not managed. Seed them explicitly. get_torch_generator creates a seeded torch.Generator (device is keyword-only), and get_random_seed derives a seed that is valid for manual_seed from another seed:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> import torch
>>> from coola.random import get_random_seed, get_torch_generator
>>> rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
>>> rng.random(3)
array([...])
>>> generator = get_torch_generator(42)
>>> torch.rand(3, generator=generator)
tensor([...])
>>> 0 <= get_random_seed(42) < 2**63 - 1
True

docs.title: Working with the Registry
docs.text:
!!! tip "Unambiguous alias"

`get_default_registry` exists in several `coola` subpackages with different return types.
`get_default_random_manager_registry` is an alias of the same function with a more explicit name, which avoids
import collisions.

The default registry manages all available random managers, in registration order:

>>> from coola.random import get_default_registry
>>> registry = get_default_registry()
>>> registry
RandomManagerRegistry(
  (random): PythonRandomManager()
  (numpy): NumpyRandomManager()
  (torch): TorchRandomManager()
)

RandomManagerRegistry is a Registry of managers (register, register_many, unregister, copy, in, [], ...) and it is itself a manager: it seeds, saves and restores all its managers, and the state is a dict that maps each key to the state of its manager.

docs.title: Using a Custom Registry
docs.text:
A registry built by the user is independent from the default one. copy() gives an independent registry that shares the managers:

>>> from coola.random import RandomManagerRegistry, PythonRandomManager, random_seed
>>> registry = RandomManagerRegistry()
>>> registry.register("random", PythonRandomManager())
>>> with random_seed(42, registry=registry):
...     pass
>>> other = registry.copy()
>>> other.register("other", PythonRandomManager())
>>> "other" in registry
False

A registry is a manager, so a registry can be registered in another registry (for example a project registry that holds the default one and its own generators). The state is then a nested dict, and the keys rule of set_rng_state applies at each level:

>>> from coola.random import RandomManagerRegistry, PythonRandomManager
>>> inner = RandomManagerRegistry({"random": PythonRandomManager()})
>>> outer = RandomManagerRegistry({"inner": inner})
>>> outer.get_rng_state().keys()
dict_keys(['inner'])
>>> outer.get_rng_state()["inner"].keys()
dict_keys(['random'])

docs.title: Strict Restore
docs.text:
set_rng_state requires the keys of the state to be the registered keys. A state saved with torch cannot be restored into a registry without torch: it raises a ValueError and nothing is restored, instead of silently restoring a part of the state.

>>> from coola.random import RandomManagerRegistry, PythonRandomManager
>>> registry = RandomManagerRegistry({"random": PythonRandomManager()})
>>> registry.set_rng_state({"random": registry.get_rng_state()["random"], "torch": None})
Traceback (most recent call last):
    ...
ValueError: The state has the keys ['random', 'torch'] but the registered keys are ['random']

If a manager fails to restore its state, the other managers are still restored before the error is raised. One error is raised as is; several errors are raised as an ExceptionGroup.

docs.title: Writing a Manager
docs.text:
To support another generator, extend BaseRandomManager. A manager has to follow this contract (checked for the built-in managers by tests/unit/random/test_contract.py):

  1. get_rng_state() returns an opaque object that does not alias the live generator.
  2. set_rng_state(get_rng_state()) leaves the draws unchanged.
  3. manual_seed(seed) validates the seed with validate_seed before it touches the generator, and the same seed gives the same draws.
  4. A manager is stateless and cheap to build: it is shared by registries, equal to another instance of its class and hashable (__eq__ and __hash__).

seed() validates the seed too, so a manager gets the seed domain even if its manual_seed does not check. This manager handles a module-level generator:

>>> import random
>>> from coola.random import BaseRandomManager, RandomManagerRegistry, validate_seed
>>> RNG = random.Random()
>>> class GlobalRngManager(BaseRandomManager):
...     def __eq__(self, other):
...         return type(other) is type(self)
...
...     def __hash__(self):
...         return hash(type(self))
...
...     def get_rng_state(self):
...         return RNG.getstate()
...
...     def manual_seed(self, seed):
...         validate_seed(seed)
...         RNG.seed(seed)
...
...     def set_rng_state(self, state):
...         RNG.setstate(state)
>>> registry = RandomManagerRegistry({"global_rng": GlobalRngManager()})
>>> with registry.seed(42):
...     first = RNG.random()
>>> with registry.seed(42):
...     second = RNG.random()
>>> first == second
True

docs.title: Registering a Manager in the Default Registry
docs.text:
register_managers adds managers to the default registry for the whole process (exist_ok is keyword-only). Use temporary_default_registries to scope the registration, for example in tests:

>>> from coola.random import PythonRandomManager, get_default_registry, register_managers
>>> from coola.utils.singleton import temporary_default_registries
>>> with temporary_default_registries():
...     register_managers({"custom": PythonRandomManager()})
...     "custom" in get_default_registry()
True
>>> "custom" in get_default_registry()
False

A package can also register its managers through the plugin group coola.random.managers (see Extending coola). The entry point is a function that takes the default registry:

# pyproject.toml of the plugin package
[project.entry-points."coola.random.managers"]
mypkg = "mypkg.coola_plugin:register"

# mypkg/coola_plugin.py
def register(registry):
    registry.register("mylib", MyLibRandomManager())

docs.title: Reproducible Experiments
docs.text:
Ensure reproducibility in scientific experiments:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> import torch
>>> from coola.random import manual_seed
>>> manual_seed(42)
>>> # All random operations are now reproducible
>>> np.random.rand(3)
array([...])
>>> torch.rand(3)
tensor([...])

docs.title: Reproducible Code Blocks
docs.text:
Make a specific code block reproducible without affecting the global state:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> from coola.random import random_seed
>>> # Generate some random data
>>> data1 = np.random.rand(5)
>>> # This block is reproducible
>>> with random_seed(123):
...     reproducible_data = np.random.rand(5)
>>> # Continue with original RNG state
>>> data2 = np.random.rand(5)

Internally, the context manager saves and restores RNG state before and after the block. It is equivalent to this code.

>>> from coola.random import get_rng_state, set_rng_state, manual_seed
>>> # Save initial state
>>> initial_state = get_rng_state()
>>> # Run test with specific seed
>>> manual_seed(42)
>>> # ... make code reproducible. ...
>>> # Restore initial state
>>> set_rng_state(initial_state)

docs.title: Cross-Library Seeding
docs.text:
Seed all libraries at once for consistent results:

>>> import random
>>> import numpy as np
>>> import torch
>>> from coola.random import manual_seed
>>> # Seed all libraries with one call
>>> manual_seed(42)
>>> # All libraries use the same seed
>>> val1 = random.random()
>>> val2 = np.random.rand()
>>> val3 = torch.rand(1).item()

docs.title: Temporary Seed Changes
docs.text:
Temporarily change seed for a specific operation:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> from coola.random import random_seed
>>> # Normal operations
>>> normal_data = np.random.rand(3)
>>> # Use specific seed for initialization
>>> with random_seed(999):
...     initialization = np.random.randn(10, 10)
>>> # Continue with normal operations
>>> more_data = np.random.rand(3)

docs.title: Available Random Managers
docs.text:
The coola.random package provides the following random managers:

  • PythonRandomManager: For Python's built-in random module (always registered)
  • NumpyRandomManager: For NumPy's random module (registered if NumPy is available)
  • TorchRandomManager: For PyTorch's random module (registered if PyTorch is available)

Each manager implements the BaseRandomManager interface with three methods:

  • manual_seed(seed): Set the random seed
  • get_rng_state(): Get the current RNG state
  • set_rng_state(state): Restore a previous RNG state

docs.title: Threads and Processes
docs.text:
The generators are process-global and coola.random does not lock them: it cannot, because other code draws from the same generators. In threads, use independent generators (numpy.random.default_rng(seed), get_torch_generator(seed)) instead of random_seed.

The CUDA state is read only if CUDA is already initialized, so get_rng_state can be called in a forked worker. A child process restores a state with set_rng_state.

docs.title: Prefer random_seed
docs.text:
Prefer the random_seed() context manager over manual_seed() for localized reproducibility: the state is restored when the block exits.

>>> from coola.random import random_seed
>>> with random_seed(42):
...     pass  # reproducible code

docs.title: Set Seeds at the Beginning
docs.text:
Set seeds at the beginning of your script for full reproducibility:

>>> from coola.random import manual_seed
>>> manual_seed(42)

docs.title: Use a Generator in Threads
docs.text: Give each thread its own generator, seeded explicitly, instead of seeding the global ones.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• Python's random module
  • NumPy's Random sampling
  • PyTorch's Reproducibility
  • coola.registry: For understanding the registry pattern used internally

docs.title: Recursive Data Transformation
docs.text:
This page describes the coola.recursive package, which provides utilities for recursively applying transformations to nested data structures using a Depth-First Search (DFS) pattern.

Prerequisites: You'll need to know a bit of Python. For a refresher, see the Python tutorial.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The coola.recursive package allows you to apply a function to all leaf values in nested data structures (lists, dicts, tuples, sets, etc.) while preserving the original structure. It provides:

  1. Clean separation between transformation logic and type dispatch
  2. Easy extensibility via registry pattern
  3. Support for custom types

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
Property Statement Leaves only func is called on the leaves, once per occurrence, never on a container. Structure-preserving A container is rebuilt from the transformed children with its original type. Keys are never transformed. Dataclasses are entered, like in equality, hashing and summary. Type dispatch The transformer is chosen from the type of the data, along the Method Resolution Order, so the most specific type wins. Registry-extensible A new type is supported by registering a transformer, without changing the existing ones. Deterministic order The leaves are visited depth first, left to right. The elements of a set are visited in the iteration order of the set, which is not specified. Pure The input is never modified. The output shares no container with the input (leaves can be shared). Any depth No RecursionError, whatever the nesting: the traversal uses an explicit stack. The depth is bounded by memory only. Cycle-safe A container that contains itself raises a ValueError. Errors propagate An exception raised by func propagates unchanged. A container that cannot be rebuilt raises a TypeError.

Not guaranteed:

  • Laziness. The output is built whole: the traversal does not use generators and does not reduce the memory usage.
  • Shared references. A container reachable by several paths is transformed once per path, so func is called once per occurrence and the cost is proportional to the number of paths.
  • Order of the calls inside a set, and the result of a func that is not deterministic.

docs.title: Transforming Nested Data
docs.text:
The main function is recursive_apply, which recursively applies a function to all items in nested data:

>>> from coola.recursive import recursive_apply
>>> recursive_apply({"a": 1, "b": "abc"}, str)
{'a': '1', 'b': 'abc'}
>>> recursive_apply([1, [2, 3], {"x": 4}], lambda x: x * 2)
[2, [4, 6], {'x': 8}]

The function traverses the data structure and applies the transformation function to each leaf value (i.e., non-container values like numbers and strings).

docs.title: More Examples
docs.text:
You can use recursive_apply with different data structures:

Nested lists and tuples:

>>> from coola.recursive import recursive_apply
>>> recursive_apply([1, 2, [3, 4, [5, 6]]], lambda x: x + 10)
[11, 12, [13, 14, [15, 16]]]
>>> recursive_apply((1, (2, 3)), str)
('1', ('2', '3'))

Nested dictionaries:

>>> from coola.recursive import recursive_apply
>>> data = {"level1": {"level2": {"level3": 42}}}
>>> recursive_apply(data, lambda x: x * 2)
{'level1': {'level2': {'level3': 84}}}

**Mixed nested structures:**

```pycon
>>> from coola.recursive import recursive_apply
>>> data = {
...     "list": [1, 2, 3],
...     "dict": {"a": 4, "b": 5},
...     "value": 8,
... }
>>> recursive_apply(data, lambda x: x + 100)
{'list': [101, 102, 103], 'dict': {'a': 104, 'b': 105}, 'value': 108}

docs.title: Custom Transformers
docs.text:
For more control over how specific types are transformed, you can create custom transformers by extending BaseTransformer. A transformer only describes the shape of a type: expand(data) returns None for a leaf, or the children and the function that rebuilds the value from the transformed children. The engine applies the function to the leaves and detects the cycles:

>>> from coola.recursive import (
...     BaseTransformer,
...     DefaultTransformer,
...     SequenceTransformer,
...     TransformerRegistry,
...     recursive_apply,
... )
>>> class MyType:
...     def __init__(self, value):
...         self.value = value
...
...     def __repr__(self):
...         return f"MyType({self.value})"
>>> class MyTransformer(BaseTransformer):
...     def expand(self, data):
...         return [data.value], lambda items: MyType(items[0])
>>> registry = TransformerRegistry(
...     {object: DefaultTransformer(), list: SequenceTransformer(), MyType: MyTransformer()}
... )
>>> recursive_apply([MyType(1), MyType(2)], lambda x: x * 10, registry=registry)
[MyType(10), MyType(20)]

docs.title: Using Custom Registry
docs.text:
You can create and use a custom registry for more control:

>>> from coola.recursive import TransformerRegistry, recursive_apply
>>> from coola.recursive import SequenceTransformer, DefaultTransformer
>>> registry = TransformerRegistry()
>>> registry.register(list, SequenceTransformer())
>>> registry.register(object, DefaultTransformer())
>>> recursive_apply([1, 2, 3], lambda x: x * 10, registry=registry)
[10, 20, 30]

docs.title: Dataclasses
docs.text:
A dataclass instance is entered, like objects_are_equal, hash_object and summarize do: the function is applied to the fields, not to the instance. The instance is rebuilt (DataclassTransformer) from a shallow copy in which every field is set with object.__setattr__, so frozen and slotted dataclasses are supported, the fields with init=False are transformed, the input is not modified and no user code (__init__, __post_init__) runs during the traversal:

>>> from dataclasses import dataclass
>>> from coola.recursive import recursive_apply
>>> @dataclass
... class Config:
...     lr: float
...     layers: list
>>> recursive_apply(Config(0.1, [1, 2]), str)
Config(lr='0.1', layers=['1', '2'])

__post_init__ is not run again, so a field that __post_init__ derives from another field is transformed like the other fields and is not recomputed. A transformer registered for the type of the dataclass has priority over the dataclass transformer, so a dataclass is kept as a leaf by registering DefaultTransformer() for its type:

>>> from coola.recursive import DefaultTransformer, get_default_registry
>>> registry = get_default_registry().copy()
>>> registry.register(Config, DefaultTransformer())
>>> recursive_apply(Config(0.1, [1, 2]), repr, registry=registry)
'Config(lr=0.1, layers=[1, 2])'

docs.title: Available Transformers
docs.text:
The coola.recursive package provides several built-in transformers:

  • DefaultTransformer: For scalar/leaf values (no children)
  • SequenceTransformer: For sequences (list, tuple) - recursive transformation preserving order
  • MappingTransformer: For mappings (dict) - recursive transformation of the values (the keys are kept)
  • SetTransformer: For sets - recursive transformation without order
  • IdentityTransformer: For leaf values that must be kept as they are: the function is never applied
  • KeyFilterTransformer: For mappings: drops the entries whose key satisfies a predicate and transforms the remaining values
>>> from coola.recursive import (
...     DefaultTransformer,
...     KeyFilterTransformer,
...     TransformerRegistry,
... )
>>> registry = TransformerRegistry(
...     {
...         object: DefaultTransformer(),
...         dict: KeyFilterTransformer(key_predicate=lambda key: key == "secret"),
...     }
... )
>>> registry.transform({"keep": 1, "secret": 2, "nested": {"secret": 3, "x": 4}}, str)
{'keep': '1', 'nested': {'x': '4'}}

docs.title: Rebuilding Containers
docs.text:
A container is rebuilt with the constructor of its type, so the subclasses keep their type. The coola.recursive.rebuild module contains the helpers (rebuild_sequence, rebuild_mapping and rebuild_set), which a custom container transformer can reuse. They handle the named tuples, the deque (maxlen) and the defaultdict (factory). A collections.ChainMap is rebuilt with a single flat map: its parents are not part of the structure.

If the constructor of a subclass differs from the one of its base type, a TypeError that names the type is raised: register a transformer for this type.

docs.title: Getting the Default Registry
docs.text:
!!! tip "Unambiguous alias"

`get_default_registry` exists in several `coola` subpackages with different return types.
`get_default_transformer_registry` is an alias of the same function with a more explicit name, which avoids
import collisions.

The package maintains a singleton default registry with transformers for common Python types:

>>> from coola.recursive import get_default_registry
>>> registry = get_default_registry()
>>> registry.transform([1, 2, 3], str)
['1', '2', '3']
>>> registry.transform({"a": 1, "b": 2}, lambda x: x * 10)
{'a': 10, 'b': 20}

The default registry includes transformers for:

  • Scalar types: int, float, complex, bool, str
  • Sequences: list, tuple, Sequence (ABC)
  • Sets: set, frozenset
  • Mappings: dict, Mapping (ABC)

docs.title: Registering Custom Types
docs.text:
You can extend the default registry to support custom types:

>>> from coola.recursive import register_transformers, BaseTransformer
>>> class Point:
...     def __init__(self, x, y):
...         self.x = x
...         self.y = y
>>> class PointTransformer(BaseTransformer):
...     def expand(self, data):
...         return [data.x, data.y], lambda items: Point(*items)
>>> register_transformers({Point: PointTransformer()})  # doctest: +SKIP

docs.title: Design Principles
docs.text:
The coola.recursive package design is inspired by the DFS pattern and provides:

  1. Type dispatch: Automatically selects the right transformer based on data type
  2. Extensibility: Easy to add support for new types via the registry pattern

docs.title: Data Type Conversion
docs.text:
Convert all numeric values in a nested structure to strings:

>>> from coola.recursive import recursive_apply
>>> data = {"metrics": [1.5, 2.3, 3.7], "count": 42}
>>> recursive_apply(data, str)
{'metrics': ['1.5', '2.3', '3.7'], 'count': '42'}

docs.title: Value Scaling
docs.text:
Scale all numeric values in a configuration:

>>> from coola.recursive import recursive_apply
>>> config = {
...     "learning_rate": 0.001,
...     "layers": [64, 128, 256],
...     "dropout": 0.5,
... }
>>> recursive_apply(config, lambda x: x * 10 if isinstance(x, (int, float)) else x)
{'learning_rate': 0.01, 'layers': [640, 1280, 2560], 'dropout': 5.0}

docs.title: Data Normalization
docs.text:
Normalize all values to a specific range:

>>> from coola.recursive import recursive_apply
>>> data = {"a": 100, "b": [200, 300], "c": {"d": 400}}
>>> recursive_apply(data, lambda x: x / 100)
{'a': 1.0, 'b': [2.0, 3.0], 'c': {'d': 4.0}}

docs.title: See Also
